name: Mitoviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: ssRNA. Genome organization: Monopartite, linear. Genome size: 2.5-2.9 kb. Key conserved domains: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment: Not specified in source. HOST/ECOLOGY: Known/predicted host range: Not specified in source, but replication occurs in the cytoplasm. Geographical distribution: Not specified in source. Transmission patterns: Horizontal transmission through mating or vertical transmission from mother to daughter cells. Additional details: Mitoviridae are viruses lacking a true virion. The genome is associated with RdRp in the cytoplasm. The virion RNA is infectious and serves as both the genome and viral messenger RNA. The genome has one ORF encoding an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Replication is cytoplasmic. Translation of genomic RNA produces viral RdRp. A dsRNA genome is synthesized from the genomic ssRNA. The dsRNA genome is transcribed/replicated thereby providing viral mRNAs/new ssRNA genomes. Source: ViralZone Type: Family Name: Mitoviridae Taxid: 2732892

name: Caulimoviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: dsDNA, non-covalently closed circular, 7.1-9.8 kbp. Encapsidated by viral coat proteins into isometric or bacilliform virions. Reverse-transcribing. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Family Caulimoviridae comprises multiple genera including Caulimovirus, Cavemovirus, Petuvirus, Rosadnavirus, Solendovirus, Soymovirus, Badnavirus, Tungrovirus, Dioscovirus, and Vaccinivirus. Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not specified. HOST/ECOLOGY: Infects a wide range of monocot and dicot plants, typically with narrow host ranges within a species. Some cause economically important diseases in tropical and subtropical crops. Insect vectors identified for Badnavirus, Caulimovirus, and Tungrovirus. Endogenous viral elements (EVEs) are known for Badnavirus, Caulimovirus, Cavemovirus, Petuvirus, and Solendovirus. Some EVEs in Musa balbisiana, Petunia hybrida, and Nicotiana edwardsonii are replication competent, leading to spontaneous infections. Most caulimovirid EVEs in vascular plants are replication defective.

name: Tymovirales
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: Positive-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA). Genome size and organization: 5.9-9.0 kb, single molecule. Polyadenylated at the 3' terminus (except Tymovirus, which has a tRNA-like structure). Capped with m7G at the 5' end. Contains a large replication-associated polyprotein (150-250 kDa) near the 5' end, translated directly from the genomic RNA. Encodes 1-5 smaller proteins translated from subgenomic RNAs (except Sclerodarnavirus). Key conserved domains: Methyltransferase (Mtr), RNA helicase (Hel), RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). Some members have a papain-like cysteine protease (P-Pro) or an OTU protease. Some have an AlkB motif. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation: Based on similarities in replication-associated polyproteins. Phylogenetic analysis supports a common ancestor excluding other characterized viruses. Forms a distinct group within the alphavirus-like superfamily. HOST/ECOLOGY: Host range: Primarily plants, some infect plant-pathogenic fungi. Geographical distribution: Not specified. Transmission patterns: Characteristic of individual genera.

name: Badnavirus
info: Genus: Badnavirus GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: dsDNA, non-covalently closed circular, 7.2-9.2 kbp. Genome has single discontinuities on each strand. Contains three ORFs (P1-P3), except in some viruses where ORF3 is divided into two. Encodes proteins P1 (unknown function), P2 (virion-associated protein), and P3 (polyprotein with movement protein, capsid protein, aspartic protease, and RT/RNase H precursors). Conserved domains include viral movement protein, retropepsin (aspartic protease), reverse transcriptase, and RNase H1. A single, greater-than-genome length, terminally redundant pregenomic RNA is transcribed. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Differs from Tungrovirus by genome organization, lack of RNA splicing, lack of helper virus dependency for transmission, and phylogenetic placement. Species are demarcated by host range, >20% difference in polymerase nucleotide sequences, and vector specificities. HOST/ECOLOGY: Narrow host range, typically restricted to one or two plant families. Geographical distribution varies. Transmission is semi-persistent via mealybugs, and sometimes aphids or lace bugs. No multiplication in mealybug vector, no transovarial transmission. Seed transmission reported in some species. Mechanical transmission possible in some species. Some members transmitted by dodder and grafting. Replication-competent endogenous badnaviral forms exist in some plant genomes, causing infection in hybrids.

name: Duamitovirus
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: ssRNA. Genome organization: Monopartite, linear, 2.5-2.9 kb. RNA is uncapped. Contains one ORF encoding an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). Genomes are associated with RdRp in the cytoplasm. No true virion or structural proteins. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment: Not specified. Genus: Duamitovirus (taxid:2948686). HOST/ECOLOGY: Host range: Fungi, plant mitochondria. Geographical distribution: Not specified. Transmission: Horizontal (mating) and vertical (mother to daughter cells). Replication: Cytoplasmic. The virion RNA is infectious and serves as both the genome and viral messenger RNA. Translation of genomic RNA produces viral RdRp. A dsRNA genome is synthesized from the genomic ssRNA. The dsRNA genome is transcribed/replicated, providing viral mRNAs/new ssRNA genomes.

name: Nudiviridae
info: Family: Nudiviridae Genome Characteristics: Nudiviruses possess a circular, double-stranded DNA genome ranging from 96 to 232 kbp, encoding 89-155 proteins. The genome contains approximately equal numbers of ORFs in either orientation. Twenty-eight core genes are conserved across nudiviruses, including 21 homologs of baculovirus core genes. Intergenic regions contain direct or tandem repeats. Evolutionary Context: Nudiviridae belongs to the order Lefavirales, class Naldaviricetes, and is related to Baculoviridae and Hytrosaviridae. Nudiviruses were previously classified within Baculoviridae but were reclassified due to virion morphology and lack of occlusion bodies. Molecular phylogeny supports their distinct lineage. Genus demarcation is based on molecular phylogeny, genome characteristics, virion dimensions, host species, tissue tropism, and transmission mode. Host/Ecology: Nudiviruses infect insects (Coleoptera, Diptera, Lepidoptera, Orthoptera) and crustaceans (Amphipoda, Decapoda). Infections can occur in both immature and adult stages. Transmission is primarily horizontal via oral ingestion, but sexual and vertical transmission have also been documented. Infection outcomes range from cell lysis and mortality to persistent asymptomatic infection. Geographical distribution is linked to host range.

name: Phycodnaviridae
info: Family: Phycodnaviridae Genome Characteristics: Virions contain large, double-stranded DNA genomes ranging from 100 to 560 kbp, with a G+C content of 40-52%. Some genomes contain methylated bases (5-methylcytosine and N6-methyladenine). Virions contain numerous proteins (over 100) ranging from <10 to >200 kDa. Genomes can be linear or circular, with terminal inverted repeats and repetitive DNA sequences. Some members have covalently closed hairpin termini. Evolutionary Context: Information not available from source. Host/Ecology: Phycodnaviruses infect a variety of marine and freshwater algae. Host range varies; some viruses are host-specific, while others infect multiple isolates within a species. Transmission occurs horizontally for chloroviruses, coccolithoviruses, prasinoviruses, prymnesioviruses, and raphidoviruses. Phaeoviruses exhibit both horizontal and vertical transmission. Geographical distribution is worldwide in freshwater and seawater environments. Virus attachment mechanisms vary depending on the virus-host system, including cell wall dissolution, fusion of host and particle surfaces, endocytosis, and envelope fusion. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm, often leading to cell lysis and virus release.

name: Alphaflexiviridae
info: Family: Alphaflexiviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome, approximately 5.9-9.0 kb in size, representing 5-6% of virion weight. The 5' end is capped with m7G, and the 3' end has a polyadenylated tail. Some members encapsidate smaller 3'-co-terminal subgenomic RNAs (sgRNAs). The genome contains five or six open reading frames (ORFs), depending on the genus. ORF1 encodes a protein with methyltransferase, helicase, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) motifs, related to alphavirus-like polymerase proteins. Some members also contain an AlkB domain. ORFs 2-4 encode the "triple gene block" (TGB) proteins involved in cell-to-cell movement. ORF5 encodes the viral coat protein (18-43 kDa, except in Lolavirus). Some genera have a final ORF encoding a zinc-binding nucleic acid-binding protein. Evolutionary Context: Genera are distinguished by genome organization and host range. Species demarcation requires less than 72% nucleotide identity (or 80% amino acid identity) in coat protein (CP) or polymerase genes. Viruses from different genera usually have less than 45% nucleotide identity in these genes. Host/Ecology: Primarily infects mono- and dicotyledonous plants, with limited host range for individual members. Transmission occurs readily by mechanical inoculation. Some members, like allexiviruses, are thought to be mite-borne. Replication is cytoplasmic. Virus particles accumulate in the cytoplasm without specific cytopathic structures. A few members infect plant-infecting fungi.

name: Tymoviridae
info: Family: Tymoviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome consists of a single molecule of positive-sense, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA), 6.0-7.5 kb in length, constituting 25-35% of the virion weight. The RNA has a high cytidine content and is capped at the 5' terminus with m7G. Most tymoviruses have a tRNA-like structure at the 3' end, while marafiviruses, maculaviruses, and Poinsettia mosaic virus (PnMV) are polyadenylated. Tymovirus genomes contain two overlapping ORFs and a third ORF for the coat protein (CP), expressed from a subgenomic RNA (sgRNA). The longest ORF encodes a replication polyprotein containing methyltransferase (Mtr), papain-like cysteine protease (P-Pro), RNA helicase (Hel), and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) domains. Evolutionary Context: Genus demarcation is based on biological criteria (mechanical transmissibility, tissue tropism) and molecular criteria (number of ORFs, presence of tRNA-like structure or poly(A) tail, presence of "tymobox" or "marafibox" sequence). Host/Ecology: Members infect dicotyledonous plants, with some marafiviruses infecting Gramineae. Host ranges are often narrow. Symptoms include yellow mosaic or mottling (tymoviruses and PnMV), chlorotic stripes, vein clearing, etched lines, or dwarfing (marafiviruses), and flecking of leaves (maculaviruses). Tymoviruses and PnMV are mechanically transmissible and invade parenchyma tissues. Marafi- and maculaviruses are phloem-limited. Some marafiviruses are vectored by leafhoppers. Some tymoviruses are seed-transmissible and spread by beetles. Maculaviruses lack recognized vectors and are disseminated through infected propagating material. Members are found worldwide, with varying geographical distributions.

name: Parvoviridae
info: Parvoviridae is a virus family characterized by small, non-enveloped virions with a T=1 icosahedral capsid, 23-28 nm in diameter. The genome consists of linear, non-permuted, single-stranded DNA, 4-6 kb in size, flanked by short palindromic sequences forming hairpin telomeres. Replication occurs via rolling hairpin replication, utilizing host DNA polymerases. The genome typically encodes two major gene cassettes: a non-structural replication initiator protein (NS) and capsid proteins (VP). Alternative splicing, non-consensus initiation, or leaky scanning mechanisms regulate protein expression. The family is divided into three subfamilies: Parvovirinae, Hamaparvovirinae and Densovirinae, primarily distinguished by host range (vertebrates vs. invertebrates). Subfamily demarcation is supported by Bayesian phylogeny of the NS1 protein sequence. Parvoviruses exhibit host and/or tissue specificity, often requiring actively dividing host cells. Some members cause diseases ranging from sub-clinical to lethal, and a few require co-infection with helper viruses. Taxonomic classification: Realm Monodnaviria, kingdom Shotokuvirae, phylum Cossaviricota, class Quintoviricetes, order Piccovirales. The family comprises 3 subfamilies, 28 genera, and 243 species.

name: Iflaviridae
info: Family: Iflaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Iflaviridae family consists of non-enveloped viruses with single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genomes, ranging from 9 to 11 kb. The genome contains a single large open reading frame (ORF) encoding a polyprotein. A genome-linked virus protein (VPg) is attached to the 5' end, and the 3' end is polyadenylated. The polyprotein is cleaved into structural (VP1, VP2, VP3, VP4) and non-structural proteins, including an RNA helicase, a 3C-like cysteine protease, and an RNA-directed RNA polymerase. Evolutionary Context: Iflaviridae belongs to the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Pisuviricota, class Pisoniviricetes, and order Picornavirales. Genus demarcation is based on >90% amino acid sequence identity in capsid proteins. Iflaviruses share properties with other Picornavirales families, including conserved replication proteins, non-enveloped virions, a VPg protein, and a polyadenylated 3' terminus. Host/Ecology: Iflaviruses infect arthropods, primarily insects, including beneficial and pest species. Infections can be symptomless or cause developmental abnormalities, behavioral changes, and premature mortality. Transmission occurs through ingestion of contaminated food, trophallaxis in social insects, and vectoring by parasitic mites (e.g., Varroa). Vertical and venereal transmission has been reported. The virus targets various tissues, including the gut, gonads, fat body, muscle, brain, and glandular tissues. Geographical distribution is not specified, but viruses have been isolated from arthropods.

name: Leishbuviridae
info: Family: Leishbuviridae Genome Characteristics: Negative-sense RNA virus with a tri-segmented genome of approximately 8.0 kb. The genome consists of three monocistronic RNA segments encoding a nucleoprotein (NP), a glycoprotein (GP), and a large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Evolutionary Context: Closely related to bunyaviral arenavirids, discoviridae, mypovirids, nairovirids, phenuivirids, and wupedevirids. Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not explicitly stated but inferred through phylogenetic analysis. Host/Ecology: Infects a broad range of hosts, including kinetoplastean protists (Blechomonas sp, Crithidia sp., Leptomonas sp., and Phytomonas sp.), dipteran insects (culicid mosquitoes, phorid and tephritid fruit flies, ephydrid shore flies, and sarcophagid flesh flies), hymenopteran insects (bumblebees and honeybees), brown salor spiders, and leeches. Geographically distributed across Madagascar, China, South Africa, the USA, the Czech Republic, and Ecuador. Transmission patterns are not explicitly established, but the virus has been detected directly in protists and various insect species.

name: Herelleviridae
info: Family: Herelleviridae Genome Characteristics: The Herelleviridae family consists of bacterial viruses with linear, non-permuted, terminally redundant dsDNA genomes ranging from 106-170 kbp. Genomes encode 126-301 proteins and 0-24 tRNAs. Some members exhibit modified DNA bases (e.g., 5-hydroxymethyluridine in place of thymidine). Genomes typically possess long terminal repeats (2-16 kbp). Phage-encoded DNA polymerase is utilized for replication. Host RNA polymerase, along with phage-encoded sigma factors, mediates transcription. Introns are present in some members. Evolutionary Context: Herelleviridae is classified within the realm Duplodnaviria, kingdom Heunggongvirae, phylum Uroviricota, and class Caudoviricetes. Genera are defined by monophyletic clades in genome-based phylogenies, sharing at least 60% nucleotide identity and conserved genome organization, and typically infecting the same bacterial genus. Species demarcation requires >95% genome nucleotide sequence identity. Phylogenetic analysis identifies five subfamilies, 34 genera, and 119 species. Host/Ecology: Herelleviruses infect bacteria of the phylum Firmicutes and exhibit a worldwide distribution. They are generally considered obligately lytic, although some may establish persistent, pseudolysogenic, or carrier states. Transmission patterns are not explicitly detailed but are assumed to follow typical bacteriophage infection cycles.

name: Salasmaviridae
info: Family: Salasmaviridae Genome Characteristics: dsDNA, linear genome of 16-20 kb, encoding 20-30 genes. Terminal protein covalently attached at the 5' end. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria not explicitly stated. Host/Ecology: Host Range: Bacteria Geographical Distribution: Worldwide Transmission: Passive diffusion through medium. Virion Structure: Non-enveloped, head-tail structure with Podo-type morphology. Prolate capsid approximately 45 x 54 nm, T=3, Q=5 symmetry. Non-contractile tail with collar and 12 appendages for host cell recognition. Capsid fibers (55) may be present for attachment. Replication: Cytoplasmic. Adsorption via tail fibers. Viral DNA injected into host cell periplasm via short tail system. Early gene transcription and translation. DNA replication by strand displacement, forming concatemers. Late gene transcription and translation. Procapsid assembly and genome packaging. Release via lysis. Key Enzymes: DNA-dependent DNA polymerase B, protease (peptidase G2), endolysin.

name: Rhabdoviridae
info: Rhabdoviridae Family Summary: Genome Characteristics: Rhabdoviridae viruses possess negative-sense, single-stranded RNA genomes, typically 10-16 kb in size. Genomes are usually single molecules with partially complementary termini, though some are bi-segmented. Most members have five core genes (N, P, M, G, L), but additional genes or alternative open reading frames are common. Some lack the G gene. Conserved domains are found within the L protein. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation relies on phylogenetic analysis of L sequences, genome architecture, antigenicity, and ecological properties. Genera form monophyletic clades based on L sequence analysis. The family includes four subfamilies (Alpharhabdovirinae, Betarhabdovirinae, Gammarhabdovirinae, Deltarhabdovirinae) and three unassigned genera. Host/Ecology: Rhabdoviruses infect a wide range of hosts, including plants, mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, and invertebrates (arthropods, flatworms, roundworms, crustaceans). Geographical distribution is worldwide. Transmission patterns vary; arthropods may act as vectors. Vertebrate transmission can occur through contact, aerosol, bite, or venereally. Plant viruses are often transmitted by arthropods or mechanically. Some viruses are transmitted vertically in insects, and one plant rhabdovirus is suggested to be transmitted vertically in seeds.

name: Autographiviridae
info: Family: Autographiviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, double-stranded DNA genome of approximately 40-42 kb, encoding about 55 genes. Key enzymes encoded include T7 RNA polymerase, DNA-directed DNA polymerase, primase, terminase, DNA ligase, kinase, endonuclease, exonuclease, nucleotide kinase, endolysin, and peptidoglycan transglycosylase (gp16). Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not specified in source. Host/Ecology: Host Range: Bacteria. Geographical Distribution: Worldwide. Transmission: Passive diffusion through medium. Virion Structure: Non-enveloped, head-tail structure with Podo-type morphology. The head is approximately 60 nm in diameter, with an icosahedral capsid exhibiting T=7 symmetry. The tail is non-contractile and possesses 6 short subterminal fibers. Replication: Cytoplasmic. The phage attaches to target cell adhesion receptors via tail fibers. Viral DNA is injected into the host cell periplasm via a short tail system. Transcription of class I genes is performed by host RNA polymerase before the viral genome completely exits the capsid. T7 RNA polymerase transcribes class II and III genes. Bacterial genome degradation occurs. Viral genome concatemers are formed via T7 DNA polymerase-mediated replication. Empty procapsids are assembled, and the viral genome is packaged. Mature virions are released through cell lysis.

name: Totiviridae
info: Family: Totiviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome consists of a single molecule of linear, uncapped, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) ranging from 4.6 to 7.0 kbp. Two large, usually overlapping open reading frames (ORFs) are present. The 5'-proximal ORF encodes the major capsid protein (CP) (Gag), which is 70-100 kDa. The 3'-proximal ORF encodes an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The polymerase is usually expressed as a gag-pol-like fusion protein. Virion-associated RdRp catalyzes end-to-end transcription of dsRNA to produce mRNA for CP and RdRp. The RdRp specifically binds (+) strands and catalyzes (−) strand synthesis to form dsRNA. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not specified in provided information. Host/Ecology: Totiviruses are associated with latent infections of fungal or protozoan hosts. Geographical distribution and transmission patterns are not specified in the provided information.

name: Betaflexiviridae
info: Family: Betaflexiviridae Genome Characteristics: Contains a single molecule of linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) of 5.9-9.0 kb. The RNA is capped at the 5' terminus and polyadenylated at the 3' terminus. Some Carlavirus members have two subgenomic RNAs (sgRNAs). The genome encodes 3-6 genes. ORF1 encodes a protein with methyltransferase (Mtr), helicase (Hel), and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) domains. Other ORFs encode proteins involved in cell-to-cell movement (MP or TGB) and capsid protein (CP). Some members encode a protein with a zinc-binding finger motif. Replication is cytoplasmic. Evolutionary Context: Genera are distinguished by genome organization and transmission mode. Species demarcation requires less than 72% nucleotide identity (or 80% amino acid identity) in CP or polymerase genes. Viruses from different genera usually have less than 45% nucleotide identity in these genes. Host/Ecology: Infects a diverse range of plant species, with individual members typically having limited host ranges. Natural infections are mostly of woody hosts, except for Carlavirus. Transmission occurs via mechanical inoculation. Some members are transmitted by mites (Trichovirus), aphids (Carlavirus), mealybugs, scale insects, or aphids (Vitivirus). Aggregates of virus particles accumulate in the cytoplasm. Many carlaviruses induce inclusions. Virions are highly immunogenic in Carlavirus, but moderate to poor antigens in other genera.

name: Totivirus
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: The Totivirus genome consists of a single linear molecule of uncapped double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), ranging from 4.6 to 6.7 kbp. Some isolates contain satellite dsRNAs encoding killer toxins, encapsidated separately. Defective dsRNAs derived from satellites may also be present. The positive strand contains two large overlapping open reading frames (ORFs). The first ORF encodes the major capsid protein (CP), while the second, via a -1 frameshift, encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) as a fusion protein. Essential sites for encapsidation, replication, and ribosomal frameshifting have been identified. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation within the genus relies on host specificity, stable co-maintenance of viruses, and response to host chromosomal mutations. Viruses found in distinct host species are considered different species. Sequence identity of less than 50% at the protein level generally indicates a species difference. HOST/ECOLOGY: Totiviruses are known to infect fungi, particularly Saccharomyces cerevisiae. They exhibit intracellular transmission during cell division, sporogenesis, and cell fusion. Saccharomyces cerevisiae virus L-A (ScV-L-A) relies on host genes MAK3, MAK10, and MAK31 for multiplication. The host antiviral gene SKI1 encodes a 5' to 3' exoribonuclease that targets uncapped RNAs. Defective SKI genes can lead to pathogenicity, particularly with M dsRNA, causing cold and temperature sensitivity.

name: Victorivirus
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Victorivirus genomes consist of a single molecule of uncapped, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) approximately 5 kbp in size. The genome contains two large open reading frames (ORFs). The upstream ORF encodes the capsid protein (CP), and the downstream ORF encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The RdRp is expressed as a separate, non-fused virion-associated minor protein. Victorivirus CPs possess a unique Ala/Gly/Pro-rich region near their C termini. The 5' end of the genomic plus strand is uncapped and contains a long 5' leader sequence predicted to be highly structured. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Species demarcation within the genus Victorivirus is based on less than 60% amino acid sequence identity in pairwise comparisons of either the CP or RdRp. Additionally, species are generally isolated from different filamentous fungi, with rare exceptions of co-maintained viruses in the same host. HOST/ECOLOGY: Victoriviruses infect filamentous fungi. They are transmitted intracellularly, both vertically during host cell division and sporogenesis, and horizontally during cell-cell fusion (hyphal anastomosis). Victoriviruses infecting ascomycetous fungi are largely excluded during ascospore formation. Geographical distribution is related to the distribution of their fungal hosts.

name: Leishmaniavirus
info: Leishmaniavirus: Genus summary based on ICTV data. Genome Characteristics: The Leishmaniavirus genome consists of a single molecule of linear, uncapped, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), approximately 5.3 kbp in size (5284 nt). The positive strand contains three open reading frames (ORFs). ORF3 exhibits motifs characteristic of viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). ORF2 encodes the major capsid protein (CP) of 82 kDa and overlaps ORF3 by 71 nucleotides, suggesting a +1 translational frameshift resulting in a gag-pol-like fusion protein of approximately 176 kDa. Sequencing data indicates abundant single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) in infected cells represents message-sense RNA. Evolutionary Context: Species demarcation within the genus relies primarily on biological criteria, similar to the genus Totivirus. Protein sequence identity of less than 50% generally indicates a species difference, although no single criterion is absolute. Host/Ecology: Leishmania RNA virus 1-1 (LRV-1-1) infects Leishmania braziliensis strain CUMC1. Viruses infecting other strains of L. braziliensis and L. guyanensis are possibly strains of LRV-1-1. A single strain of L. major is known to be infected with an LRV-1-1-like virus, designated LRV-2-1.

name: Botourmiaviridae
info: Family: Botourmiaviridae Genome Characteristics: Positive-sense RNA. Genomes are either monopartite (2-5.3 kb) in Botoulivirus, Betabotoulivirus, Magoulivirus, Scleroulivirus, Betascleroulivirus, Gammascleroulivirus, Deltascleroulivirus, Epsilonscleroulivirus, Penoulivirus, Rhizoulivirus, and Betarhizoulivirus genera, or tripartite (2.8 kb, 1.1 kb, 0.97 kb) in Ourmiavirus. Each RNA segment typically encodes a single protein. The RNA segment or RNA1 encodes an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) containing a conserved GDD domain. Ourmiaviruses also encode a coat protein (CP) and a movement protein (MP). Some members have polyadenylated 3' ends. Evolutionary Context: Belongs to the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Lenarviricota, class Miaviricetes, and order Ourlivirales. The family includes 12 genera: Ourmiavirus, Botoulivirus, Betabotoulivirus, Magoulivirus, Scleroulivirus, Betascleroulivirus, Gammascleroulivirus, Deltascleroulivirus, Epsilonscleroulivirus, Penoulivirus, Rhizoulivirus, and Betarhizoulivirus, comprising 159 species. Host/Ecology: Infects plants and fungi. Ourmiaviruses infect a wide range of dicotyledonous plants, causing systemic symptoms. Other genera infect fungal genera such as Botrytis, Sclerotinia, Magnaporthe, Rhizoctonia, Epicoccum, Acremonium, Phaeoacremonium, Neofusicoccum, Cladosporium, Entoleuca, Colletotrichum, Penicillium, Pyricularia, Phoma, Aspergillus, Phomopsis, Macrophomina and Oidiodendron. Some have been associated with oomycetes or grapevine leaves infected with oomycetes. Ourmia melon virus is mechanically transmitted. Horizontal transmission is suspected via weeds. Seed transmission occurs at low rates. Mycoviruses can transfer via hyphal anastomosis.

name: Yueviridae
info: Family: Yueviridae Genome Characteristics: Yueviridae viruses possess a bi-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome, ranging from 7.8 to 8.2 kb in total length. The large (L) segment (6.6-6.9 kb) encodes an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) containing a GDP:polyribonucleotidyltransferase (PRNTase) domain. The small (S) segment (1.2-1.3 kb) encodes a nucleocapsid protein. The RdRP domain shows similarity to those of Mononegavirales viruses. Evolutionary Context: Yueviridae is classified within the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Negarnaviricota, class Yunchangviricetes, and order Goujianvirales. They are closely related to aspivirids, jingchuvirals, mononegavirals, and qinvirids within the subphylum Haploviricotina. Species demarcation is based on phylogenetic analysis of the RdRP, but numerical thresholds are not defined. The family currently contains a single genus, Yuyuevirus. Host/Ecology: Yueviridae viruses have been detected in a broad range of hosts, including branchiopod, decapod, and isopod crustaceans; dipteran and thysanopteran insects; lycopodiopsid and polypodiopsid plants; various macrophytes; and stramenopiles. Specific viruses have been isolated from sesarmid crabs and freshwater isopods in China. Unclassified yuevirids have been found in brine shrimp, stramenopiles, onion thrips in Italy; mosquitoes in Finland; and meadow spikemoss, threeleaf goldback ferns, and unspecified macrophytes in the USA. Transmission patterns and replication cycles are currently unknown.

name: Straboviridae
info: Straboviridae: Genome Characteristics: Linear, double-stranded DNA genome of approximately 169 kb, encoding around 300 proteins. Genes are transcribed by operons. Encodes enzymes including DNA-dependent DNA polymerase B, DNA topoisomerase, DNA primase, serine protease, ADP-ribosyltransferase, DNA ligase, RNA ligase, exonuclease, endonuclease, DNA adenine methylase, terminase, NAD(+)-arginine ADP-ribosyltransferase, deoxycytidylate deaminase, polynucleotide kinase, ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase, deoxynucleotide monophosphate kinase, dihydrofolate reductase, thymidylate synthase, thymidine kinase, ribonuclease H, exodeoxyribonuclease, and endolysin. Evolutionary Context: Not specified. Host/Ecology: Infects Gram-negative bacteria. Geographical distribution is worldwide. Transmission occurs via passive diffusion through the medium. No antiviral drugs are currently available. Virion: Non-enveloped with a head-tail structure exhibiting Myo-type morphology. The prolate head measures 120 nm in length and 86 nm in width. The contractile tail features 6 long terminal fibers, 6 short spikes, and a small base plate. The capsid displays elongated icosahedral symmetry (T=13 Q=21), composed of 152 capsomers. Replication: Cytoplasmic. Adsorption to the host cell is mediated by tail fibers. Viral exolysin degrades the host cell wall locally. Viral DNA is ejected into the host cell cytoplasm via tail sheath contraction. Early gene transcription and translation are followed by genomic DNA replication, late gene transcription and translation, procapsid assembly, genome packaging, tail fiber assembly, and tail assembly. Mature virions are released through cell lysis.

name: Arenaviridae
info: Family: Arenaviridae Genome Characteristics: Arenaviridae are ambisense RNA viruses with genomes approximately 10.5 kb in size. The genome consists of two or three single-stranded RNA segments (S, M, L). Open reading frames (ORFs) encode nucleoproteins (NPs), glycoproteins (GPs), and large (L) proteins containing RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domains. Some members encode zinc-binding proteins (Z). The RNAs are uncapped and lack poly(A) tracts. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation relies on phylogenetic analysis of L protein/RdRP and NP sequences. Genus classification requires >40% S-segment and >35% L-segment nucleotide sequence identity. Criteria also include genome architecture, virion antigenicity, and virus ecology. Host/Ecology: Arenaviridae infect a diverse range of hosts, including fish (Antennavirus), snakes (Hartmanivirus, Reptarenavirus), mammals (Mammarenavirus), and unknown hosts (Innmovirus). Geographical distribution is linked to host distribution. Transmission patterns vary; some mammarenaviruses can infect humans, causing diseases ranging from mild to fatal. Infection starts with attachment to cell-surface receptors, followed by entry via the endosomal route.

name: Phenuiviridae
info: Family: Phenuiviridae Genome Characteristics: The family Phenuiviridae comprises viruses with segmented, negative-sense or ambisense RNA genomes, ranging from 8.1 to 25.1 kb in total size, distributed across 2 to 8 segments. Genomes typically encode four structural proteins: L (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase), Gn and Gc (glycoproteins), and N (nucleocapsid protein). Some members lack Gn and Gc genes and encode non-structural proteins involved in interferon response inhibition, apoptosis inhibition, movement in plant/fungal hosts, or RNA silencing suppression. Individual RNA segments have partially complementary termini. Evolutionary Context: Genus demarcation is based on phylogenetic relationships, genome organization, and ecological factors such as host range, pathobiology, and transmission patterns. Phenuiviridae is closely related to Arenaviridae, Discoviridae, Leishbuviridae, Mypoviridae, Nairoviridae, and Wupedeviridae, and more distantly related to Cruliviridae, Fimoviridae, Peribunyaviridae, Phasmaviridae, Tospoviridae, and Tulasviridae. Host/Ecology: Phenuiviridae members infect a diverse range of hosts, including humans, livestock, birds, crustaceans, plants, and fungi. They are also found in invertebrates, particularly arthropods, which can serve as biological vectors for transmission or act as unique hosts. Transmission occurs via arthropod vectors (e.g., sandflies, ticks, mosquitoes, planthoppers), transovarial transmission, or venereal transmission. Some members are important pathogens of humans, livestock, seafood, and agricultural crops. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm, utilizing a cap-snatching mechanism for mRNA transcription.

name: Nodaviridae
info: Family: Nodaviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, bipartite, single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome. RNA1 is approximately 3.1 kb, and RNA2 is approximately 1.4 kb. Both segments are capped at the 5' end but lack a poly(A) tail at the 3' end. RNA1 encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). RNA2 encodes the capsid protein. A subgenomic RNA3, co-linear to RNA1, encodes proteins B1 and B2. Evolutionary Context: Alphanodavirus CP sequences share 44-87% amino acid identity, while betanodavirus CP sequences share 80% or greater identity. Some unclassified viruses may be reclassified as betanodavirus strains based on RNA2 sequence similarity. Alphanodavirus and betanodavirus CP sequences share only about 10% identity. Host/Ecology: Nodaviridae members infect insects (alphanodaviruses) and fish (betanodaviruses). Betanodaviruses cause viral nervous necrosis in fish. Alphanodaviruses are named after their place of isolation or host. Betanodaviruses are named after the host fish. Virion: Non-enveloped, approximately 30 nm in diameter, with T=3 icosahedral symmetry (180 protein subunits). Replication: Cytoplasmic. The viral RNA acts as mRNA. RNA1 is translated to produce RdRp. Replication occurs in cytoplasmic viral factories, producing dsRNA intermediates. Subgenomic RNA3 is expressed. RNA2 is translated to produce the capsid protein. Virus assembly occurs in the cytoplasm. The assembled capsid protein is cleaved. Release of infectious particles occurs (possibly via lysis). Enzymes: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), Alphavirus-type capping enzymes (RNA triphosphatase, N7 methyltransferase, guanylyltransferase, 2'O methyltransferase), Self-cleaving capsid peptidase N1.

name: Alphanodavirus
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: The Alphanodavirus genome consists of two positive-sense single-stranded RNA molecules, RNA1 (3.1 kb) and RNA2 (1.4 kb), both required for infectivity and encapsidated in the same virion. The RNAs are capped at the 5' end but lack poly(A) tails. RNA1 encodes protein A (112 kDa), the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). RNA2 encodes protein α (44 kDa), the capsid protein (CP) precursor. A subgenomic RNA3 (0.39 kb) is produced, encoding one or two small proteins (B1 and B2). The capsid comprises 180 subunits of protein α or its cleavage products, proteins β (39 kDa) and γ (4 kDa), arranged in a T=3 lattice. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Species demarcation within the Alphanodavirus genus relies on biological properties (host range, vectors, transmission), antigenic properties (cross-reactivity), virion characteristics (electrophoretic mobility, sedimentation coefficient, buoyant density), structural protein characteristics (electrophoretic mobility of CP), and genome characteristics (RNA electrophoretic mobilities, hybridization properties, sequence). Definitive demarcation is based on nucleotide sequence of the viral CP gene (RNA2). HOST/ECOLOGY: Alphanodaviruses primarily infect insects. Nodamura virus (NoV) can also infect vertebrates (pigs, herons, mice, hamsters). Viruses can be propagated in Galleria mellonella larvae and cultured Drosophila melanogaster cells. Some, like Flock House virus (FHV), have a broader host range, including mammalian cells, plants, yeast, and nematodes. Transmission of NoV to suckling mice occurs via Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. In insects, infection typically causes stunting, paralysis, and death.

name: Betanodavirus
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Betanodavirus has a genome consisting of two positive-sense single-stranded RNA molecules, RNA1 (3.1 kb) and RNA2 (1.4 kb), both capped at the 5' end and lacking poly(A) tails. Both RNAs are required for infectivity and are encapsidated in the same virion. Infected cells also contain a subgenomic RNA3 (0.4 kb) derived from RNA1, which is not packaged. RNA1 encodes protein 1a (110 kDa), the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). RNA2 encodes protein 2a (42 kDa), the capsid protein (CP). SJNNV RNA3 encodes protein B2, an RNA silencing suppressor. The capsid contains 180 copies of the CP, which does not undergo maturation cleavage. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Species demarcation relies on biological properties, antigenic properties, virion characteristics, structural protein characteristics, and genome molecular characteristics. Definitive demarcation is based on the nucleotide sequence of the viral CP gene (RNA2). HOST/ECOLOGY: Betanodaviruses infect marine fish, causing viral nervous necrosis (VNN) or viral encephalopathy and retinopathy (VER), leading to behavioral abnormalities and high mortalities. Some species like SJNNV and TPNNV have limited host ranges, while others like RGNNV and BFNNV infect a wide range of fish. The viruses replicate in cultured fish cells and, at low levels, in mammalian cells. Transmission occurs both horizontally and vertically, with viral antigens and CP genes detected in eggs, larvae, and ovaries of infected fish.

name: Hypoviridae
info: Family: Hypoviridae Genome Characteristics: The Hypoviridae family consists of capsidless viruses with linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genomes ranging from 7.3 to 18.3 kb. Genomes contain either a single large open reading frame (ORF) or two ORFs, translated via non-canonical mechanisms like internal ribosome entry sites (IRES) and stop/restart translation. The predominant dsRNA form found in infected mycelia is regarded as a replicative intermediate or replicative form RNA. Evolutionary Context: Hypoviruses are classified within the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Pisuviricota, class Duploviricetes, and order Durnavirales. Phylogenetic analysis of protease, polymerase, and helicase domains suggests relatedness to the family Fusariviridae and, more distantly, to the genus Bymovirus in the family Potyviridae. Genera are distinguished based on phylogenetic analysis of polyprotein sequences including the RdRP domain. Host/Ecology: Hypoviridae infect ascomycetous and basidiomycetous filamentous fungi. Some members induce hypovirulence in their hosts, while others have little discernible effect. Replication occurs cytoplasmically in Golgi body-derived, lipid vesicles containing dsRNA. Transmission occurs through hyphal fusion (anastomosis), with variable rates through asexual spores (conidia). Sexual spore (ascospore) transmission is not known. The family includes eight genera: Alphahypovirus, Betahypovirus, Gammahypovirus, Deltahypovirus, Epsilonhypovirus, Zetahypovirus, Thetahypovirus, and Etahypovirus, comprising 39 species.

name: Aspiviridae
info: Family: Aspiviridae Genome Characteristics: The Aspiviridae family comprises viruses with single-stranded, negative-sense (possibly ambi-sense) RNA genomes. The genome size ranges from 11.3 to 12.5 kb, divided into 3 or 4 segments. The largest segment (RNA1) contains two ORFs, one encoding a protein involved in miRNA misprocessing and another encoding an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) with conserved motifs (A-E), including the SDD sequence. Other segments encode a cell-to-cell movement protein (MP) and a coat protein (CP). Evolutionary Context: Aspiviridae belongs to the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Negarnaviricota, subphylum Haploviricotina, class Milneviricetes, and order Naedrevirales. Phylogenetic analysis of RdRP sequences supports its classification as a distinct monophyletic group within negative-stranded RNA viruses. Host/Ecology: Aspiviruses infect a wide range of plants, including trees, shrubs, vegetables, and ornamentals (both monocots and dicots). Known hosts include citrus, blueberry, lettuce, tulip, ranunculus, and freesia. Some species are soil-transmitted and transmitted by zoospores of Olpidium spp. Geographical distribution varies by species, with some having wide distributions (e.g., Citrus psorosis virus) and others being more localized. Transmission patterns include vegetative propagation and vector transmission by Olpidium spp.

name: Potyviridae
info: Family: Potyviridae Genome Characteristics: Viruses possess a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genome, typically monopartite (8.2-11.5 kb) but bipartite in Bymovirus (RNA1: 7.3-7.6 kb, RNA2: 3.5-3.7 kb). Genomes have a VPg covalently linked to the 5′-end and are usually polyadenylated at the 3′-terminus. The genome encodes a large polyprotein that is self-cleaved into functional proteins, with conserved gene order. A trans-frame protein (PIPO) is also produced. Key proteins include P1, HC-Pro, P3, 6K1, CI, 6K2, VPg, NIa-Pro, NIb, and CP, each with specific functions in replication, movement, and transmission. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation is based on biological criteria (vector transmission) and molecular data (nucleotide sequence identity). Genus demarcation requires <46% nucleotide identity across the open reading frame (except for Rymovirus and Potyvirus). Species demarcation requires <76% nucleotide and <82% amino acid identity in complete ORF sequences. Host/Ecology: The host range is primarily plants, with some members having a narrow host range and others infecting species across many plant families. Geographical distribution is wide, aided by seed transmission in some cases. Transmission occurs via arthropods (aphids, eriophyid mites, whiteflies), plasmodiophorids (Bymovirus), seeds, or pollen. Aphid transmission requires conserved HC-Pro and CP motifs. Some members are mechanically transmissible.

name: Secoviridae
info: Family: Secoviridae Genome Characteristics: Secoviridae viruses possess non-enveloped virions, 25-30 nm in diameter, with icosahedral symmetry. The genome consists of one or two linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA molecules, ranging from 9 to 13.7 kb in total. Genomes typically have a 3' poly(A) tail, with some genera also having a 5' VPg protein. Viral proteins are expressed as large polyproteins, cleaved by RNA1-encoded 3C-like proteinases, and in some cases, by RNA2-encoded glutamic proteases. The replication block contains conserved domains characteristic of NTP-binding proteins, 3C-like proteinases, and RNA-directed RNA polymerases. Evolutionary Context: Secoviridae belongs to the order Picornavirales. Genera are demarcated by the number of genomic RNAs, protein domains, capsid proteins, presence of ORFs, and phylogenetic analysis of the Pro-Pol region. Species are demarcated by CP and Pro-Pol amino acid sequence identity, antigenic reactions, host range, vector specificity, and reassortment potential. Host/Ecology: Secoviridae members infect plants, primarily dicotyledonous species. Transmission occurs mainly via insect vectors (aphids, beetles, whiteflies, leafhoppers), nematodes, or through seed and pollen. Some genera require helper viruses for insect transmission. Geographical distribution varies among genera and species. Host range and symptoms also vary, with some causing mild or asymptomatic infections.

name: Tolecusatellitidae
info: Family: Tolecusatellitidae Genome Characteristics: Circular, single-stranded DNA genome ranging from 700 to 1,350 nucleotides. Lacks sequence identity to helper begomoviruses or mastreviruses. Contains an adenine-rich region and a satellite conserved region (SCR). Encodes none or one protein. Evolutionary Context: Satellite virus status defined by dependence on helper Begomoviruses or Mastreviruses for replication and packaging. Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not explicitly stated. Host/Ecology: Host range includes plants susceptible to helper begomoviruses or mastreviruses. Geographical distribution is linked to the distribution of its helper viruses. Transmission occurs via mechanisms associated with helper virus transmission, including vector-mediated spread. Replication occurs in the nucleus. The single-stranded DNA genome is converted to double-stranded DNA using cellular factors. Bidirectional transcription produces viral mRNAs and proteins. Replication is initiated by REP protein cleavage and proceeds via rolling circle replication. Newly synthesized single-stranded DNA can be converted to double-stranded DNA, encapsidated, or transported to neighboring cells via plasmodesmata with the help of viral movement proteins.

name: Closteroviridae
info: Family: Closteroviridae Genome Characteristics: The Closteroviridae family comprises plant viruses with long, flexible filamentous particles, 650-2,200 nm in length. The genome consists of a large, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA, which can be mono-, bi-, or tripartite, ranging from 13,000 to nearly 19,000 nucleotides. Key conserved domains include methyltransferase (Mtr), helicase (Hel), and RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP). A cellular HSP70 homolog and a duplicated, diverged copy of the capsid protein (CPm) are characteristic features. Genome expression involves proteolytic processing, a +1 ribosomal frameshift, and sub-genomic messenger RNAs. Evolutionary Context: Closteroviruses are considered a monophyletic lineage, possibly evolved from a smaller filamentous virus. Recombination events and horizontal gene transfer have contributed to genetic diversity and genome organization. Taxonomic demarcation is based on phylogenetic relationships in RdRP, CP, and HSP70h amino acid sequences, vector type, number of genomic RNAs, ORF number and organization, and virion length. Host/Ecology: Closteroviridae members primarily infect plants, mainly dicots. Transmission occurs via aphids, whiteflies, pseudococcid mealybugs, or soft scale insects in a semi-persistent manner. Mechanical inoculation is difficult, and seed transmission is not known. Viruses are mostly phloem-restricted, inducing cytoplasmic aggregates of virus particles with membranous vesicles derived from the endoplasmic reticulum and possibly mitochondria. Geographical distribution varies, mostly in temperate or subtropical regions.

name: Filoviridae
info: Family: Filoviridae Genome Characteristics: Filoviridae are negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses. Genomes are linear and non-segmented, ranging from 13.1 to 20.9 kb. The genome encodes 6-10 proteins depending on the genus, including a nucleoprotein (NP), polymerase cofactor (VP35), glycoprotein (GP1,2), transcriptional activator (VP30), and a large protein (L) with an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Gene order is generally 3′-NP-VP35-(VP40)-(GP)-L-5′, with variations in additional genes and gene overlaps. Evolutionary Context: Filoviridae form a monophyletic clade based on RdRP sequences. Genus demarcation relies on Pairwise Sequence Comparison (PASC) of complete genomes (≥55% difference between genera), genomic features (gene overlaps, ORFs), host range, geographic distribution, and pathogenicity. The family includes 9 genera and 17 species. Host/Ecology: Filoviridae infect fish (Oblavirus, Striavirus, Thamnovirus), mammals (Cuevavirus, Dianlovirus, Orthoebolavirus, Orthomarburgvirus), and reptiles (Tapjovirus). Geographic distribution includes Africa, Asia, Europe, and South America. Natural hosts include bats, fish, snakes, and potentially other animals. Some filoviruses, such as Ebola virus and Marburg virus, are highly pathogenic to humans, with transmission occurring through direct contact. Reston virus has been found in domestic pigs.

name: Narnaviridae
info: Narnaviridae: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Single molecule of non-encapsidated, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA+) ranging from 2.3 to 2.9 kb. Genome is linear and monopartite, encoding a single protein (80-104 kDa) with RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) motifs. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Phylogenetic analysis of RdRp sequences distinguishes Narnavirus and Mitovirus genera within the family. RdRp proteins show distant relationship to those of bacteriophages in the family Leviviridae. 3'-end secondary structures of Narnavirus members resemble those of Leviviridae coliphages. Taxonomic demarcation is based on RdRp sequence and phylogenetic clustering. HOST/ECOLOGY: Host range includes fungi. Geographical distribution is not specified in provided information. Transmission occurs horizontally through mating or vertically from mother to daughter cells. Replication is cytoplasmic. The virus lacks a capsid and is not assigned to a Baltimore classification. REPLICATION: The virion RNA serves as both the genome and viral messenger RNA. Translation of genomic RNA produces viral RdRp. A double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genome is synthesized from the genomic ssRNA(+). The dsRNA genome is transcribed/replicated, providing viral mRNAs/new ssRNA(+) genomes. Mature genomes can be transmitted to new cells by cytoplasmic exchange, sporogenesis, or hyphal anastomosis.

name: Narnavirus
info: Genus: Narnavirus Genome Characteristics: The genome is a linear, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) molecule, approximately 2.5 kb in size, with a high G+C content (around 60%). It lacks a poly(A) tail at the 3' end, and the presence of a 5' cap is unknown. The genome contains one major open reading frame (ORF) encoding a protein of 91 kDa (p91), which exhibits sequence similarity to RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRps), particularly those of ssRNA enterobacteria phages. Evolutionary Context: Species demarcation within the genus relies on biological criteria such as stable co-maintenance of different species within the same cell, segregation patterns during cell growth, and recombination potential. Sequence identity at the protein level, with less than 50% identity generally indicating a species difference, also contributes to species demarcation. Host/Ecology: Narnaviruses primarily infect the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. ScNV-20S, a representative narnavirus, infects a high percentage of laboratory strains. Transmission occurs through mating or cytoplasmic mixing, without an extracellular stage. Narnaviruses are stable and resistant to curing procedures effective against other yeast viruses. Geographical distribution is linked to the distribution of its yeast host. No specific phenotype is associated with narnavirus presence in the host.

name: Mitovirus
info: Genus: Mitovirus Genome Characteristics: The genome consists of a single molecule of single-stranded RNA, 2.3-2.7 kb in size. Double-stranded RNA forms are found in infected mitochondria. The coding strand has 62-73% A+U content and lacks a poly(A) tail. The 5' and 3' ends can form stem-loop structures, sometimes complementary. The coding strand is predicted to be translatable only in mitochondria, yielding an 80-97 kDa protein containing RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) motifs. RdRp activity and an 80 kDa RdRp protein have been detected in infected mitochondria. No structural proteins are known. Evolutionary Context: Species demarcation is based on RdRp amino acid sequence identity. Different species show less than 40% identity, while strains within a species show greater than 90% identity. Host/Ecology: Mitoviruses infect fungi, including Cryphonectria parasitica, Ophiostoma novo-ulmi, O. ulmi, and Sclerotinia homoeocarpa. They are localized in mitochondria and can be transmitted through hyphal fusion. Transmission rates through asexual spores vary from 10-100%. Sexual spore transmission in C. parasitica occurs at 20-50% when the infected parent is female, but not when male. In O. novo-ulmi, viruses are usually excluded from ascospores. Interspecies and intergenus transmission may occur. Some mitoviruses reduce fungal virulence (hypovirulence).

name: Nairoviridae
info: Family: Nairoviridae Genome Characteristics: Nairoviridae viruses possess bisegmented or trisegmented negative-sense RNA genomes, ranging from 17.2 to 21.1 kb. The genome segments are designated S, M, and L. The S RNA encodes the nucleoprotein (N), the M RNA encodes a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and the L RNA encodes a large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Viral mRNAs are capped but not polyadenylated, acquiring 5' caps via cap-snatching from host cell mRNAs. Key conserved domains include the RdRP domain within the L protein. Evolutionary Context: Genus demarcation is based on phylogenetic relationships, genome architecture, virion antigenicity, and virus ecology. Species demarcation requires coding-complete sequences of all genome segments and is determined by RdRP amino acid sequence identity, with <93% identity indicating different species. Host/Ecology: Nairoviridae viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by arthropods, including ticks, cockroaches, spiders and water striders, among birds and mammals. Known hosts include arthropods (ticks, cockroaches, spiders, water striders), birds, and mammals. Some members, such as Norwavirus and Orthonairovirus, can infect humans, causing diseases ranging from mild to fatal. Transmission patterns primarily involve arthropod vectors.

name: Chuviridae
info: Family: Chuviridae Genome Characteristics: Negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes ranging from 9.1 to 12.2 kb. Genomes can be nonsegmented linear, nonsegmented circular, bisegmented linear, or bisegmented circular. Genomes contain two to four open reading frames (ORFs) encoding a glycoprotein (GP), a nucleoprotein (NP), a large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain, and/or proteins of unknown function. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation is based on L protein sequence identity. Genus demarcation requires L protein sequence identity <31%. Species demarcation requires L protein sequence identity <90%. Host/Ecology: Associated with a broad range of hosts including arachnids (spiders and ticks), barnacles, crustaceans (crabs and shrimp), insects (cockroaches, glow-worms, earwigs, louse flies, mosquitoes, stink bugs, water bugs, whiteflies, wasps, damselflies/dragonflies, termites), fish (atheriniform and syngnathiform), and reptiles (snakes). Also associated with cephalopods and turtles. Geographical distribution includes Africa, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. Transmission patterns are largely unknown.

name: Caliciviridae
info: Family: Caliciviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome of 6.4-8.5 kb. The genome has a 5'-terminal VPg and a 3'-terminal poly(A) tail. Non-structural and structural proteins are encoded by different ORFs. A subgenomic RNA of 2.2-2.4 kb is synthesized intracellularly. The virion consists of a major capsid protein VP1 (58-60 kDa), a minor structural protein VP2 (8.5-23 kDa), and VPg (13-16 kDa). Evolutionary Context: Eleven genera are classified based on VP1 amino acid sequence differences (>60%). Caliciviruses share similarities with viruses in the order Picornavirales and the family Potyviridae, including a VPg and poly(A) tail. Host/Ecology: Infects a wide range of hosts, including mammals (Lagovirus, Norovirus, Nebovirus, Recovirus, Sapovirus, Valovirus, Vesivirus), birds (Bavovirus, Nacovirus), and fish (Minovirus, Salovirus). Human noroviruses are a leading cause of acute gastroenteritis. Transmission occurs via direct contact with infected hosts or indirectly through fecal material, vomitus, respiratory secretions, contaminated food, water, and fomites. Mechanical arthropod vector transmission has been described for some viruses. Associated with various disease syndromes, including gastroenteritis, vesicular exanthema, liver necrosis, and enteritis.

name: Ascoviridae
info: Family: Ascoviridae Genome Characteristics: Circular dsDNA, 100-200 kbp, containing 117-180 genes. G+C content ranges from 42-60%. Replication occurs in the nucleus, leading to cell cleavage into virion-containing vesicles. Virions contain at least 20 proteins. Evolutionary Context: Classified within the realm Varidnaviria, kingdom Bamfordvirae, phylum Nucleocytoviricota, class Megaviricetes, order Pimascovirales. Two genera: Ascovirus and Toursvirus. Genus demarcation based on virion morphology, phylogenetic analysis, DNA hybridization, host range, and association with hymenopteran parasites. Host/Ecology: Primarily infects lepidopteran larvae, especially Noctuidae (Ascovirus) and Yponomeutidae (Toursvirus). Ascovirus has a broader experimental host range. Toursvirus replicates in both lepidopteran host and ichneumonid vector. Geographically widespread, including the United States, Europe, Australia, Indonesia, Japan, China, and Mexico. Transmitted horizontally by parasitoid wasps (Braconidae and Ichneumonidae) via contaminated ovipositors. Toursvirus (DpTV) is transmitted vertically in the wasp Diadromus pulchellus. Causes chronic, fatal disease in larvae, retarding development.

name: Schitoviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: dsDNA, linear. Genome size: ~70 kb. Gene count: 72. Key feature: Encodes a viral RNA polymerase (vRNAP). EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation: Family Schitoviridae (taxid:2842329). HOST/ECOLOGY: Host range: Bacteria. Geographical distribution: Worldwide. Transmission: Passive diffusion. Virion Structure: Non-enveloped, head-tail structure with Podo-type morphology. Capsid: Icosahedral, ~70 nm diameter, T=9 symmetry. Contains ~4 copies of vRNAP. Replication Cycle: Cytoplasmic. Adsorption via tail fibers. Ejection of viral DNA and vRNAP into host cytoplasm. Transcription of early genes by vRNAP. Replication of genomic DNA. Transcription of late genes by host RNAP. Assembly of procapsid and genome packaging. Tail fiber and tail assembly. Release via lysis. Gene Expression: Encodes DNA-directed DNA polymerase B (DNA pol B).

name: Virgaviridae
info: Family: Virgaviridae Genome Characteristics: ssRNA, positive-sense genome ranging from 6.3 to 13 kb. Genome can be monopartite (Tobamovirus) or multipartite (2 or 3 segments in other genera). Possesses a 3′-terminal tRNA-like structure and a 5′-cap (m7GpppG). Encodes an alpha-like replication protein with methyltransferase (Mtr) and helicase (Hel) domains. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) is part of the replication protein, except in Hordeivirus. Evolutionary Context: Realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Kitrinoviricota, class Alsuviricetes, order Martellivirales. Seven genera are differentiated based on genome organization, number of genomic RNAs, type of movement protein (30K or TGB), and transmission mode. Replication proteins are related to those of Closteroviridae, Bromoviridae, and unassigned genera Idaeovirus, Blunervirus, Cilevirus and Higrevirus. Host/Ecology: Plant viruses infecting a wide range of herbaceous, monocotyledonous, and dicotyledonous plants. Host range of individual viruses is usually limited. Transmitted mechanically (all members), by soil-borne vectors (Furovirus, Pecluvirus, Pomovirus, Tobravirus), or through pollen and seed (Hordeivirus, Goravirus). Geographical distribution varies depending on the virus. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm. Virions: Non-enveloped, rod-shaped particles approximately 20 nm in diameter and up to 300 nm long. Capsid comprises multiple copies of a single polypeptide (17-24 kDa). Some viruses encode a readthrough capsid protein.

name: Picornaviridae
info: Picornaviridae is a family of small, non-enveloped, icosahedral viruses with single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genomes ranging from 6.7 to 10.1 kb. The genome contains a single long open reading frame (ORF), except for cadiciviruses which have two ORFs. A small protein, VPg, is covalently linked to the 5′-terminus. Translation is initiated by an internal ribosomal entry site (IRES). The polyprotein is cleaved by virus-encoded proteinases (3Cpro, 2Apro, Lpro). Replication occurs in cytoplasmic replication organelles, using a RNA-directed RNA polymerase with a YGDD motif. The family is classified within the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Pisuviricota, class Pisoniviricetes, and order Picornavirales. Genus demarcation is based on homologous IRES structures and proteins, monophyly, distinctive genome maps, significant sequence divergence in P1cap, 2Chel, 3Cpro, and 3Dpol, and lack of homology in L, 2B, 3A, and 3B proteins. Species demarcation requires significant amino acid identity in P1, 2C, 3C, and 3D proteins, monophyly, identical genome maps, and compatibility in proteolytic processing, replication, encapsidation, and genetic recombination. Picornaviruses infect vertebrates, causing a range of diseases from mild to severe. Transmission is primarily horizontal, via fecal-oral, fomite, or airborne routes. Most picornaviruses are specific to one or a few host species.

name: Solemoviridae
info: Family: Solemoviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome is a 4-6 kb, positive-sense, monopartite, polycistronic RNA with a 5′-terminal VPg and no poly(A) tail. Genomes contain 4-10 ORFs, encoding a viral suppressor of RNA silencing, a polyprotein, and a capsid protein. The polyprotein contains domains for a membrane anchor, serine protease, VPg, and either a C-terminal domain protein or an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) expressed via ribosomal frameshifting. Some members encapsidate small circular satellite RNAs. Evolutionary Context: Genera are differentiated by phylogenies of individual ORFs or proteins. Solemovirus RdRPs are closely related to those of Alvernaviridae and Barnaviridae. Polerovirus and Enamovirus CPs share a common origin with Luteovirus, while Polemovirus and Sobemovirus CPs are related to Necrovirus. Host/Ecology: The host range is plants (monocotyledons and dicotyledons). Transmission occurs via mechanical wounding, vegetative propagation, soil, or insects (beetles, aphids, thrips, hoppers, mirid bugs, and moths). Poleroviruses and Enamoviruses are primarily transmitted by aphids in a persistent, circulative, non-propagative manner. Some viruses infecting legumes or Chenopodiaceae may be seed-transmissible. Genera include Sobemovirus, Polemovirus, Polerovirus, and Enamovirus.

name: Geminiviridae
info: Family: Geminiviridae Genome Characteristics: Geminiviruses possess small, non-enveloped virions with genomes consisting of one or two circular, single-stranded DNA molecules ranging from 2.5 to 5.2 kb. Replication occurs in the host cell nucleus utilizing host replication factors via rolling-circle and recombination-dependent mechanisms. A conserved nonanucleotide sequence (5′-TAATATTAC-3′ or 5′-TAAGATTCC-3′) is present at the origin of virion strand replication. Evolutionary Context: Geminiviridae belongs to the realm Monodnaviria, kingdom Shotokuvirae, phylum Cressdnaviricota, class Repensiviricetes, and order Geplafuvirales. The family is divided into 15 genera based on host range, insect vector, genome organization, and phylogenetic relationships. Similar replication mechanisms and conserved sequences are observed in other ssDNA virus families like Nanoviridae, Circoviridae, Anelloviridae and Genomoviridae. Host/Ecology: Geminiviruses infect a wide range of monocot and dicot plants, causing economically significant diseases in tropical and subtropical regions. Transmission occurs via various insect vectors, including whiteflies, leafhoppers, aphids, and treehoppers. Some genera exhibit specific host ranges and vector associations. For example, Begomoviruses are transmitted by whiteflies and infect dicots, while Mastreviruses primarily infect monocots and are transmitted by leafhoppers. Some members can replicate in insect vectors.

name: Iridoviridae
info: Iridoviridae is a family of large, icosahedral, double-stranded DNA viruses classified into two subfamilies: Alphairidovirinae and Betairidovirinae. Alphairidovirinae genera (Ranavirus, Megalocytivirus, Lymphocystivirus) primarily infect ectothermic vertebrates, while Betairidovirinae genera (Iridovirus, Chloriridovirus, Decapodiridovirus) mainly infect invertebrates. Genomes are linear, dsDNA, 103-220 kbp (unique portion), circularly permuted, and terminally redundant, encoding 92-211 proteins. G+C content ranges from 27-55%. Vertebrate iridovirus genomes are typically methylated. Replication involves both nuclear (early stages) and cytoplasmic (late stages) compartments. Virion assembly occurs in cytoplasmic assembly sites. Mature virions may be released by cell lysis or acquire an envelope by budding. Taxonomic demarcation is based on host range, nucleotide/amino acid sequence identity, G+C content, phylogenetic relatedness, genome co-linearity, disease manifestations, and antigenicity. Alphairidovirinae and Betairidovirinae are distinguished by primary host and genome characteristics. Iridovirids infect ectothermic vertebrates and invertebrates in aquatic environments. Transmission in invertebrates can be peroral or via parasites. Vertebrate iridoviruses are transmitted by co-habitation, feeding, or injection. Host range and virulence vary widely. Members of different genera are serologically distinct. Iridovirids share sequence similarity with other large DNA viruses like African swine fever virus, Ascoviridae, Phycodnaviridae, Mimiviridae and Poxviridae, suggesting a common origin.

name: Hantaviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Hantaviridae viruses possess a tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome, ranging from 10.5 to 14.6 kb in total size. The genome segments are designated S, M, and L. The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein (N), the M segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and the L segment encodes a large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Viral mRNAs are capped but not polyadenylated, acquiring 5' caps via cap-snatching from host mRNAs. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Hantaviridae is a family within the order Elliovirales, class Bunyaviricetes, phylum Negarnaviricota, kingdom Orthornavirae, and realm Riboviria. The family is divided into four subfamilies and eight genera. Genus demarcation relies on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein, and N sequences, using a Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) threshold of 0.95. Species demarcation uses a PED threshold of 0.1. Subfamilies are demarcated based on distinct clustering in phylogenetic trees and a PED threshold of 3.5. Hantaviridae is closely related to other bunyavirus-like families. HOST/ECOLOGY: Hantaviruses are maintained in diverse hosts, including actinopterygian and agnathan fish (Actinovirus, Agnathovirus, Percilovirus), bats (Loanvirus, Mobatvirus), eulipotyphla and rodents (Orthohantavirus, Thottimvirus), and reptiles (Reptillovirus). Geographical distribution is linked to host ranges. Transmission patterns vary, with some orthohantaviruses capable of infecting humans and causing diseases.

name: Astroviridae
info: Family: Astroviridae Genome Characteristics: Virions contain a single molecule of infectious, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA, ranging from 6.4 to 7.7 kb. A poly(A) tail is present at the 3' end. The 5' end structure is unknown. A small protein with VPg similarity has been identified. The genome contains three ORFs: ORF1a and ORF1b (encoding non-structural proteins), and ORF2 (encoding structural proteins). A frame-shifting mechanism facilitates RNA-dependent RNA polymerase translation. A subgenomic RNA (approximately 2.8 kb) corresponding to ORF2 is produced. Recombination may occur. Evolutionary Context: Serotypes are defined by immune electron microscopy, neutralization tests, and sequence comparisons of the ORF2 carboxy-terminal hypervariable domain. Eight serotypes of classical human astroviruses (HAstV) are recognized. Distinct serotypes exist for bovine, turkey, avian nephritis, and chicken astroviruses. Novel human astroviruses have been identified since 2008. Host/Ecology: Astroviruses infect a wide range of mammals and birds, including humans, cats, cattle, deer, dogs, ducks, mice, pigs, sheep, mink, turkeys, chickens, bats, cheetahs, guinea fowl, rats, and marine mammals. Infections are primarily associated with gastroenteritis in young individuals. Other diseases include hepatitis in ducks and interstitial nephritis in chickens. Transmission occurs via the fecal-oral route. Astrovirus pathogenesis varies by genus. HAstV-1 capsid protein binds complement proteins C1q and MBL, inhibiting complement activation.

name: Avastrovirus
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Information not provided in source. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria for Avastrovirus species are currently under redefinition. The original classification was based on host species, which did not align with genetic phylogenies. A revised classification based on genetic analysis of the complete capsid region at the amino acid level is proposed, dividing avian astroviruses into two main genogroups (I and II). Genogroups include astroviruses infecting different host species and can be further subdivided into genotype species based on both genetic and host species criteria. Mean amino acid genetic distances between the two genogroups is 0.704±0.013. Within each genogroup, amino acid genetic distances between genotypes range between 0.576 and 0.741. HOST/ECOLOGY: Avastrovirus species infect various avian hosts, including ducks, turkeys, guinea fowl, and chickens. Infection often involves extra-intestinal manifestations, such as damage to the liver, kidney, or the immune system. Duck astrovirus (DAstV) causes often-fatal hepatitis in ducklings. Astroviruses infecting turkeys (TAstV-1, TAstV-2 and ANV), guinea fowl (TAstV-2) and chickens (ANV and CAstV) affect multiple organs, including the kidney and thymus. Duck astrovirus grows in embryonated hens’ eggs. Turkey astroviruses grow in embryonated turkey eggs. Certain strains of chicken astrovirus grow in LMH cells.

name: Mamastrovirus
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Information not provided in source. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria for Mamastrovirus species were originally based on host species, which did not align with genetic phylogenies. Reclassification is underway, dividing mammalian astroviruses into two main genogroups (I and II) based on amino acid analysis of the complete capsid region. Genogroups include astroviruses infecting different host species and can be further subdivided based on genetic and host species criteria. Mean amino acid genetic distance between genogroups is 0.671±0.016. Within genogroups, amino acid genetic distances between genotypes range from 0.338 to 0.783. Serotypes within genotypes are defined by 20-fold or greater two-way cross-neutralization titers. HOST/ECOLOGY: Mamastroviruses primarily cause gastroenteritis in mammals. In humans, astroviruses have been detected in duodenal biopsies. In experimentally infected sheep, astrovirus was found in the small intestine. In calves, astrovirus infection was localized to M cells overlying Peyer’s patches. Human astroviruses are distributed worldwide and associated with 2–8% of acute, non-bacterial gastroenteritis in children, as well as gastroenteritis outbreaks and infections in immunocompromised individuals.

name: Chrysoviridae
info: Family: Chrysoviridae Genome Characteristics: The Chrysoviridae family consists of non-enveloped, isometric viruses approximately 40 nm in diameter. The genome is composed of 3-7 segments of double-stranded (ds) RNA, totaling 8.9-16.0 kbp. Each segment is individually encapsidated. The dsRNA1 segment typically encodes the RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP), and dsRNA2 encodes the major capsid protein (CP). Other segments encode proteins of unknown function. Conserved sequences are found in the 5' and 3' non-coding regions (NCRs). Evolutionary Context: Chrysoviruses are classified within the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Duplornaviricota, class Chrymotiviricetes, and order Ghabrivirales. The family includes two genera: Alphachrysovirus and Betachrysovirus, containing 20 and 11 species, respectively. Genus demarcation is based on phylogenetic analysis, nucleotide and amino acid sequence data, and the number of dsRNA genome segments. Host/Ecology: Chrysoviruses primarily infect ascomycetous and basidiomycetous fungi, plants, and possibly insects. They lack an extracellular phase and are transmitted intracellularly through cell division, sporogenesis (vertical transmission), and hyphal anastomosis (horizontal transmission). Infections are often latent, although some can cause deleterious effects in fungal hosts. Geographical distribution is linked to host range.

name: Demerecviridae
info: Family: Demerecviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, double-stranded DNA genome of approximately 121 kb, encoding about 160 genes. Key enzymes include DNA-directed DNA polymerase A, serine proteases (Peptidase S78, Peptidase S74), exonuclease, ribonuclease H, and DNA ligase. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not specified. Host/Ecology: Host Range: Bacteria. Geographical Distribution: Worldwide. Transmission: Passive diffusion through medium. Virion Structure and Replication: Non-enveloped virus with a head-tail structure and Sipho-type morphology. The capsid is about 90 nm in diameter with T=13 icosahedral symmetry, composed of 11 pentamers and 120 hexamers. The tail is about 160 nm in length and 9 nm in width, featuring a subterminal disk and three long kinked fibers (120 nm), plus a conical tip with a single straight central fiber (50 nm). Replication occurs in the cytoplasm. The virus attaches to host cell receptors via tail fibers. Viral exolysin degrades the host cell wall. Viral DNA is injected into the host cytoplasm via a long flexible tail ejection system. Replication involves DNA strand displacement. Virions are released by cell lysis. Antiviral Drugs: None reported.

name: Poxviridae
info: Family: Poxviridae Genome Characteristics: The Poxviridae family comprises enveloped viruses, generally oval or brick-shaped, with virions measuring 220-450 nm x 140-260 nm x 140-260 nm. The genome consists of a single, linear molecule of dsDNA, ranging from 128 to 375 kbp, with covalently closed ends. Genomes encode 120-300 proteins. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm, mediated by virus-encoded proteins. Evolutionary Context: Poxviridae belongs to the Nucleocytoplasmic Large DNA Viruses (NCLDV) group. The family is divided into two subfamilies: Chordopoxvirinae (infecting vertebrates) and Entomopoxvirinae (infecting insects). Subfamily demarcation is based on host range and genetic differences, with only 49 conserved gene products between the two. Host/Ecology: Chordopoxvirinae members infect vertebrates, including humans, livestock, and wildlife, often causing lesions, skin nodules, or disseminated rash. Transmission occurs through droplets/aerosols, direct contact, arthropods (mechanical), or fomites. Entomopoxvirinae members infect insects, with transmission occurring mechanically. Host range in nature is generally narrow. Infections by Entomopoxvirinae are invariably fatal.

name: Endornaviridae
info: Family: Endornaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Endornaviridae family comprises viruses with linear, single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genomes ranging from 9.7 to 17.6 kb. The genome is monocistronic, encoding a large polyprotein (3,217-5,825 aa). A conserved RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain is present in all members. Other domains, such as viral helicase, methyl transferase, glycosyl transferase, cysteine-rich regions, phytoreo_S7 domain, and capsular polysaccharide synthase, may also be present. The 3' end of most endornavirus RNAs contains a short stretch of repeated cytosine residues. The dsRNA of several plant endornaviruses contains a site-specific break (nick) in the coding strand. Evolutionary Context: The family is divided into two genera, Alphaendornavirus and Betaendornavirus, based on genome size, host, presence/absence of a site-specific nick, and phylogenetic clustering of RdRP sequences. Endornaviruses likely acquired genetic material through lateral gene transfer from plants, fungi, and bacteria. The RdRP and helicase domains are related to those of the "alpha-like" superfamily of positive-sense RNA viruses. Host/Ecology: Endornaviruses infect plants, fungi, and oomycetes. They are host-specific and distributed throughout all tissues. Transmission in plants occurs vertically through gametes (seeds and pollen). Fungal endornaviruses are transmitted vertically through spores and horizontally via hyphal anastomosis. Most endornaviruses have no obvious effect on host phenotype, though some have been associated with cytoplasmic male sterility in plants and hypovirulence in fungi.
