Endornavirus-derived small RNAs (siRNAs) have been detected in infected plants.

name: Circoviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Family Circoviridae members possess circular, covalently closed, single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) genomes ranging from 1.7 to 2.1 kb. Genomes are monopartite and have an ambisense organization, encoding at least two major open reading frames (ORFs) for the replication-associated protein (Rep) and capsid protein (Cp). Replication occurs via rolling circle replication (RCR), initiated by the Rep protein at a conserved nonanucleotide motif within the origin of replication (ori). Key conserved domains include endonuclease and helicase domains within the Rep protein. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: The family includes two genera: Circovirus and Cyclovirus. Genus demarcation is based on the location of the ori relative to coding regions. Species demarcation within the family is set at 80% genome-wide nucleotide sequence identity. Circoviridae is related to other ssDNA viruses, including Anelloviridae, Geminiviridae, Nanoviridae and Genomoviridae. HOST/ECOLOGY: Circovirus members have been identified in vertebrates (mammals, birds, and fish). Cyclovirus members have been identified in vertebrates (mammals and birds) and invertebrates (arthropods). The true host for Cyclovirus is often unknown. Biological information is primarily derived from porcine circoviruses (PCV1 and PCV2) and beak and feather disease virus (BFDV). Antigenic relationships among Circoviridae members are mostly unknown, with PCV1 and PCV2 being antigenically distinct from BFDV. Transmission patterns and host range for Cyclovirus are largely uncharacterized.

name: Hepeviridae
info: Family: Hepeviridae Genome Characteristics: ssRNA, positive-sense, linear genome of 6.4-7.2 kb with a m7G cap and poly(A) tail. Genome contains 3 ORFs (ORF1, ORF2, ORF3), with some strains of Orthohepevirus ratti containing an additional ORF4. ORF1 encodes non-structural proteins with domains similar to methyltransferases, cysteine proteases, macro domains, RNA helicases, and RdRP. ORF2 encodes the major capsid protein (CP). ORF3 encodes a small phosphoprotein. Evolutionary Context: Realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Kitrinoviricota, class Alsuviricetes, order Hepelivirales. Two subfamilies: Parahepevirinae (infects trout and salmon) and Orthohepevirinae (infects mammals and birds). Five genera and ten species are currently recognized. Host/Ecology: Members infect mammals (Chirohepevirus, Paslahepevirus, Rocahepevirus), birds (Avihepevirus), and salmonid fish (Piscihepevirus). Geographical distribution varies depending on the specific virus and host. Transmission occurs primarily via the fecal-oral route, through contaminated water or consumption of undercooked meat. Zoonotic transmission to humans can occur, leading to acute or chronic hepatitis. Vertical transmission from mother to fetus is also possible.

name: Flaviviridae
info: Family: Flaviviridae Genome Characteristics: Positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome, ranging from 9.0 to 13 kb. Genome organization includes a single long open reading frame (ORF) flanked by 5' and 3' non-coding regions (NCRs). Genera Orthoflavivirus utilizes a type I cap for translation initiation, while Pestivirus, Hepacivirus, and Pegivirus use an internal ribosome entry site (IRES). Encodes a polyprotein that is cleaved into structural and nonstructural proteins, including a serine protease, RNA helicase, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP). Evolutionary Context: Realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Kitrinoviricota, class Flasuviricetes, order Amarillovirales. Four genera: Orthoflavivirus, Pestivirus, Hepacivirus, and Pegivirus. Taxonomic demarcation based on genetic and biological properties. Host/Ecology: Most infect mammals and birds. Orthoflavivirus members are primarily arthropod-borne, infecting mosquitoes or ticks, with mammals and birds as primary hosts. Pestiviruses infect pigs and ruminants, transmitted through contact with infected secretions. Hepacivirus members infect mammals, targeting the liver. Pegivirus members are associated with persistent infections in a wide range of mammalian species. Geographical distribution varies depending on the specific virus and host range. Transmission patterns differ among genera, with arthropod-borne transmission for Orthoflavivirus and direct contact for Pestivirus.

name: Bornaviridae
info: Family: Bornaviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome consists of a linear, negative-sense, non-segmented RNA molecule of approximately 9 kb. It contains three transcription units and at least six open reading frames (ORFs). Key proteins expressed include nucleoprotein (N), phosphoprotein (P), matrix protein (M), glycoprotein (G), and a large protein (L) with RNA-directed RNA polymerase domain, plus an accessory protein (X). Replication occurs intranuclearly, utilizing anti-genomic RNA as an intermediate. Genomic and anti-genomic RNA are neither capped nor polyadenylated. Evolutionary Context: Bornaviruses belong to the order Mononegavirales. Genus demarcation is based on genomic characteristics, including pairwise sequence comparison (PASC), phylogeny, and genome organization, with a cutoff of approximately 45% complete genome nucleotide identity. The family includes the genera Carbovirus, Cultervirus, and Orthobornavirus. Endogenous bornavirus-like (EBL) sequences are found in various chordate genomes. Host/Ecology: Bornaviruses infect a wide range of hosts, including mammals, birds, reptiles, and fish. Orthobornaviruses, specifically Orthobornavirus bornaense and Orthobornavirus sciuri, can cause fatal encephalitis in humans. Transmission patterns vary depending on the specific virus and host. Geographical distribution is broad, reflecting the wide host range.

name: Paramyxoviridae
info: Family: Paramyxoviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome consists of a single molecule of linear, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA, ranging from 14.6 to 20.1 kb. Genomes are multiples of 6 nt. The RNA is encapsidated in ribonucleocapsids (RNPs). The genome encodes 6-10 proteins. Virion proteins include nucleocapsid protein (N), phosphoprotein (P), large protein (L), matrix protein (M), fusion protein (F), and receptor-binding protein (RBP). RNA-directed RNA polymerase and mRNA guanylyl- and methyltransferases are encoded in the L protein. Evolutionary Context: Belongs to the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthrnavirae, phylum Negarnaviricota, class Monjiviricetes, order Mononegavirales. Contains 9 subfamilies, 23 genera, and 153 species. Shares a similar gene expression, replication strategy, and gene order with filoviruses and rhabdoviruses. Host/Ecology: Infects mammals, birds, reptiles, and fish. Transmission is horizontal, mainly through direct contact and airborne routes. No vectors are known. Infection typically begins in the respiratory tract and may spread to secondary sites. Some viruses exhibit narrow host ranges, while others can infect a broader range of cultured cells. Infections can be lytic, temperate, or persistent.

name: Retroviridae
info: Family: Retroviridae Genome Characteristics: Retroviruses possess a diploid genome consisting of two identical molecules of linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA, typically 7-13 kb in length. Spumaretroviruses contain some dsDNA due to reverse transcription within the virion. The RNA monomers are capped, polyadenylated, and associated with a tRNA primer. The genome encodes Gag (structural proteins), Pro (protease), Pol (reverse transcriptase and integrase), and Env (envelope proteins). Some retroviruses contain additional regulatory or accessory genes, or oncogenes. The proviral DNA form contains long terminal repeats (LTRs). Evolutionary Context: Retroviruses are classified within the order Ortervirales, sharing evolutionary relationships with Caulimoviridae, Metaviridae, Pseudoviridae, and Belpaoviridae. Genus demarcation is based on phylogenetic analysis of reverse transcriptase, presence/absence of regulatory proteins, Env protein characteristics, and host association (for Spumaretrovirinae). Endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) provide insights into retroviral evolution. Host/Ecology: Retroviruses infect a wide variety of vertebrate hosts and are globally distributed. Transmission occurs horizontally (e.g., blood, sexual contact) and vertically (e.g., germline inheritance of ERVs). Retroviruses are associated with various diseases, including malignancies, immunodeficiencies, and autoimmune disorders. Some retroviruses are non-pathogenic.

name: Hepadnaviridae
info: Family: Hepadnaviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome consists of partially double-stranded DNA, approximately 3.0-3.4 kb in size. It is circular due to a cohesive overlap. The genome contains three or four open reading frames (precore/core, polymerase, env/surface, and X in orthohepadnaviruses). Replication occurs via reverse transcription of a pregenomic RNA within nucleocapsids in the cytoplasm. Evolutionary Context: The family belongs to the realm Riboviria, order Blubervirales, based on reverse transcriptase homology with RNA viruses. Genera are distinguished by nucleotide sequence divergence, genome size, core protein size, presence of MHBs surface protein, X protein essentiality, and host range. There are five genera: Parahepadnavirus, Metahepadnavirus, Herpetohepadnavirus, Avihepadnavirus, and Orthohepadnavirus. Host/Ecology: Hepadnaviruses infect a range of hosts: teleost fish (Parahepadnavirus, Metahepadnavirus), reptiles and frogs (Herpetohepadnavirus), birds (Avihepadnavirus), and mammals (Orthohepadnavirus). Infections are hepatotropic and can be transient or persistent. Transmission patterns vary depending on the virus and host. Persistent infections can lead to high levels of virions and subviral particles in the blood.

name: Arteriviridae
info: Arteriviridae is a family of viruses with spherical, enveloped virions, 50-74 nm in diameter, containing a linear, positive-sense RNA genome of 12.7-15.7 kb. The genome is multi-cistronic, encoding nonstructural proteins (nsps) from ORF1a and ORF1b, and structural proteins from 3'-ORFs. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm on double-membrane vesicles derived from the endoplasmic reticulum, mediated by a viral ribonucleoprotein transmembrane complex. Discontinuous transcription produces subgenomic mRNAs. Taxonomic demarcation is based on evolutionary distances of five replicative protein domains: 3CLpro, NiRAN, RdRp, ZBD, and HEL1. The family includes six subfamilies, thirteen genera, eleven subgenera, and twenty-three species. Arteriviruses infect vertebrates, predominantly mammals, without vector involvement. Infection can be asymptomatic or cause overt disease. Host range varies, with some members infecting specific species like horses (equine arteritis virus), pigs (porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus), mice (lactate dehydrogenase-elevating virus), monkeys (simian hemorrhagic fever virus), and marsupials (wobbly possum disease virus). Geographical distribution is worldwide. Transmission patterns vary, with some viruses establishing persistent infections in reproductive tracts or lymph nodes. Key conserved domains include a zinc finger, papain-like proteinases (PLPs), a chymotrypsin-like serine proteinase (SP), a nidovirus RNA-polymerase associated nucleotidyl-transferase (NiRAN), an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRp), a nidovirus conserved zinc binding domain (ZBD), an NTPase/RNA helicase (HEL1), a nidovirus uridylate-specific endoribonuclease (NendoU), and an arterivirus-specific replicase subunit (AsD). NiRAN and ZBD are conserved in all nidoviruses.

name: Sedoreoviridae
info: Family: Sedoreoviridae Genome Characteristics: dsRNA, segmented linear genome of 10-12 segments, totaling 18-26 kbp. Segments range from 0.6-5.8 kbp. Each segment has a 5′-terminal cap but no 3′-poly(A) tail. Viral RNAs are mostly monogenic. The transcriptionally active core particle is made of two protein layers. The inner layer contains 120 copies of a single protein with T=2 symmetry. The outer layer contains 780 copies of another single protein with T=13 symmetry. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation relies on genome segment number, host range, disease signs, capsid structure, and sequence divergence (RdRP amino acid identity <26% between genera, >30% within a genus). Species demarcation considers reassortment capability, sequence similarity, serological comparisons, electropherotype analysis (AGE), and conserved terminal regions of genome segments. Closely related to Spinareoviridae within the order Reovirales. Host/Ecology: Host range includes mammals, birds, crustaceans, arthropods, algae, and plants. Virus cell entry varies between genera but usually results in loss of outer-capsid components. Replication occurs in cytoplasmic viroplasms. Progeny virions are released from some cell types without compromising cell viability (e.g., budding), or from other types of cells following cell lysis. Biological properties vary by genus.

name: Spinareoviridae
info: Family: Spinareoviridae Genome Characteristics: The Spinareoviridae family comprises viruses with segmented, linear, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genomes, ranging from 23 to 29 kbp, divided into 9-12 segments (0.5-4.8 kbp each). The positive-sense strand of each segment has a 5' cap but lacks a 3' poly(A) tail. Viral RNAs are mostly monocistronic. Replication occurs in cytoplasmic viral inclusions (viroplasms). Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation relies on genome segment number, host range, disease signs, capsid structure, and sequence divergence (especially RdRP). Genus demarcation typically shows <26% amino acid identity in RdRP comparisons, while species demarcation considers genetic exchange capacity, sequence similarity, serological comparisons, electropherotype analysis, and conserved terminal regions. Spinareoviridae is closely related to Sedoreoviridae within the order Reovirales. Host/Ecology: Spinareoviridae viruses infect a broad range of hosts, including mammals, aquatic animals (fish, mammals, crustaceans, molluscs), birds, reptiles, arthropods, fungi, and plants. Transmission patterns and biological properties vary by genus. Some members, like cypoviruses, are occluded within proteinaceous crystals (polyhedra). Virus entry varies between genera but usually results in loss of outer-capsid components.

name: Anelloviridae
info: Family: Anelloviridae Genome Characteristics: Virions contain a single molecule of circular, negative-sense ssDNA, ranging from 2 to 3.9 kb. The genome includes a non-coding region with high G+C content (ca. 90%) and conserved sequences. Two main open reading frames, ORF1 and ORF2, are present, along with additional ORFs. ORF1 is believed to encode the capsid protein and replication-associated protein. ORF2 may encode a protein with phosphatase activity or suppress NF-κB pathways. Anelloviruses likely replicate via a rolling circle mechanism. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation is based on ORF1 nucleotide sequence analysis, with genus divergence >56% and species divergence >35%. Anelloviruses share similarities with Circoviridae, including circular ssDNA genomes, similar genome organization, and conserved motifs in capsid proteins and ORF2. Host/Ecology: Anelloviruses have a global distribution and high prevalence (>90%) in the general population. They have been detected in humans, non-human primates, tupaia, pets, farm animals, and marine mammals. Transmission is suggested to occur through saliva droplets, blood transfusion, maternal routes, and sexual routes. The link between anellovirus infection and specific pathologies remains unproven.

name: Orthoherpesviridae
info: Orthoherpesviridae is a family of enveloped viruses with spherical virions containing a linear, double-stranded DNA genome of 125-241 kbp, encoding 70-170 genes. A core set of 43 genes is conserved across the family. Genome architecture varies, with classes defined by the presence and arrangement of terminal and internal repeats, influencing isomeric forms. Replication involves a lytic and latent phase, with transcription and DNA replication occurring in the nucleus.                     Orthoherpesviruses exhibit a broad host range, infecting mammals, birds, and reptiles. They typically coevolve with their hosts, establishing lifelong latent infections. Severe disease is usually limited to specific conditions such as fetal infection, immunocompromised individuals, or infection of alternative hosts. Transmission routes vary, including aerosol spread, oral contact, sexual contact, and airborne dander. Some members can be transmitted via the host germ line.                     Taxonomic demarcation within the Orthoherpesviridae family relies on genetic content, epidemiological and biological characteristics, and genome sequence analysis. The family is classified within the order Herpesvirales, alongside Alloherpesviridae and Malacoherpesviridae, based on virion morphology and conservation of DNA packaging terminase subunits. Evolutionary relationships extend to bacteriophages in the order Caudovirales. The family exhibits distant relationships with cellular genes, likely acquired through capture or convergent evolution.

name: Adenoviridae
info: Adenoviridae is a family of non-enveloped viruses with icosahedral virions containing linear, double-stranded DNA genomes ranging from 25 to 48 kb. The genome has inverted terminal repeats and a covalently linked terminal protein. Approximately 40 viral polypeptides are produced, with about one-third composing the virion. The family is divided into six genera: Mastadenovirus (mammals), Aviadenovirus (birds), Ichtadenovirus (fish), Testadenovirus (turtles), Barthadenovirus (squamate reptiles, birds, ruminants, marsupials, tortoises), and Siadenovirus (birds, frog, tortoise). Host range varies among genera, and infections range from subclinical to lethal. Adenoviruses infect a wide range of vertebrate hosts, from fish to humans, with some members capable of crossing host species barriers. Transmission occurs directly or indirectly via throat, feces, eye, urine, or fomites, depending on the virus type. Geographical distribution is worldwide, reflecting the broad host range. Genus demarcation is based on phylogenetic distance, genome organization, and host range. Adenoviruses share evolutionary links with bacteriophages (e.g., Enterobacteria phage PRD1) and linear plasmids in fungi and plants, indicated by similar virion architecture and conserved genes. Higher taxonomic classification places Adenoviridae within the realm Varidnaviria, kingdom Bamfordvirae, phylum Preplasmiviricota, subphylum Polisuviricotina, class Pharingeaviricetes, and order Rowavirales.

name: Benyviridae
info: Family: Benyviridae Genome Characteristics: The Benyviridae family possesses multipartite, single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genomes. Genomes are capped at the 5' end (m7G) and polyadenylated at the 3' end. Genome size varies among members, with beet necrotic yellow vein virus (BNYVV) having four or five linear RNAs ranging from approximately 1.3 to 6.7 kb. Viral replicase undergoes post-translational cleavage. Conserved 3' structures are essential for RNA replication initiation. Evolutionary Context: Benyviridae is classified within the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Kitrinoviricota, class Alsuviricetes, and order Hepelivirales. The family currently contains one genus and four species. Host/Ecology: Benyviridae members infect plants. BNYVV and beet soil-borne mosaic virus (BSBMV) naturally infect Beta vulgaris. Experimental hosts include Chenopodium species. Transmission occurs via root-infecting vectors in the family Plasmodiphorales (Cercozoa), such as Polymyxa betae for BNYVV and BSBMV, and Polymyxa graminis for rice stripe necrosis virus (RSNV). Mechanical transmission is also possible. BNYVV is globally distributed in sugar beet-growing regions. BSBMV is found in the United States. RSNV occurs in Africa, South and Central America. Burdock mottle virus (BdMV) has been identified in Japan. BNYVV causes rhizomania disease in sugar beet.

name: Casjensviridae
info: Casjensviridae (taxid:2943001) GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: dsDNA, linear genome of approximately 59 kb, containing about 75 genes. Genome has cohesive ends. Key enzymes encoded include DNA polymerase I, DNA primase, protease (Peptidase S49), terminase, and phosphoadenosine phosphosulphate reductase. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not specified. HOST/ECOLOGY: Host Range: Bacteria. Bacteriophage chi attaches to the filament of a bacterial flagellum, with the entry receptor site located at the base of the flagellum. Geographical Distribution: Worldwide. Transmission: Passive diffusion through medium. Replication: Cytoplasmic. Adsorption to host cell adhesion receptors via tail fibers. Ejection of viral DNA into host cytoplasm via long flexible tail ejection system. Transcription and translation of early genes, followed by genomic DNA replication, and transcription/translation of late genes. Assembly of an empty procapsid, genome packaging, tail fiber and tail assembly. Mature virions released by lysis. Virion Structure: Non-enveloped, head-tail structure with Sipho-type morphology. Icosahedral head is about 66 nm in diameter. Non-contractile tail is about 220-230 nm in length and 13 nm in width with about 55 cross-striations. Extremely long tail fiber measuring approximately 200-220 nm in length. Antiviral Drugs: None specified.

name: Bromoviridae
info: Family: Bromoviridae Genome Characteristics: The Bromoviridae family comprises plant viruses with tri-segmented, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genomes, totaling approximately 8 kb. The 5' ends possess cap structures, while the 3' ends, though not polyadenylated, exhibit conserved secondary structures, sometimes tRNA-like. Genomes are packaged in separate virions. RNA1 and RNA2 encode replicase components (1a and 2a proteins). RNA3 encodes a movement protein (3a) and coat protein (CP), expressed from a subgenomic RNA. Evolutionary Context: Bromoviridae belongs to the "alpha-like" supergroup, sharing sequence similarities in replicase domains with Virgaviridae and Togaviridae. Genera are demarcated based on host range, transmission, morphology, genome structure, and ability to support defective/satellite RNAs. Host/Ecology: The host range varies from narrow to broad, affecting fruit, vegetable, and fodder crops like tomato, cucurbits, bananas, and alfalfa. Transmission occurs mechanically, via pollen, seeds, and non-persistently by insect vectors. Virions are spherical or bacilliform. Replication occurs on cytoplasmic membranes. The coat protein (CP) is involved in systemic movement and may be required for cell-to-cell spread, virus expression and replication or activation of replication.

name: Ackermannviridae
info: Ackermannviridae: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Linear, dsDNA genome of approximately 155 kb, encoding 190-216 proteins and 1-7 tRNAs. Genes are transcribed by operons. Encodes DNA-directed DNA polymerase B, cysteine proteases (Peptidase C51, Peptidase S77), endonuclease, topoisomerase, and ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria not specified. HOST/ECOLOGY: Infects bacteria. Geographical distribution is worldwide. Transmission occurs via passive diffusion through the medium. No antiviral drugs are available. VIRION STRUCTURE: Non-enveloped with a head-tail structure exhibiting Myo-type morphology. Icosahedral head is ~93 nm in diameter. Features a neck without a collar and a small base plate. Contractile tail is ~140 nm in width and ~20 nm in length. Tail fibers are ~38 nm in length. REPLICATION: Cytoplasmic replication cycle. Adsorption via tail fibers. DNA ejection into host cytoplasm via tail sheath contraction. Early and late gene transcription/translation. Genome replication. Procapsid assembly and genome packaging. Tail fiber and tail assembly. Virion release via cell lysis.

name: Microviridae
info: Family: Microviridae Genome Characteristics: Circular, positive-sense, single-stranded DNA genomes. Genome size varies by genus: Microvirus (5.3-6.1 kb), Gokushovirus (4.4-4.9 kb). Genome arrangement is highly conserved within genera (Microvirus, Chlamydiamicrovirus). Bdellomicrovirus φMH2K genome organization is similar to Chlamydiamicrovirus, except for gene 5 location. Sequence similarities and structural analyses provide insights into viral proteins across genera. Evolutionary Context: ssDNA genome organization is similar to Inoviridae. Structural similarities exist with Parvoviridae, particularly in capsid protein interactions at three-fold symmetry axes. Antibodies often cross-react with other genus members. Host/Ecology: Host Range: Microvirus: Enterobacteria. Chlamydiamicrovirus and Bdellomicrovirus: Intracellular parasitic bacteria. Spiromicrovirus: Spiroplasma. Microvirus phages are sensitive to host cell alleles of rep, slyD, and mraY. Some proteins exhibit cross-functional or cross-inhibitory properties. PhiX174 utilizes LPS as a cell receptor. Geographical Distribution: Worldwide. Transmission: Not specified. Antiviral Drugs: None reported.

name: Coronaviridae
info: Family: Coronaviridae Genome Characteristics:  Nucleic acid type: Positive-sense, single-stranded RNA.  Genome size: 26-32 kb, linear, unimolecular.  Organization: 5′-UTR-replicase-S-M-N-UTR-3′. Genome functions as mRNA for the replicase gene.  Key conserved domains: ADP-ribose-1″-phosphatase (ADRP), 3CLpro, RdRp, Helicase (Hel), ExoN, NendoU, O-MT. Replicase gene comprised of overlapping ORFs 1a and 1b, coding for polyproteins pp1a and pp1ab. Evolutionary Context:  Taxonomic demarcation: Based on rooted phylogeny and pairwise evolutionary distances of conserved replicase domains (ADRP, nsp5, nsp12, nsp13, nsp14, nsp15, nsp16).  Genus demarcation: Phylogenetic outliers sharing <46% sequence identity in conserved replicase domains may represent a new genus.  Species demarcation: >90% amino acid sequence identity in conserved replicase domains indicates the same species. Host/Ecology:  Host range: Mammals, birds, and fish.  Geographical distribution: Not specified.  Transmission: Virions attach to host cell receptors via spikes, genome released via membrane fusion. Replication cycle in cytoplasm.

name: Torovirus
info: Genus: Torovirus Genome Characteristics: The torovirus genome consists of a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA molecule, approximately 28 kb in length. The genome is capped and polyadenylated, and infectious upon transfection into mammalian cells. Encodes structural proteins S, HE, M, and N. The HE protein is dispensable for replication in vitro. Evolutionary Context: Host preference has been a primary criterion for species demarcation. Phylogenetic analyses support the distinction of bovine, equine, and porcine toroviruses. Recombination events have been observed, suggesting cross-species transmission. The existence of human torovirus remains uncertain. Host/Ecology: Known hosts include ungulates: horses (equine torovirus), cattle (bovine torovirus), and swine (porcine torovirus). Serological evidence suggests possible infection in goats and sheep. Claims of infection in humans, turkeys, and carnivores require further confirmation. Toroviruses have a worldwide distribution. Transmission likely occurs via the oral/nasal route through contact with contaminated feces or nasopharyngeal secretions. Bovine torovirus is an established respiratory and enteric pathogen of cattle, while equine and porcine toroviruses are associated with asymptomatic enteric infections.

name: Alphacoronavirus
info: Genus: Alphacoronavirus Genome Characteristics: Alphacoronaviruses possess a distinct nsp1, differing in size and sequence from betacoronavirus nsp1, with no apparent counterpart in deltacoronaviruses or gammacoronaviruses. They also contain an accessory gene, typically ORF3, encoding a dispensable multi-spanning alphacoronavirus membrane protein (αmp). Some members have up to six accessory genes. Forms a monophyletic group within the Orthocoronavirinae subfamily. Evolutionary Context: Alphacoronaviruses are demarcated as a distinct monophyletic group within the Orthocoronavirinae subfamily based on phylogenetic relationships and unique genomic characteristics. Host/Ecology: Alphacoronaviruses infect a wide range of mammals, including bats, pigs, humans, rats, mink, and shrews. Specific subgenera exhibit host preferences: Colacovirus, Decacovirus, Duvinacovirus, Minuacovirus, Myotacovirus, Nyctacovirus, Pedacovirus, Rhinacovirus and Setracovirus infect bats. Pedacovirus and Rhinacovirus can cause enteric diseases in pigs. Human coronavirus 229E (subgenus Duvinacovirus) and human coronavirus NL63 (subgenus Setracovirus) are members of this genus. Other members include Lucheng Rn rat coronavirus (Luchacovirus), Mink coronavirus (Minacovirus), Common shrew coronavirus Tibet-2014 (Soracovirus), Suncus murinus coronavirus Xingguo-74 (Sunacovirus). Alphacoronavirus 1 (Tegacovirus) infects dogs, cats, and pigs.

name: Bafinivirus
info: Genome Characteristics: Bafinivirus contains a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genome of approximately 26.6 kb. The genome is capped, polyadenylated, and infectious. It encodes five open reading frames (ORFs): ORF1a, ORF1b (replicase), ORF2 (spike protein S), ORF3 (membrane protein M), and ORF4 (nucleocapsid protein N). The replicase gene is composed of ORF1a and ORF1b. Structural proteins are expressed from three subgenomic (sg) mRNAs that are 3' co-terminal with the genome. A conserved nonanucleotide sequence, CA(G/A)CACUAC, is located upstream of each structural protein gene. The spike protein S is a glycosylated type I membrane glycoprotein with features of class I fusion proteins. The membrane protein M is a glycosylated integral membrane protein with three predicted transmembrane regions. The nucleocapsid protein N is a basic protein. Evolutionary Context: Viruses are assigned to the genus Bafinivirus based on rooted phylogeny and pairwise comparisons of Coronaviridae-wide conserved domains in replicase polyprotein pp1ab. Host/Ecology: Bafinivirus has been isolated from white bream (Blicca bjoerkna), a freshwater fish species (family Cyprinidae). The virus has been found in Europe. Virions assemble through budding at intracellular membranes of the ER and/or Golgi complex and egress via exocytosis. Transmission patterns and detailed ecological and pathogenic properties are not well-established.

name: Mesyanzhinovviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: dsDNA, circular genome of approximately 60 kb, containing about 77 genes. Encodes DNA-dependent DNA polymerase A. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not specified. HOST/ECOLOGY: Host Range: Bacteria. Geographical Distribution: Passive diffusion through medium. Transmission: Passive diffusion through medium. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm. Adsorption to host cell adhesion receptors via tail fibers. Viral DNA is ejected into the host cytoplasm via a long flexible tail ejection system. The DNA genome is circularized or integrated into the host chromosome. Early and late genes are transcribed and translated. Genomic DNA replication occurs. An empty procapsid is assembled, and the genome is packaged. Viral tail fiber and tail assembly occur. Mature virions are released by cell lysis. Virion: Non-enveloped with a head-tail structure and Sipho-type morphology. The prolate head measures approximately 72 by 51 nm, and the tail length is about 145 nm. Antiviral Drugs: None specified.

name: Redondoviridae
info: Family: Redondoviridae Genome Characteristics: Redondoviruses possess circular, single-stranded DNA genomes of approximately 3.0 kb. The genome contains three open reading frames (ORFs): one encoding a capsid protein (Cp), another encoding a replication-associated protein (Rep), and a third ORF with no known homology. A stem-loop structure with a conserved nonanucleotide motif is present upstream of the Rep coding sequence, likely serving as the origin of replication. The Rep protein contains rolling-circle replication (RCR) endonuclease and superfamily 3 helicase (SF3) domains. Evolutionary Context: Redondoviruses are classified within the realm Monodnaviria, kingdom Shotokuvirae, phylum Cressdnaviricota, class Arfiviricetes, and order Recrevirales. Taxonomic demarcation is based on genome characteristics and protein sequence identity. Host/Ecology: The definitive host range of redondoviruses is not fully established, but they are inferred to replicate primarily in humans. They have been predominantly detected in oro-respiratory specimens, and less frequently in the gut. Geographical distribution is widespread, with detection in various human populations. Transmission patterns are not well-defined, but persistent colonization or infection is suggested by detection over extended periods in some individuals. Redondovirus DNA levels are associated with periodontitis and critical illness, but their etiological role remains unproven. Co-occurrence with Anelloviridae members has been observed, but the significance is undetermined.

name: Drexlerviridae
info: Family: Drexlerviridae Genome Characteristics: dsDNA, linear genome of approximately 50 kb, terminally redundant and circularly permuted, containing about 80 genes. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria not explicitly assessed in provided information. Host/Ecology: Host Range: Bacteria. Receptor: FhuA. Geographical Distribution: Worldwide. Transmission: Passive diffusion through medium. Replication: Cytoplasmic. Attachment via tail fibers to FhuA receptor. Viral DNA ejected into host cytoplasm. Early gene transcription and translation. Genomic DNA replication, forming concatemers. Late gene transcription and translation. Procapsid assembly and genome packaging via headful mechanism. Tail fiber and tail assembly. Virion release via cell lysis. Virion: Non-enveloped, head-tail structure with Sipho-type morphology. Head diameter approximately 60 nm. Non-contractile, flexible tail approximately 151 nm long and 8 nm wide, with 4 short kinked terminal fibers. Antiviral Drugs: None reported.

name: Peduoviridae
info: Family: Peduoviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, double-stranded DNA genome of approximately 34 kb, encoding about 45 proteins. Genome has cohesive ends (cos sites). Genes are transcribed by operons. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation based on shared genomic and structural features. Host/Ecology: Host Range: Bacteria. Geographical Distribution: Worldwide. Transmission: Passive diffusion through medium. Virion Structure and Morphology: Non-enveloped, head-tail structure with Myo-type morphology. Icosahedral head is about 60 nm, with T=7 dextro symmetry, composed of 72 capsomers. Contractile tail is about 135 x 18 nm, with 6 short kinked fibers. Replication: Cytoplasmic. Adsorption to host cell via tail fibers. Viral DNA ejection into host cytoplasm via tail sheath contraction. Early gene transcription and translation. Synthesis of linear concatemers of viral DNA by rolling circle replication. Late gene transcription and translation. Assembly of procapsid and genome packaging. Viral tail fiber and tail assembly. Virion release by cell lysis. Enzymes: Serine protease (Peptidase S73), Integrase. Antiviral Drugs: None.

name: Deltaflexiviridae
info: Family: Deltaflexiviridae Genome Characteristics: RNA(+), single-stranded. Genome size is approximately 6-8 kb, capped and polyadenylated. Encodes an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). Replication involves dsRNA intermediates. Possible subgenome-sized mRNA for translation. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation is based on sequence analysis and phylogenetic relationships. Belongs to Realm Riboviria, Kingdom Orthornavirae, Phylum Kitrinoviricota, Class Alsuviricetes, Order Tymovirales. Contains one genus (Deltaflexivirus) and four species. Host/Ecology: Known host range is fungi. Geographical distribution is not specified. Transmission patterns are not established. Name Derivation: Deltaflexiviridae and Deltaflexivirus are derived from the Ancient Greek "delta" (number 4) and "flexi," referring to its origin as the fourth family created from the division of the old Flexiviridae family. The suffixes "-viridae" and "-virus" denote family and genus taxa, respectively. Source: ICTV (Interim Report, established 2018, Master Species List #32) Type: Family

name: Peribunyaviridae
info: Family: Peribunyaviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome consists of three distinct, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA segments, totaling 10.7-12.5 kb. These segments encode the nucleocapsid protein (N), envelope glycoproteins (Gn and Gc), and an RNA-directed RNA polymerase/endonuclease (L protein). Conserved terminal sequences facilitate panhandle structure formation. Some viruses encode non-structural proteins (NSs, NSm). Evolutionary Context: Genera are monophyletic based on L protein analysis, sharing genomic organization and transmission cycles. Phylogenetically related to Fimoviridae and Tospoviridae. Genus demarcation is based on L protein phylogeny, NSs/NSm encoding, and Gc protein truncation. Host/Ecology: Primarily maintained in vertebrate-arthropod transmission cycles, including transovarial transmission in arthropods. Some are arthropod-specific. Host and geographic ranges are generally restricted, with some overlap. Human infection occurs via arthropod vectors, leading to diverse clinical outcomes. Found on every continent except Antarctica. Additional Information: Virions are enveloped, spherical or pleomorphic, 80-120 nm in diameter. Replication is cytoplasmic, involving "cap snatching." Gn and Gc proteins mediate host cell attachment and entry via endocytosis. The L protein functions in transcription and replication. Genetic reassortment occurs. Orthobunyavirus Gn and Gc proteins elicit neutralizing antibodies. The family includes eight genera: Orthobunyavirus, Gryffinivirus, Herbevirus, Khurdivirus, Lakivirus, Lambavirus, Pacuvirus, and Shangavirus.

name: Alternaviridae
info: Family: Alternaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Alternaviridae family comprises viruses with double-stranded (ds) RNA genomes. The genome consists of 3-4 dsRNA molecules, ranging from 8.4 to 10.7 kbp. These segments encode RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP), capsid protein, and proteins with unknown functions. The dsRNA is multipartite, polyadenylated, and likely capped. Virions are isometric, approximately 33 nm in diameter. Evolutionary Context: The family was established in 2023. Taxonomy: Realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Duplornaviricota, class Chrymotiviricetes, order Ghabrivirales. The family includes one genus (Alternavirus) and five species. The name Alternaviridae is derived from Alternaria alternata, the original fungal host, and RNA, referring to the nucleic acid type. Host/Ecology: Alternaviridae viruses infect fungi, specifically ascomycetes. The replication and translation mechanisms are currently unknown. Example species: Alternavirus alternariae, exemplified by Alternaria alternata virus 1.

name: Partitiviridae
info: Family: Partitiviridae Genome Characteristics: The Partitiviridae family comprises non-enveloped viruses with isometric virions, containing bisegmented dsRNA genomes ranging from 3 to 4.8 kbp. Each segment is individually encapsidated. The two essential genome segments, dsRNA1 and dsRNA2, each contain one large ORF. dsRNA1 encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP), and dsRNA2 encodes the coat protein (CP). Evolutionary Context: Partitiviridae is classified within the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Pisuviricota, class Duplopiviricetes, and order Durnavirales. Genus demarcation is based on host range (plants, fungi, or protozoa), genome segment/protein lengths, RdRP amino acid sequence identity (<24% between genera), and RdRP phylogenetic grouping. Similarities exist with Picobirnaviridae (bisegmented genomes, small capsids), but picobirnaviruses infect vertebrates. Host/Ecology: Partitiviruses infect plants, fungi, and protozoa. Genera Alphapartitivirus and Betapartitivirus include viruses from both plants and fungi; Gammapartitivirus infects only fungi; Deltapartitivirus infects only plants; and Cryspovirus infects only protozoa. Transmission occurs intracellularly via seeds (plants), oocysts (protozoa), or hyphal anastomosis, cell division, and sporogenesis (fungi). No natural vectors are known. Infections are typically persistent.

name: Discoviridae
info: Family: Discoviridae Genome Characteristics: Discoviridae are negative-sense RNA viruses with tri-segmented genomes ranging from 6.2 to 9.7 kb. The segments are designated S (1.1-1.2 kb), M (1.7-1.9 kb), and L (3.4-6.5 kb). The genome encodes a nucleoprotein (NP), a nonstructural (Ns) protein, and a large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Evolutionary Context: Discoviridae belongs to the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Negarnaviricota, class Bunyaviricetes, and order Hareavirales. They are related to bunyaviral arenavirids, leishbuvirids, mypovirids, nairovirids, phenuivirids, and wupedevirids. Species demarcation is based on <80% RdRP amino acid sequence identity. Host/Ecology: Discoviridae have been detected in fungi (Eurotiomycetes, Sordariomycetes, Dothideomycetes, Leotiomycetes) and stramenopiles (Peronosporaceae). Specific viruses have been found in Coniella diplodiella, Plasmopara viticola, Penicillium atramentosum, Penicillium roseopurpureum, and Oryza sativa. Geographical distribution includes Italy, Spain, USA and China. Transmission patterns are currently unknown. The family includes the genus Orthodiscovirus and six species.

name: Polymycoviridae
info: Family: Polymycoviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome consists of 4 to 8 linear, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) segments, totaling 7.5–12.5 kbp. Each segment is monocistronic. The RNA dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) contains conserved motifs (MSDITKWDANMC, YGCMPSGSFYTSLVNTTGNNL and YGDNQLFSEHL). The dsRNAs are coated by the intrinsically disordered proline-alanine-serine rich protein (PASrp; 18–32 kDa). Evolutionary Context: Belongs to the realm Riboviria. Related to Hadakaviridae, Astroviridae, Caliciviridae, Picornaviridae and Partitiviridae. The GDNQ motif, typically found in negative-sense ssRNA viruses of the order Monogenavirales, is conserved in the RdRPs encoded by all members of Polymycoviridae. Host/Ecology: Infects fungi (ascomycetes and basidiomycetes) and oomycetes. Lacks an extracellular phase, transmitted intracellularly during cell division and sporogenesis (vertical transmission) and by cell fusion (horizontal transmission). Virions accumulate in the cytoplasm. Polymycovirus infection has been associated with various morphological alterations in the host cells, decreased host growth, and host virulence against plants, insects and mammals, or increased sporulation, host growth and host virulence in the greater wax moth. Taxonomic Demarcation: Contains one genus, Polymycovirus, including 10 species. Genus demarcation is based on virus classification within the family Polymycoviridae.

name: Xinmoviridae
info: Family: Xinmoviridae Genome Characteristics: Negative-sense RNA, 10-16 kb in size. Contains 3-6 ORFs encoding a glycoprotein, nucleoprotein, and RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP). Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation is based on RdRP amino acid identity. Genera have RdRP identities of 60% or less. Species within a genus have RdRP identities of 66% or less. Closely related to Bornaviridae and Nyamiviridae within the order Mononegavirales. Host/Ecology: Typically infects beneficial and pest insects. Detected in insects from Africa, Asia, Europe, and Oceania. May infect insects of more than 12 orders, including Blattodea, Coleoptera, Diptera, Hemiptera, Hymenoptera, Lepidoptera, Mantodea, Neuroptera, Odonata, Orthoptera, Psocodea, Trichoptera, and Zygentoma. Host range and geographic distribution may be broader than currently known. Taxonomy: Realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Negarnaviricota, class Monjiviricetes, order Mononegavirales. Contains 22 genera and 25 species.

name: Polyomaviridae
info: Family: Polyomaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Polyomaviridae family consists of small, non-enveloped viruses with approximately 5 kbp circular double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) genomes. Genome size varies across species, ranging from 3,962 bp to 7,369 bp. Genomes encode early regulatory proteins (large tumor antigen (LTAg) and small tumor antigen (STAg)) and late capsid proteins (VP1, VP2, VP3). Some members encode additional proteins like ALTO, MTAg, VP4, or agnoprotein. The genome contains early and late transcriptional regions separated by a non-coding control region (NCCR). Evolutionary Context: Phylogenetic relationships are determined based on LTAg amino acid sequences. The family includes 122 species classified into 6 genera: Alphapolyomavirus, Betapolyomavirus, Gammapolyomavirus, Deltapolyomavirus, Epsilonpolyomavirus, and Zetapolyomavirus. Recombination events have shaped polyomavirus evolution. Host/Ecology: Polyomaviruses infect mammals, birds, and fish. Each member typically has a restricted host range. Some are human and veterinary pathogens, causing symptomatic infection or cancer, primarily in immunocompromised individuals. Human polyomaviruses include BKPyV (associated with nephropathy), JCPyV (associated with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy), and MCPyV (linked to Merkel cell carcinoma). Geographical distribution varies depending on the specific virus and host. Transmission patterns are not explicitly detailed but are likely related to host contact and shedding.

name: Papillomaviridae
info: Family: Papillomaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Papillomaviridae family comprises non-enveloped viruses with circular, double-stranded DNA genomes ranging from 5,748 to 8,607 base pairs. The GC content varies from 36% to 59%. Genomes are organized into early (E) and late (L) regions, encoding proteins involved in replication, transcription, and capsid formation, respectively. The upstream regulatory region (URR) contains the origin of replication and transcription factor binding sites. Key proteins include E1 (helicase), E2 (transcriptional regulator), E6 and E7 (cellular manipulation), L1 (major capsid protein), and L2 (minor capsid protein). Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic classification is primarily based on pairwise nucleotide sequence identity within the L1 open reading frame. Subfamilies are demarcated by less than 45% L1 sequence identity, while genera are delineated by phylogenetic analysis of concatenated E1, E2, L1, and L2 sequences. Genera within the Firstpapillomavirinae subfamily are named using the Greek alphabet, while those in the Secondpapillomavirinae use the Semitic abjad. Host/Ecology: Papillomaviruses infect a broad range of hosts, including mammals, reptiles, birds, and fish, primarily targeting mucosal and keratinized epithelia. Transmission occurs via skin-to-skin contact, with genital human papillomavirus (HPV) being a common sexually transmitted infection. Infections are often subclinical, but certain types, particularly within the Alphapapillomavirus genus, are associated with cancers. The virus evades the immune system, promoting persistence.

name: Genomoviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Family Genomoviridae; taxid:1910928. Non-enveloped, round virions with T=1 icosahedral symmetry, approximately 20 nm in diameter. Genome is monopartite, circular, single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) of about 2.17 kb. Coding regions present on both positive and negative sense strands. Contains a replication (Rep) protein that initiates and terminates rolling circle replication. Two intergenic regions separate the two open reading frames (ORFs). Short intergenic region contains bidirectional polyadenylation signals. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not specified. HOST/ECOLOGY: Natural hosts include humans, mammals, birds, and fungi. Virus attaches to host cell, and genomic DNA penetrates into the cytoplasm. Presumably the ssDNA is converted to dsDNA. Transcription is bidirectional from the long intergenic region (LIR) which contains two divergent promoters. The resulting transcripts encode a capsid protein and a replication-associated protein. Genome replication, possibly by rolling circle. Assembly and release of virions. Cress-type Endonuclease [Rep] is present. Host-virus interaction occurs via cell receptors.

name: Aliusviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Family Aliusviridae viruses possess non-segmented, linear, negative-sense RNA genomes ranging from 9.9 to 15.3 kb. Genomes contain two to four open reading frames (ORFs) encoding a glycoprotein (GP), nucleoprotein (NP), a large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain, and/or proteins of unknown function. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Aliusviridae is a family within the order Jingchuvirales. Genus demarcation is based on L protein sequence identity (<31%). Species demarcation is based on L protein sequence identity (<90%). HOST/ECOLOGY: Aliusviridae viruses have been found in coleopteran, dipteran, hemipteran, hymenopteran, and siphonapteran insects. They have been geographically identified in Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. Transmission patterns and replication cycle remain to be elucidated. Taxonomic Information: Realm: Riboviria Kingdom: Orthornavirae Phylum: Negarnaviricota Class: Monjiviricetes Order: Jingchuvirales Family: Aliusviridae Genera: Ollusvirus, Obscuruvirus Species: 12 species, including Ollusvirus culvertonense

name: Phasmaviridae
info: Family: Phasmaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Phasmaviridae family consists of negative-sense RNA viruses with tri-segmented genomes ranging from 9.7 to 15.8 kb. The three segments are designated small (S), medium (M), and large (L). The L segment encodes an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP). Viral mRNAs are capped but not polyadenylated, acquiring caps via cap-snatching from host mRNAs. Evolutionary Context: Viruses within the Phasmaviridae family are classified into seven genera based on phylogenetic analysis of the L protein/RdRP sequences. Species demarcation requires less than 95% amino acid identity in the L protein. The availability of coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for classification. Phasmaviridae is closely related to the crulivirids, fimovirids, hantavirids, peribunyavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids. Host/Ecology: Phasmaviruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by various insects, including blattodean, coleopteran, dipteran, hemipteran, hymenopteran, neuropteran, and odonatan insects. They are found in Africa, Asia, Europe, Northern America, and South America. Putative phasmavirids have been associated with branchiopods, collembolan hexapods, myriapods, zorapteran insects, eulipotyphla, mammals, plants, and fungi in Asia, Europe, Northern America, and Oceania.

name: Tospoviridae
info: Family: Tospoviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, segmented, negative-sense RNA genome. The genome consists of three segments: L (~8.8kb), M (~4.8kb), and S (~3kb). Encodes six proteins. mRNAs are capped via cap-snatching by the L protein but are not polyadenylated. The S and M segments utilize an ambisense strategy. Evolutionary Context: TaxID: 1980419. Host/Ecology: Natural hosts include plants and insect vectors. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm of both plant and insect cells. In plants, the virus enters via effraction or plasmodesmata transport. In insects, attachment is mediated by viral G glycoproteins, followed by membrane fusion. Transcription is performed by a viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (L). Replication starts when sufficient nucleoprotein is available for encapsidation. Transmission occurs via arthropod bite. Geographical distribution is not specified. Associated diseases include mosaic.

name: Tobaniviridae
info: Family: Tobaniviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, monopartite, single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome of approximately 28 kb. Genome is capped and polyadenylated. Encodes ORF1a and ORF1b (translated via ribosomal frameshifting), producing polyproteins pp1a and pp1ab, which are processed into viral polymerase (RdRp) and other non-structural proteins. Structural proteins are expressed from subgenomic RNAs. A putative 30K protein overlapping ORF1a may be expressed from an alternative CUG codon. Conserved domains include RNA-directed RNA polymerase, Nido-type capping enzymes (GDP polyribonucleotidyltransferase, N7methyltransferase, 2'O methylase), EndoU ribonuclease, and polyprotein major protease (Peptidase S75). Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not specified in source. Host/Ecology: Natural hosts include vertebrates: humans, cattle, pigs, horses, reptiles, and fish. Geographical distribution is worldwide. Transmission patterns not explicitly stated, but replication occurs in the cytoplasm involving endocytosis, membrane fusion, and exocytosis. Viral S protein (and HE if present) mediates endocytosis. Replication occurs in viral factories. Assembly and budding occur at membranes of the endoplasmic reticulum, intermediate compartments, and/or the Golgi complex. Virions are released by exocytosis. Virion is enveloped, spherical, 120-140nm in diameter, with a tubular nucleocapsid bent into an open torus.

name: Konkoviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Family Konkoviridae members possess segmented, linear, single-stranded negative-sense RNA (ssRNA(-)) genomes. Some viruses may have both ssRNA(-) and ssRNA(+/-) segments. The genome comprises 4 segments, ranging from 10.2 to 10.3 kb in total length, with pan-handle termini. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: The family Konkoviridae was established in 2024. It is classified within the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Negarnaviricota, subphylum Polyploviricotina, class Bunyaviricetes, and order Hareavirales. The family contains one genus, Olpivirus, and two species. Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment details are not provided. HOST/ECOLOGY: Konkoviridae members are known to infect plants. The type member, tulip streak virus, infects tulips and is transmitted by the fungal vector Olpidium. The geographical distribution and detailed transmission patterns of other members are not specified. ICTV Source.

name: Inoviridae
info: Family: Inoviridae Genome Characteristics: The Inoviridae family comprises viruses with non-enveloped, flexible filamentous virions, typically 6-10 nm in diameter and 600-2500 nm in length. The genome consists of a supercoiled, circular, positive-sense single-stranded DNA ((+) ssDNA) molecule, ranging from 5.5 to 10.6 kb. Genomes encode 7-15 proteins. The GC content varies depending on the host. Genes are densely packed, with some overlapping or contained within larger genes. Genomes may contain insertion sequences and genes for latent stage regulation. Evolutionary Context: Inoviridae is classified within the realm Monodnaviria, kingdom Loebvirae, phylum Hofneiviricota, class Faserviricetes, and order Tubulavirales. Genus demarcation relies on significant similarity in DNA sequences (BLASTn) and the Zot and Coat B proteins. Genera differ by >50% in amino acid sequence of the major coat (CoaB; p8) and morphogenesis (Zot; p1) proteins. Shares similarities with Plectroviridae and Paulinoviridae. Host/Ecology: Inoviridae members infect Gram-negative bacteria, including Escherichia, Salmonella, Pseudomonas, Xanthomonas, Stenotrophomonas, Vibrio, and Ralstonia. Adsorption occurs via bacterial pili. Replication proceeds through a rolling-circle mechanism, with virions released by extrusion without host cell lysis, establishing a chronic productive infection. Phage DNA can persist extrachromosomally or integrate into the bacterial genome. Some phages encode virulence factors or influence bacterial fitness. Prophages are frequently detected in bacterial genomes.

name: Tombusviridae
info: Family: Tombusviridae Genome Characteristics: Virions contain single-stranded, positive-sense, linear RNA, typically 3.7 to 4.8 kb, except Dianthovirus which has two segments (3.8 kb and 1.4 kb). Genomes are uncapped at the 5' end and lack polyadenylation at the 3' end. Double-stranded RNAs corresponding to genomic and subgenomic RNAs are found in infected tissues. Defective interfering RNAs and satellite RNAs/viruses may be present. Capsids are composed of a single coat protein subunit, ranging from 25-30 kDa or 37-48 kDa depending on the genus. A conserved RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) domain is present, interrupted by a termination codon or frameshifting element. Evolutionary Context: RdRp is related to those of Luteovirus and Umbravirus. Coat proteins of Necrovirus are related to Sobemovirus. Dianthovirus movement protein is related to movement proteins of several other virus families. Host/Ecology: Natural host range is relatively narrow, infecting either monocots or dicots. Experimental host range is wider. Infections may be localized or systemic, often causing necrosis, mottling, or deformation. Transmitted by mechanical inoculation, plant material, contact, and seeds. Some members are transmitted by fungi (Olpidium) or beetles. Geographical distribution varies, with most species in temperate regions. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm within membranous vesicles associated with endoplasmic reticulum or modified organelles. Virions accumulate in high concentrations in cells, often with "multivesicular bodies".

name: Tombusvirus
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Tombusvirus has a linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome of approximately 4.7-4.8 kb. The genome contains four open reading frames (ORFs). ORF1 encodes a 32-36 kDa protein and a readthrough product of 92-95 kDa, both involved in RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) activity. ORF2 encodes the coat protein (CP), expressed from a 2.2 kb subgenomic RNA (sgRNA). ORFs 3 and 4, located at the 3' terminus, encode proteins of approximately 22 kDa (p22) and 19 kDa (p19), respectively, and are expressed from a 0.9 kb sgRNA. The 3' terminus lacks a poly(A) tail or tRNA-like structure. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Species demarcation criteria include serological relationships, less than 85% CP sequence identity, differential cytopathological features (organelle origin of multivesicular bodies), and natural/artificial host range. HOST/ECOLOGY: Tombusviruses infect a wide range of monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plants. Most species have a narrow natural host range but a wider experimental host range. They are readily transmitted mechanically and are primarily soil-borne. Cucumber necrosis virus (CNV) is transmitted by the fungus Olpidium bornovanus. Tombusviruses are found globally, wherever their primary hosts exist, with diseases prevailing in temperate climates. Virions are found in various parts of the host cell, including the cytoplasm, nuclei, and mitochondria. A characteristic cytopathic effect is the formation of multivesicular bodies (MVBs).

name: Dianthovirus
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Dianthoviruses possess a bipartite, linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome. The genome consists of two RNA molecules, approximately 3.8 kb (RNA1) and 1.4 kb (RNA2). RNA1 encodes the viral polymerase via ribosomal frameshifting, producing 27 kDa and 88 kDa proteins, and the coat protein (CP) from a 1.5 kb subgenomic RNA (sgRNA). RNA2 encodes a 34-35 kDa movement protein (MP). The MP amino acid sequence is unique to dianthoviruses. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria include serological relationships, sequence identity of gene products (less than 93% amino acid identity in the polymerase and less than 75% in the CP), ability to form pseudorecombinants, soil transmission, natural host range, and artificial host range. HOST/ECOLOGY: Dianthoviruses infect dicotyledonous plants, with a moderately broad natural host range. Experimental host range is broader, including Solanaceae, Leguminosae, Cucurbitaceae, and Compositae. Infections are typically local (non-systemic). Viruses are transmitted mechanically and through the soil without a biological vector. Geographical distribution is widespread throughout temperate regions. Virions are approximately 37 nm in diameter with T=3 icosahedral symmetry. They sediment at 126-135S, with a buoyant density of 1.363-1.366 g/cm3.

name: Aureusvirus
info: Aureusvirus Genus Summary Genome Characteristics: Aureusviruses possess a single molecule of linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome, approximately 4.2-4.4 kb in size. The genome is uncapped and non-polyadenylated, constituting about 17% of the virion weight. The genome contains four open reading frames (ORFs). Two subgenomic RNAs (sgRNAs) of approximately 2.0 kb and 0.8 kb are produced. Key conserved domains show similarity to Tombusviruses, particularly in the polymerase and pre-readthrough regions. Evolutionary Context: Species demarcation criteria within the genus include serological specificity, sequence identity of gene products (less than 40% amino acid identity for the coat protein and less than 80% for the polymerase), differential cytopathological features, vector transmission, natural host range, and artificial host range reactions. Host/Ecology: Aureusviruses infect a range of plant hosts. Pothos latent virus (PoLV) naturally infects Pothos (Scindapsus aureus) and pigeonpea (Cajanus cajan), while cucumber leaf spot virus (CLSV) infects cucumber (Cucumis sativus). Maize white line mosaic virus (MWLMV) infects sweet corn. Experimental host range can be moderately wide. Geographical distribution includes several European countries, Canada, the US, Jordan, and India. Transmission occurs through the soil, with or without the aid of a vector. CLSV is transmitted by the fungus Olpidium bornovanus, and MWLMV may be transmitted by the protist Polymyxa graminis. Mechanical inoculation can also transmit PoLV and CLSV.

name: Avenavirus
info: Genus: Avenavirus Genome Characteristics: The genome consists of a single-stranded positive-sense RNA molecule of 4114 nucleotides. It contains three open reading frames (ORFs). ORF1 encodes a 23 kDa protein that can be readthrough to produce an 84 kDa polymerase. ORF2 encodes a 48 kDa coat protein (CP). ORF3, within ORF2, encodes a unique 8 kDa polypeptide. A single 3' co-terminal subgenomic RNA (sgRNA) of 1772 nucleotides is expressed. The CP is significantly larger (48K) than other Tombusviridae members, with limited amino acid sequence identity (11-28%). Evolutionary Context: The genus is distinguished by a unique genome organization intermediate between tombusviruses and carmoviruses. The 8K protein overlapping the CP ORF does not share sequence similarity to small proteins encoded by other Tombusviridae members. Host/Ecology: The known host range is limited to oats (Avena sativa). The virus has been reported only in the United Kingdom. It is readily transmitted mechanically from oat plant to oat plant. Infection patterns suggest soil-borne transmission, possibly by zoosporic fungi. The virus is a moderate immunogen, with no cross-reactivity observed with other icosahedral viruses of oats or representative members of Carmovirus and Machlomovirus genera. Virions are isometric, approximately 35 nm in diameter, with presumed T=3 icosahedral symmetry.

name: Carmovirus
info: Carmovirus: Genus Description Genome Characteristics: The Carmovirus genome consists of a single molecule of linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA, ranging from 3.9 to 4.5 kb. The genome contains four open reading frames (ORFs). ORF1 encodes a 28 kDa protein and an 88 kDa readthrough polymerase. ORFs 2 and 3 encode 7 kDa and 9 kDa proteins involved in cell-to-cell movement. ORF4 encodes a 38 kDa coat protein (CP) with a P domain. The genome is not capped and lacks a poly(A) tail. Evolutionary Context: Species demarcation criteria include serological relationships, sequence identity of gene products (less than 52% amino acid identity for CP, less than 57% for polymerase), cytopathological features (presence/absence of multivesicular bodies), fungal vector transmission, and natural/artificial host range. Host/Ecology: Carmoviruses infect a wide range of monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plants. Most species have a narrow natural host range but a wider experimental host range. Geographical distribution is likely worldwide, with most species found in temperate regions and those infecting legumes reported from tropical areas. Transmission occurs readily mechanically. Some species are seed-borne or soil-borne, and some are transmitted by the fungus Olpidium bornovanus or beetles (Coleoptera). Virion Properties: Virions are 32–35 nm in diameter with T=3 icosahedral symmetry. The buoyant density is 1.33–1.36 g cm−3 in CsCl, and the Mr is 8.2×106. Virions are composed of 180 identical protein subunits with R, S, and P structural domains. The CP subunit ranges from 35–42 kDa.

name: Necrovirus
info: Genus: Necrovirus Genome Characteristics: Viruses contain a single molecule of linear, positive-sense, ssRNA of approximately 3.7 kb. The genome has four major ORFs, with a potential fifth in some species. The 5' end is not capped and lacks a 3' poly(A) tail. Three virus-specific dsRNA species are found in infected cells. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation is based on serological relationships, sequence identity of gene products (less than 93% amino acid identity in polymerase, less than 87% in CP), transmission by fungal vector, and host range. Host/Ecology: Necroviruses infect a wide range of monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plants, primarily in roots. Transmission occurs via mechanical inoculation and soil. Some species are transmitted by the chytrid fungus Olpidium brassicae, while others are transmitted through soil without a vector. TNV-A and TNV-D are ubiquitous. OLV-1 is found in Mediterranean countries, LWSV in France, and BBSV in China and the US. Virion Properties: Virions are approximately 28 nm in diameter with T=3 icosahedral symmetry and a smooth surface. The sedimentation coefficient is 118S, and the buoyant density in CsCl is 1.40 g cm−3. The Mr is 7.6×106. Thermal inactivation occurs between 85 and 95 °C, and the isoelectric point is pH 4.5. Virions are insensitive to ether, chloroform, and non-ionic detergents. Cytopathic Effects: Virus particles form crystalline arrays in infected cells of all tissue types. Some species induce electron-dense amorphous material accumulations. LWSV and OLV-1 elicit membranous vesicles with fibrillar material lining the tonoplast or derived from the endoplasmic reticulum.

name: Panicovirus
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: Positive-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA). Genome size and organization: 4.3 kb genome with five ORFs, one initiating with a non-canonical GUG codon. Produces a 1.5 kb subgenomic RNA (sgRNA) for expression of ORFs 2-5. Genome organization similar to Machlomovirus but lacks the additional 5'-proximal ORF. Key conserved domains identified: Polymerase with a unique 20 kDa N-terminal region. ORF2 protein (p8) similar to MP1 of carmoviruses, necroviruses, and machlomoviruses. p6.6 similar to MP2 proteins of Tombusviridae. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment: Not applicable (at genus level). HOST/ECOLOGY: Known/predicted host range: Primarily restricted to grass species in the Paniceae tribe (Poaceae). Experimental hosts include Zea mays. Cocksfoot mild mosaic virus (CMMV) infects various grass species. Geographical distribution: Panicovirus reported in the US and Mexico. CMMV present in Europe and Canada. Transmission patterns: Readily transmitted by mechanical inoculation and transport of infected sod. Possible seed transmission reported for St Augustine grass decline virus strain in Setaria italica. Virion properties: Icosahedral virions approximately 30 nm in diameter. Sedimentation coefficient of 109S, buoyant density of 1.365 g/cm3 in CsCl, and virion Mr of 6.1×106. Thermally stable, insensitive to ether, chloroform, and non-ionic detergents, and stabilized by divalent cations.

name: Machlomovirus
info: Genus: Machlomovirus GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: The genome is a single molecule of linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) of approximately 4.4 kb (4437 nt). It contains four open reading frames (ORFs). The polymerase ORF has an N-terminal extension not found in other family members and is not the 5'-most proximal ORF. Two subgenomic RNAs (sgRNAs) of 1.47 kb and 0.34 kb are present in infected plants. The 1.47 kb sgRNA encodes the capsid protein (CP). The function of the 0.34 kb sgRNA is unknown. The genome organization is similar to Panicovirus, but Machlomovirus encodes an additional 5'-proximally located ORF encoding a 32 kDa protein of unknown function. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria at the genus level are not applicable in the provided source. HOST/ECOLOGY: The known host range is restricted to monocotyledonous plants, particularly maize (Zea mays) in nature and members of the family Gramineae in the laboratory. Geographical distribution includes Argentina, Mexico, Peru, and the United States (Kansas, Nebraska, and Hawaii). Transmission occurs readily by mechanical inoculation and seed transmission. Some isolates can be transmitted by chrysomelid beetles and thrips. The virus causes a mild mosaic on maize, but in combination with certain potyviruses, it can cause corn lethal necrosis. Virions are approximately 30 nm in diameter with icosahedral symmetry, sediment at 109S, and have a buoyant density of 1.365 g cm−3 in CsCl.

name: Mesoniviridae
info: Family: Mesoniviridae Genome Characteristics: Enveloped, spherical virions, 60-80 nm in diameter. Genome is monopartite, linear, single-stranded positive-sense RNA, approximately 20 kb in size. Encodes ORF1a and ORF1b (translated via ribosomal frameshifting), producing pp1a and pp1ab, which are processed into viral polymerase (RdRp) and other non-structural proteins. Structural proteins are expressed from subgenomic RNAs. Each RNA typically translates the 5'-most ORF, except ORF2b (possibly via leaky scanning). Viral enzymes include RNA-directed RNA polymerase, proofreading exoribonuclease (ExoN), Nido-type capping enzymes (GDP polyribonucleotidyltransferase, N7methyltransferase, 2'O methylase), and polyprotein major protease (Peptidase C107). Replication: Cytoplasmic. Attachment to host receptors mediates endocytosis. Fusion releases ssRNA(+) genome into cytoplasm. Replicase polyprotein synthesis and cleavage. Replication in viral factories, producing dsRNA intermediate. Transcription/replication yields viral mRNAs/new ssRNA(+) genomes. Structural protein synthesis from subgenomic mRNAs. Assembly and budding at ER, intermediate compartments, and/or Golgi complex membranes. Virion release. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not specified. Host/Ecology: Natural hosts are mosquitoes. Geographical distribution includes Vietnam and Ivory Coast. Transmission patterns not explicitly stated, but presumed via mosquito vectors.

name: Dicistroviridae
info: Family: Dicistroviridae Genome Characteristics: Dicistroviridae viruses possess a single molecule of linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome, ranging from 8 to 10 kb with a GC content of 34-45%. The genome is monopartite and contains two non-overlapping open reading frames (ORFs) encoding non-structural and structural protein precursors, separated by an intergenic untranslated region (IGR). A genome-linked virus protein (VPg) is covalently attached to the 5′-end, and the 3′-terminus is polyadenylated. The non-structural polyprotein includes an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP), cysteine protease, RNA helicase, and VPg. Translation is cap-independent, initiated at internal ribosome entry site (IRES) elements in the 5′-UTR and IGR. Evolutionary Context: Dicistroviridae belongs to the order Picornavirales, sharing similarities with Iflaviridae, Picornaviridae, Marnaviridae, and Secoviridae families. Genus demarcation is based on IGR IRES sequence and topology, and phylogenetic analysis. Host/Ecology: Dicistroviridae viruses infect arthropods, with some causing significant economic damage in honeybees (e.g., acute bee paralysis virus) and the seafood industry (e.g., taura syndrome virus). Some members are being explored as biopesticides. Transmission occurs via ingestion, with virus shedding into the gut lumen. Horizontal transmission can occur via glandular secretions in honeybees. Vertical transmission is also observed. Viruses exhibit tissue tropism to the alimentary canal, nervous tissue, fat body, epidermal cells, and gonads. Geographical distribution is wide. Many members are serologically distinguishable.

name: Permutotetraviridae
info: Family: Permutotetraviridae Genome Characteristics: ssRNA(+) genome, 5.6-5.7 kb, linear, one segment. Contains a 5'-terminal VPg and a 3'-terminal pseudoknot. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm, associated with host cell membranes, via dsRNA intermediates. Translation occurs from genomic and subgenomic mRNAs with autoproteolytic cleavage. Evolutionary Context: Realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae. Contains one genus (Alphapermutotetravirus) and two species. Taxonomic demarcation is based on RdRP active site permutation and T=4 capsid architecture. Permutotetraviridae name is derived from Latin "permutare" (to change thoroughly) and Greek "tetra" (four). Alphapermutotetravirus name is derived from Greek "alpha" (first). Host/Ecology: Infects invertebrates, specifically Lepidoptera. Example virus: Euprosterna elaeasa virus. Virions are icosahedral, 40 nm in diameter, with T=4 quasi-symmetry. Geographical distribution not specified. Transmission patterns not established.

name: Nyamiviridae
info: Family: Nyamiviridae Genome Characteristics: Nyamiviridae viruses possess linear, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA genomes, either non-segmented or bi-segmented, ranging from 10 to 13 kb. Genomes encode 4-8 structural proteins, including a nucleocapsid protein (N), glycoprotein (G), and a large protein (L) with an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Conserved domains are identified based on sequence similarity with other mononegavirals. Evolutionary Context: Nyamiviridae belongs to the order Mononegavirales. The family includes seven genera: Berhavirus, Crustavirus, Formivirus, Nyavirus, Orinovirus, Socyvirus, and Tapwovirus. Genus demarcation criteria are based on phylogeny and host range. Host/Ecology: Nyamiviridae viruses infect a broad range of hosts, including invertebrates (ticks, insects, echinoderms, sipunculids, crustaceans, nematodes, tapeworms) and vertebrates (land- and seabirds). Geographical distribution varies depending on the specific virus and host. Transmission patterns are established for Nyavirus, which are tick-borne, and some can infect birds. Socyvirus infect plant parasitic nematodes. Other genera are associated with marine animals (Berhavirus and Crustavirus), moths and beetles (Orinovirus), tapeworms (Tapwovirus), and ants and wasps (Formivirus). Virions of Nyavirus and Socyvirus are enveloped and spherical. Virion information for other genera is unavailable.

name: Marseilleviridae
info: FAMILY: Marseilleviridae TAXID: 944644 GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: dsDNA, circular genome of 372 kb, encoding 457 ORFs. Icosahedral capsid, 250 nm diameter. Major capsid protein with double jelly roll-fold (D2XAY2). Pentons with single jelly roll-fold (D2XAB2?). EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment unavailable. HOST/ECOLOGY: Host Range: Amoeba. Geographical Distribution: France and Senegal. Transmission: Undocumented. Enzymes: DNA-directed RNA polymerase, cell-type capping enzyme, protease (peptidase S74), thymidine kinase, endonuclease, kinase, ribonuclease H, ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase. Gene Expression: Undocumented. Replication: Undocumented. Antiviral Drugs: None. Source: ViralZone Type: Family Name: Marseilleviridae

name: Togaviridae
info: Family: Togaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Togaviridae family consists of enveloped viruses with single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genomes ranging from 10 to 12 kb. Alphavirus genomes have a 5' cap and a poly(A) tail, encoding non-structural proteins (nsP1-nsP4) for replication and structural proteins (capsid, E3, E2, 6K/TF, E1) for virion assembly. The non-structural proteins are translated from genomic RNA, while structural proteins are translated from subgenomic RNA. Evolutionary Context: Species demarcation within the Alphavirus genus considers nucleotide and amino acid sequences, antigenic characteristics, vector and host associations, disease association, and ecological characteristics. Significant sequence divergence may exist within a species due to variations in vector usage and virulence. Historically, Togaviridae included Rubivirus, now in Matonaviridae, and shares distant relationships with Flaviviruses and members of an alphavirus-like superfamily. Host/Ecology: Togaviridae, specifically Alphavirus, primarily includes mosquito-borne viruses, though other hematophagous insects can be vectors. Vertebrate hosts include humans, non-human primates, equids, birds, amphibians, reptiles, rodents, and pigs. Some alphaviruses infect aquatic mammals and fish. Alphaviruses are geographically widespread, found on all continents except Antarctica, with distribution influenced by ecological conditions, reservoir hosts, and vector species. Transmission typically occurs between vertebrate and invertebrate hosts, though some viruses exhibit horizontal or vertical transmission.

name: Chaseviridae
info: Family: Chaseviridae Genome Characteristics: dsDNA, linear, 52-56 kbp with terminal repeats. G+C content ranges from 39.3-52.5%. Encodes 63-92 genes, including 0-1 tRNAs. Contains a phage-encoded Autographiviridae-like RNA polymerase. 25 conserved proteins representing 33.7% of the viral proteome have been identified. Evolutionary Context: Belongs to the realm Duplodnaviria, kingdom Heunggongvirae, phylum Uroviricota, and class Caudoviricetes. Subfamilies are identified by phylogenetic analysis of RNA polymerase and terminase large subunit proteins, with 25-29% whole genome sequence similarity within each subfamily. Genera form monophyletic clades with at least 70% nucleotide identity across the genome. Species share over 95% genome nucleotide sequence identity. Host/Ecology: Infects bacteria of the phylum Proteobacteria, class Gammaproteobacteria. Obligately lytic. Has a worldwide distribution. Virion: Head-tail morphology with a contractile tail and icosahedral head. Head diameter is 53-65 nm, and uncontracted tail length is 116-166 nm. Taxonomy: Contains 2 subfamilies (Cleopatravirinae, Nefertitivirinae), 13 genera, and 30 species.

name: Rountreeviridae
info: Family: Rountreeviridae Genome Characteristics: dsDNA, linear genome ranging from 16 to 20 kb, encoding 20-30 genes. Terminal proteins are covalently attached at both DNA ends. Key enzymes include DNA-dependent DNA polymerase B and cysteine protease (Peptidase C51). Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria not specified. Host/Ecology: Host Range: Gram-positive bacteria. Geographical Distribution: Worldwide. Transmission: Passive diffusion through medium. Replication: Cytoplasmic. Adsorption occurs via tail fibers.
