Viral DNA is injected into the host cell periplasm. Early gene transcription and translation are followed by genomic DNA replication using viral DNA polymerase, forming concatemers. Late gene transcription and translation occur. Empty procapsids are assembled, and the viral genome is packaged. Mature virions are released by cell lysis. Virion Characteristics: Non-enveloped, head-tail structure with Podo-type morphology. The capsid is approximately 55 nm in diameter, likely with T=4 icosahedral symmetry. The non-contractile tail is about 27 nm long and features a collar with 12 appendages attached to the neck region, which are important for host cell recognition and entry.

name: Fusariviridae
info: Family: Fusariviridae Genome Characteristics: Positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome, ranging from 5.9 to 10.7 kb. Genomes are typically bicistronic, but can range from one to four open reading frames (ORFs). The 5'-proximal ORF encodes a protein with RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) and RNA helicase (Hel) domains. The 3'-terminus is generally polyadenylated. Replicative form is dsRNA, accumulating intracellularly. No virions have been purified. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation is based on phylogenetic analysis of the RdRP domain. Species within the same genus form monophyletic clades. Species share >80% identity in the full-length sequence of the protein that includes the RdRP domain. Phylogenetically related to Hypoviridae, but with distinct genome organization. Host/Ecology: Known hosts are primarily ascomycetes and basidiomycetes fungi. One confirmed host is a stramenopiles oomycete. Experimentally confirmed hosts are members of the kingdom Fungi and in one case a confirmed stramenopiles oomycetes host. Additional members of two species have been associated with peronosporaceaen stramenopiles from a metatranscriptomic sample. Transmission patterns are not well-established. Some fusariviruses can induce hypovirulence in their fungal hosts.

name: Tectiviridae
info: Family: Tectiviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, double-stranded DNA genome of approximately 15 kb. Contains inverted terminal repeats (approximately 100 bp) and covalently linked 5'-terminal proteins used as primers for replication. G+C content is around 48%. Evolutionary Context: Species demarcation is based on sequence comparison, with Enterobacteria phages (PRD1-types) showing high nucleotide sequence similarity (91.9-99.8%) and Bacillus phages (Bam35-types) exhibiting more diversity (59-99% identity). Tectiviruses share similarities with adenoviruses, including genome structure, replication mechanisms, and capsid architecture. Similar capsid protein folds are observed in other viruses across different domains of life. Host/Ecology: Infects bacteria, including Enterobacteria (e.g., Escherichia coli), Bacillus, and Thermus species. Enterobacteria phages are virulent, while Bacillus phages can be temperate. Thermus phages are found in volcanic hot springs. Transmission involves a tail-like membranous tube for DNA injection. Geographical distribution varies depending on the host.

name: Fimoviridae
info: Family: Fimoviridae Genome Characteristics: The Fimoviridae family comprises plant viruses with multipartite negative-sense single-stranded RNA (-ssRNA) genomes. Genomes consist of four to ten segments, totaling 12.3–18.5 kb. Genomic RNAs are not capped or polyadenylated but contain complementary sequences at their 5′ and 3′ termini. Each RNA segment typically encodes a single protein. RNA1 encodes the RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP), RNA2 encodes a glycoprotein precursor (GP), RNA3 encodes the nucleocapsid protein (NP), and RNA4 encodes a putative movement protein (MP). The remaining RNAs (RNA5 to RNA9) encode proteins with unknown functions. The RdRP shares conserved motifs with related viruses. Evolutionary Context: Fimoviridae belongs to the order Elliovirales and shares similarities with Tospoviridae and Peribunyaviridae, including a multipartite -ssRNA genome, sequence identity in RdRP, GP, and NP, conserved RdRP motifs, enveloped virions, and complementary terminal sequences on RNA segments. The family contains one genus, Emaravirus, with consideration for future division into multiple genera based on phylogeny, encoded proteins, and genomic terminations. Host/Ecology: Fimoviridae members primarily infect dicotyledonous plants, including woody species (fig, grapevine) and ornamentals (camellia, rose). A few infect monocotyledonous plants (wheat, maize). Symptoms vary from leaf mottling to mosaic patterns. Transmission occurs through grafting and eriophyid mites. Mechanical transmission to herbaceous hosts is rare.

name: Mamonoviridae
info: Mamonoviridae: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Circular, dsDNA genome of 362 kb. Encodes 429 ORFs. Icosahedral capsid of 260 nm diameter with T=277 symmetry. Encodes DNA-directed DNA polymerase, DNA primase, cap-specific mRNA (nucleoside-2'-O-)-methyltransferase, 3'-5' exonuclease, dCMP deaminase, thymidylate synthase, dTMP kinase, multiple Ser/Thr protein kinases, protein phosphatase 2C, ribonuclease H, ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase, Nudix hydrolase, deoxyuridine triphosphatase, and protease (Peptidase C14). Gene expression and replication mechanisms are undocumented. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not available. HOST/ECOLOGY: Host: Amoeba. Geographical distribution: Isolated in Japan. Transmission patterns: Unknown. Antiviral drugs: None.

name: Cystoviridae
info: Family: Cystoviridae Genome Characteristics: The Cystoviridae family comprises enveloped viruses with a tri-segmented, linear, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genome, ranging from 12.7 to 15.0 kbp in total size. The genome is organized into three segments: L (6.4–7.1 kbp), M (3.6–4.7 kbp), and S (2.3–3.2 kbp), with a GC content of 53.4–58.8%. The genome encodes structural and non-structural proteins, with distinct noncoding regions at the termini of the segments containing signals for genome packaging and replication. Key proteins include P1 (major capsid protein), P2 (viral replicase and transcriptase), P3 (receptor binding spike), P4 (nucleoside triphosphatase), P5 (lytic enzyme), P6 and P9 (envelope proteins). Evolutionary Context: Cystoviruses share similarities in genome replication strategy with eukaryotic dsRNA viruses. The structure, organization, and functions of the polymerase complex are similar to those of members of families Chrysoviridae, Reoviridae, Totiviridae, Partitiviridae, Megabirnaviridae, Quadriviridae and Picobirnaviridae. The T=13 architecture of the capsid layer is also shared with reoviruses. Taxonomic demarcation includes seven genera and nine species within the order Mindivirales, class Vidaverviricetes, phylum Duplornaviricota, kingdom Orthornavirae, and realm Riboviria. Host/Ecology: Cystoviruses infect Gram-negative bacteria, primarily plant-pathogenic Pseudomonas syringae strains. They are lytic bacteriophages that induce host cell lysis. Virions adsorb to the host bacterium, and the viral envelope fuses with the host outer membrane. Viral lipids are derived from the host plasma membrane.

name: Amalgaviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Family Amalgaviridae members possess a monopartite, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genome of approximately 3.5 kbp. The genome contains two partially overlapping open reading frames (ORFs). These ORFs encode an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) and a protein of unknown function. Translation involves +1 ribosomal frameshifting. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: The family Amalgaviridae belongs to the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Pisuviricota, class Duplopiviricetes, and order Durnavirales. It comprises 3 genera and 23 species. The name Amalgaviridae derives from the Medieval Latin "amalgama," reflecting the family's blended properties of Partitiviridae and Totiviridae viruses. HOST/ECOLOGY: Amalgaviridae viruses infect plants, often resulting in asymptomatic infections. Seed transmission is a known transmission pattern. An example is the southern tomato virus (species Amalgavirus lycopersici, genus Amalgavirus).

name: Alphatetraviridae
info: Family: Alphatetraviridae Genome Characteristics: ssRNA(+) genome, 6.6-8.0 kb, 1-2 linear segments, 3'-terminal tRNA-like structure. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm via dsRNA intermediates. Translation involves genomic and subgenomic mRNAs, possibly with read-through. Evolutionary Context: Realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Kitrinoviricota, class Alsuviricetes, order Hepelivirales. Contains 2 genera and 10 species. The name Alphatetraviridae refers to the relationship to viruses of the Alpha-like supergroup and the T=4 capsid architecture. Host/Ecology: Infects invertebrates, specifically Lepidoptera. Geographical distribution is not specified. Transmission patterns are not established. Virion: Icosahedral, 32-40 nm diameter, T=4 quasi-symmetry.

name: Birnaviridae
info: Family: Birnaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Birnaviridae family comprises viruses with bisegmented, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genomes, totaling approximately 6 kbp. The genome is organized into two linear segments, A and B, with a high G+C content (53-58%, lower in some insect viruses). The positive-sense strand of each segment is covalently linked to a viral protein (VP1) at the 5' terminus. Segment A encodes a polyprotein (preVP2-VP4-VP3), while segment B encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP), VP1. Evolutionary Context: Birnaviruses exhibit no nucleic acid sequence similarity to other taxa. However, structural similarities exist between the capsid protein VP2 and capsid proteins of Nodaviridae and Tetraviridae (positive-sense ssRNA viruses). The VP4 protease shares homology with bacterial ATP-dependent Lon proteases. The RdRP VP1 shares motif rearrangement with Permutotetraviridae. Genus demarcation is based on host range and amino acid identity of RdRP and capsid proteins. Host/Ecology: Birnaviridae members infect a diverse range of hosts, including vertebrates (fish, birds), invertebrates (insects, molluscs, rotifers). Genera are demarcated by host: Aquabirnavirus, Avibirnavirus, and Blosnavirus infect vertebrates; Entomobirnavirus and Dronavirus infect insects; Ronavirus infects rotifers; and Telnavirus infects molluscs. Transmission patterns vary depending on the virus, including horizontal and vertical transmission. Some members, such as infectious pancreatic necrosis virus (IPNV) and infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV), are economically important pathogens. Geographical distribution is worldwide for some members.

name: Picobirnaviridae
info: Family: Picobirnaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Picobirnaviridae family consists of viruses with a bisegmented, linear, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genome. Segment 1 is approximately 2.4-2.6 kbp and contains three open reading frames (ORFs). ORF1 functionality is unclear, ORF2 encodes a protein with unknown function, and ORF3 encodes the capsid protein (CP) precursor. Segment 2 is 1.5-1.9 kbp and encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), containing a canonical A-B-C motif. No lipids are present. Evolutionary Context: Species demarcation within the Picobirnavirus genus is based on host, country of origin, and year of isolation. Genetic diversity is high, particularly in the RdRp-encoding segment (segment 2), leading to the identification of two genogroups (I and II). Capsid protein sequence identity between rabbit and human picobirnaviruses is low (25%). Host/Ecology: Picobirnaviruses have a broad host range, infecting humans, mammals, birds, and reptiles. They are geographically widespread and are often detected in fecal samples and raw sewage, suggesting fecal-oral transmission. While pathogenicity is not fully established, they are suspected to be opportunistic pathogens, potentially causing diarrhea, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Animal-to-animal transmission is evident, but host-specific virus clusters have not been identified.

name: Marnaviridae
info: Family: Marnaviridae Genome Characteristics: Non-enveloped viruses with positive-sense, monopartite RNA genomes ranging from 8.6 to 9.6 kb, including a 3'-poly(A) tail. Genomes contain one or two open reading frames (ORFs). Conserved domains include helicase, RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP), and structural (VP) domains, with some members containing regions resembling 3C cysteine proteinases. Internal ribosome entry sites (IRES) are present. Four conserved proteins (VP1-4) share similarities with structural proteins of Picornavirales. Evolutionary Context: Belongs to the order Picornavirales. Phylogenetic analysis of RdRP sequences places Marnaviridae as a monophyletic group. Metagenomic studies have identified related viruses, potentially representing new genera. Genera are defined based on phylogenetic relationships between virus amino acid sequences. Species demarcation uses 90% RdRP and 75% capsid amino acid identity cut-offs. Host/Ecology: Infect marine single-celled eukaryotes (protists). Some members are known from ocean virioplankton metagenomic studies, with additional viruses from marine and freshwater metagenomic datasets. Replication is cytolytic, with latent periods of 8-48 hours. Cytopathic effects include endoplasmic reticulum swelling, crystalline arrays, vacuolation, and cytoplasm disintegration. Burst sizes range from 66 to 105 particles per cell. Seven genera and 20 species are currently classified.

name: Lispiviridae
info: Family: Lispiviridae Genome Characteristics: Negative-sense RNA, 6.5-15.5 kb. Genomes typically contain five to six open reading frames (ORFs). Encoded proteins include a glycoprotein and a large protein (L) with an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Evolutionary Context: Belongs to the order Mononegavirales, sharing similar genome organization. Genus demarcation: <50% RdRP amino acid sequence identity. Species demarcation: <85% RdRP amino acid sequence identity within a genus. Host/Ecology: Primarily detected in arthropods (hemipterans, odonatans, hymenopterans, orthopterans, arachnids), nematodes, mammals (mice) and bird faeces. Geographical distribution includes Africa, America, Asia, Europe, and Oceania. Specific hosts include short-horned grasshoppers, whiteflies, parasitoid wasps, orb-weaver spiders, stink bugs, ticks, termites, diving beetles, dragonflies, damselflies, ants, wood cockroaches, water striders, insect endoparasites of bees, and true mice. Transmission patterns are currently unknown.

name: Solinviviridae
info: Family: Solinviviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome is a non-segmented, linear, positive-sense RNA molecule of 10-11 kb. It has a 3'-poly(A) tail and is presumed to have a viral protein genome-linked (VPg) covalently attached to the 5'-end. The genome encodes picorna/calici-like superfamily III helicase, 3C-like chymotrypsin-related cysteine protease, and superfamily I RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) domains. Capsid proteins are encoded towards the 3'-end and comprise a single jelly-roll fold domain with a large extension domain, plus an additional capsid-associated protein. A subgenomic capsid-encoding RNA is produced. Evolutionary Context: Genera are separated based on phylogenetic clustering based on protein sequence identities and genome organization. Formal genus demarcation criteria have not yet been established. Solinviviridae genomes encode picorna/calici-like domains. Similar to Caliciviridae, there is only a single jelly-roll fold capsid domain. Host/Ecology: Known hosts include arthropods, specifically ants (Solenopsis invicta). Viruses appear to have high host specificity. Transmission occurs through feeding. Geographical distribution is not specified but related unclassified viruses derive from a large variety of insects and other arthropods. Solenopsis invicta virus 3 (SINV3) infection is largely specific to workers and is highly pathogenic. Nyfulvavirus 1 (NfV1) has been detected in larvae, pupae, worker and queen ants, with the highest viral load and active replication detected in larvae.

name: Orthomyxoviridae
info: Family: Orthomyxoviridae Genome Characteristics: Virions contain segmented, linear, negative-sense ssRNA. Influenza A and B viruses, and infectious salmon anemia virus (ISAV) have eight segments; influenza C virus and Dhori virus (DHOV) have seven; Thogoto virus (THOV) has six. Segment lengths range from 736 to 2396 nt, with a total genome size of 10.0 to 14.6 kb. RNA segments possess conserved 5′ and 3′ ends with promoter activity. Key proteins include RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) subunits (e.g., PA, PB1, PB2), nucleoprotein (NP), hemagglutinin (HA, HE [HEF], or GP), and matrix protein (M1 or M). Genera may also encode neuraminidase (NA) and small integral membrane proteins (M2, NB, BM2, or CM2). Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation is based on genetic and antigenic properties. Gene reassortment occurs within genera but not between different genera. Host/Ecology:  Host Range: Influenza A viruses infect humans, other mammals, and birds. Influenza B viruses primarily infect humans. Influenza C viruses infect humans and pigs. Thogoto and Dhori viruses infect mammals and ticks. Isaviruses infect salmon.  Geographical Distribution: Worldwide.  Transmission: Influenza viruses are transmitted by aerosol or waterborne routes. Thogoto and Dhori viruses are transmitted by ticks. Isaviruses are transmitted via water.

name: Bicaudaviridae
info: Family: Bicaudaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Bicaudaviridae family possesses a circular, double-stranded DNA genome of approximately 62,730 base pairs with a GC content of 41.2%. The genome encodes 72 predicted proteins and contains four putative transposable elements. Several genes may have arisen from gene duplication. Key proteins include structural proteins (11 major types), a putative integrase, glycosyltransferase, ParB-like partitioning protein, DNA repair photolyase, acyltransferase, and three AAA+ ATPases. Some structural proteins contain coiled-coil or low complexity sequence domains. Evolutionary Context: Bicaudaviruses share a conserved DnaA-like AAA+ ATPase with Fuselloviridae and Guttaviridae, suggesting a possible evolutionary relationship. Taxonomic demarcation is based on shared characteristics and host range. Host/Ecology: Bicaudaviruses infect hyperthermophilic archaea of the genus Acidianus. The type member, Acidianus two-tailed virus, was isolated from a hot acidic spring in Pozzuoli, Italy. Infection can result in either lytic or lysogenic cycles. Lysogeny involves integration of the viral genome into the host chromosome, potentially mediated by a virus-encoded integrase. The virus relies on host machinery for genome replication and transcription. Virions are released as spindle-shaped particles that develop two tails.

name: Fiersviridae
info: FAMILY: Fiersviridae GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Non-enveloped, icosahedral virions, approximately 26 nm in diameter. Genome is monopartite, linear, single-stranded positive-sense RNA, ranging from 3.4 to 4.3 kb. The 5' end has a triphosphate group. Encodes 3-4 proteins. Virion RNA serves as both genome and mRNA. Encodes 4 ORFs. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Formerly named Leviviridae. Taxonomic demarcation not explicitly assessed. HOST/ECOLOGY: Infects Enterobacteria, Caulobacter, Pseudomonas, and Acinetobacter. Geographical distribution is worldwide. Transmission occurs via adsorption to F pili of target cells, inducing maturation protein cleavage and release. Genomic RNA enters the bacterium, viral proteins are translated, and viral replicase assembles with host proteins to form active RNA polymerase. Replication produces new positive-strand genomes. CP protein binds to RNA hairpin on the genome, and new virus particles assemble in the cytoplasm. Release occurs via cell lysis. No associated diseases reported.

name: Graaviviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: dsDNA genome, linear, 39-42 kbp. Encodes proteins with conserved domains (details not specified). EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Family Graaviviridae; Realm Duplodnaviria, kingdom Heunggongvirae, phylum Uroviricota, class Caudoviricetes, order Kirjokansivirales. Contains 2 genera and 2 species. Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment details not provided. Established in 2022. HOST/ECOLOGY: Infects hyperhalophilic archaea of Halorubrum sp. Geographical distribution not specified. Transmission patterns not established. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION: Virions consist of an icosahedral capsid (55 nm diameter) and a non-contractile tail (70 nm length), exhibiting siphovirus morphology. The name Graaviviridae derives from the Finnish word "graavi," referring to the raw cooking of fish with salt. Example virus: Halorubrum virus BJ1 (species Beejeyvirus bagaejinnorense, genus Beejeyvirus).

name: Qinviridae
info: Family: Qinviridae Genome Characteristics: The Qinviridae family comprises viruses with bi-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes, ranging from 7.3 to 8.2 kb in total length. The large (L) segment (5.6-6.6 kb) encodes an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) with a GDP:polyribonucleotidyltransferase (PRNTase) domain. The small (S) segment (1.6-1.9 kb) encodes a nucleocapsid protein. The RdRP domain shows similarity to those of viruses in the order Mononegavirales. Evolutionary Context: Qinviridae is classified within the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Negarnaviricota, class Chunqiuviricetes, and order Muvirales. The family contains a single genus, Yingvirus, with eight species. Species demarcation is based on phylogenetic analysis of the RdRP, without established numerical cutoffs. Qinvirids are closely related to aspivirids, jingchuvirals, mononegavirals, and yuevirids within the subphylum Haploviricotina. Host/Ecology: Qinvirids have been associated with a broad range of hosts, including decapod crustaceans, insects (blattodean and dipteran), gastropods, and nematodes. Geographical distribution includes China, and unclassified qinvirids have been found worldwide. Specific transmission patterns remain largely unknown.

name: Steitzviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: ssRNA(+) Genome size and organization: Monopartite, linear genome of approximately 3.4-4.3 kb. The 5' end has a triphosphate. Encodes at least 3 proteins. Key conserved domains: RNA-directed RNA polymerase. CP protein binds to a RNA hairpin on the genome. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment: Not specified. Family Steitzviridae (taxid:2842332). HOST/ECOLOGY: Known/predicted host range: Enterobacteria, Caulobacter, Pseudomonas, and Acinetobacter. Adsorption to F pili of target cells. Geographical distribution: Worldwide. Transmission patterns: Not specified. Release by cell lysis. Virion RNA is infectious and serves as both the genome and viral messenger RNA. Genomic RNA enters the bacterium. Viral proteins are translated. Replication of genomic RNA into a minus strand, which serves as template to produce new positive strand genomes. Late in infection CP protein bind to a RNA hairpin on the genome, and new virus particles are assembled in the cytoplasm. Virion: Non-enveloped, spherical virion about 26 nm in diameter with T=3 icosahedral symmetry composed of 178 CP proteins and a single maturation protein. Associated Diseases: None reported.

name: Carmotetraviridae
info: Family: Carmotetraviridae Genome Characteristics: ssRNA(+) genome, linear, 6.1-6.2 kb in size. Encodes proteins translated from genomic and subgenomic mRNAs via autoproteolytic cleavage and read-through. Evolutionary Context: Realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Kitrinoviricota, class Tolucaviricetes, order Tolivirales. Established in 2011. Includes viruses with carmo-like replicase and T=4 capsid architecture. Contains one genus, Alphacarmotetravirus, and one species, Alphacarmotetravirus providencense. Host/Ecology: Infects invertebrates, primarily lepidopteran insects. Possible infection of mammalian cells and plants. Infections can be asymptomatic and persistent. Example member is Providence virus. Virions are icosahedral, 40 nm in diameter, with T=4 quasi-symmetry. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm, associated with host cell membranes, involving dsRNA intermediates.

name: Lipothrixviridae
info: Family: Lipothrixviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, double-stranded DNA genomes ranging from 15.9 to 56 kbp. Genomes encode structural proteins and proteins with homology to rudiviruses. Some members contain terminal repeats and modified DNA ends. Evolutionary Context: Shares a common ancestor with Rudiviridae, indicated by conserved genes and structural similarities in major virion proteins. Phylogenetic relationships are supported by sequence similarities in specific ORFs. Host/Ecology: Infect hyperthermophilic archaea. Host genera include Thermoproteus, Sulfolobus, and Acidianus. Geographical distribution corresponds to the habitats of their archaeal hosts. Transmission patterns vary; some cause cell lysis, while others establish persistent infections without lysis. Virions attach to host pili or cell surfaces via terminal structures. Genera:  Alphalipothrixvirus: Rigid rod-shaped virions, infects Thermoproteus.  Betalipothrixvirus: Flexuous filamentous virions, infects Sulfolobus and Acidianus. Genomes contain large inverted terminal repeats.  Gammalipothrixvirus: Filamentous virions with claw-like terminal structures, infects Acidianus.  Deltalipothrixvirus: Flexuous filamentous virions with bottle brush-like terminal structures, infects Acidianus. Lipids not detected.

name: Barnaviridae
info: Family: Barnaviridae Genome Characteristics:  Nucleic acid type: ssRNA, positive sense, linear  Genome size: 4.0 kb (4009 nt)  Genome organization: Contains four major and three minor ORFs with 5′- and 3′-UTRs. Encodes polypeptides including a putative serine protease (related to chymotrypsin), an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), and a capsid protein (CP). VPg linked, lacks poly(A) tail. Evolutionary Context:  Taxonomic demarcation: Family description corresponds to the genus description due to only one recognized genus (Barnavirus).  Phylogenetic relationships: Shows similarity to ssRNA positive sense plant viruses like poleroviruses, sobemoviruses, and enamoviruses based on serine protease and RdRp sequences. Host/Ecology:  Host range: Primarily infects the cultivated button mushroom (Agaricus bisporus). Also observed in the field mushroom A. campestris.  Geographical distribution: Coincides with commercial cultivation of A. bisporus; reported in most major mushroom-growing countries.  Transmission: Horizontal transmission via mycelium and possibly basidiospores.  Additional notes: Often found as a double infection with LaFrance isometric virus (LFIV). Role in La France disease pathogenesis is not fully determined. Virion Properties:  Morphology: Bacilliform, non-enveloped, lacking prominent surface projections. Dimensions typically 19x50 nm (range 18-20 nm width, 48-53 nm length).  Physicochemical properties: Mr 7.1×106, buoyant density in Cs2SO4 is 1.32 g cm−3. Stable between pH 6 and 8 and ionic strength of 0.01 to 0.1M phosphate, and are insensitive to chloroform.  Proteins: Single major CP of 21.9 kDa (approximately 240 molecules per capsid).

name: Mymonaviridae
info: Family: Mymonaviridae Genome Characteristics:  Nucleic acid type: Single-stranded, negative-sense RNA  Genome size: Approximately 10 kb, linear  Organization: Typically contains 4-7 open reading frames (ORFs), separated by non-coding intergenic regions with conserved gene-junction sequences. Some members have ORFs on both strands.  Key conserved domains: RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain in the large (L) protein. Evolutionary Context:  Taxonomic demarcation: Belongs to Realm Riboviria, Phylum Negarnaviricota, Subphylum Haploviricotina, Class Monjiviricetes, Order Mononegavirales. Genus demarcation is based on <32% amino acid sequence identity in the L protein. Includes nine genera: Auricularimonavirus, Botrytimonavirus, Hubramonavius, Lentimonavirus, Penicillimonavirus, Phyllomonavirus, Plasmopamavirus, Rhizomonavirus, and Sclerotimonavirus. Host/Ecology:  Host range: Primarily infects filamentous fungi (plant-pathogenic, edible, and endophytic fungi). Also detected in insects, oomycetes, plants, and soil via metagenomics, but true hosts in these cases are unclear.  Geographical distribution: Not specified, but viruses have been isolated from various locations, including China.  Transmission patterns: Horizontal transmission occurs through hyphal fusion in fungi. Transmission through sexual or asexual spores is not known. Sclerotinia sclerotiorum negative-stranded RNA virus 1 (SsNSRV-1) induces hypovirulence in its fungal host and reduces pathogenicity on plants. Virion: Enveloped, filamentous virions, 25-50 nm in diameter and about 1,000 nm in length.

name: Curvulaviridae
info: Curvulaviridae: Genome Characteristics: Linear, segmented, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genome. Consists of 2 segments, potentially encoding 3 proteins. Each segment is monocistronic. Encodes an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). Possibly non-enveloped icosahedral capsid. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria not explicitly assessed. Host/Ecology: Natural hosts are fungi. First characterized in Curvularia protuberata. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm. Virus penetrates into the cytoplasm. Transcription of the dsRNA genome by viral polymerase occurs inside the virion, producing a plus-strand transcript used for translation. Plus-strand RNAs are encapsidated and transcribed into negative-strand RNAs, forming dsRNA genomes. Transmission occurs via cytoplasmic exchange, sporogenesis, or hyphal anastomosis. Reference strain: Fusarium graminearum orthocurvulavirus (FgV).

name: Inseviridae
info: Family: Inseviridae Genome Characteristics: dsRNA, linear, single segment (5.3-6.6 kbp). Genome contains two non-overlapping open reading frames. The upstream ORF encodes the capsid protein (approximately 122 kDa), and the downstream ORF encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP, approximately 90 kDa) via a -1 ribosomal frameshift. Some inseviruses have a hypothetical protein upstream of the capsid protein. Evolutionary Context: Realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Duplornaviricota, class Chrymotiviricetes, order Ghabrivirales. Species demarcation criteria include host species assignment, sequence validation, and RdRP amino acid sequence identity (<70% for different species, regardless of host; >=70% for same species, even in different hosts). Host/Ecology: Invertebrates, including ants (Camponotus yamaokai), mosquitoes (Aedes, Anopheles, Culex), white-backed planthopper (Sogatella furcifera), fruit fly (Bactrocera dorsalis), tick, Diptera, crab, and Spirurian nematodes. Found worldwide. Transmission patterns are unknown. Additional Information: Virions are non-enveloped, icosahedral particles, 30 nm in diameter. Replication details are unknown, but translation involves a -1 ribosomal frameshift. The family comprises one genus, Insevirus, and 16 species (as of 2024).

name: Megabirnaviridae
info: Family: Megabirnaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Megabirnaviridae family consists of non-enveloped viruses with a bisegmented, linear, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genome. The total genome size is approximately 16.1 kbp, with segments ranging from 7.2 to 8.9 kbp. Each segment contains two open reading frames (ORFs). dsRNA1 encodes a major capsid protein (CP) and an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) via -1 ribosomal frameshifting. dsRNA2 encodes two non-overlapping ORFs, with one processed into smaller proteins. The 5' untranslated regions are large (over 1.6 kb) and likely contain internal ribosome entry sites (IRES). Evolutionary Context: Megabirnaviridae belongs to the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Duplornaviricota, class Chrymotiviricetes, and order Ghabrivirales. It is related to the family Chrysoviridae based on RdRP sequence, but differs in genome segment number, virion size, and coding capacity. Taxonomic demarcation criteria for the single genus, Megabirnavirus, are not yet defined. Host/Ecology: Megabirnaviruses infect filamentous fungi, including Rosellinia necatrix (white root rot fungus) and Cryphonectria parasitica (chestnut blight fungus). Rosellinia necatrix megabirnavirus 1 (RnMBV1) confers hypovirulence to its host. Transmission occurs horizontally via hyphal anastomosis. Vertical transmission is infrequent. RnMBV1 is targeted by antiviral RNA silencing in C. parasitica and is considered a potential biological control agent.

name: Nanoviridae
info: Family: Nanoviridae Genome Characteristics: Multipartite, circular, single-stranded DNA genome with 6 components (Babuvirus) or 8 components (Nanovirus). Genome components range from 0.9-1.1 kb. Each virion contains a single genome component. All DNAs have a similar structural organization, including conserved inverted repeat sequences potentially forming a stem-loop structure that are the origin of replication and part of the common region-stem loop [CR-SL], and a second common region named CR-M (for babuviruses) or CR-II (for nanoviruses). Encodes 5-7 non-structural proteins. Evolutionary Context: Realm Monodnaviria, kingdom Shotokuvirae, phylum Cressdnaviricota, class Arfiviricetes, order Mulpavirales. Two genera: Babuvirus and Nanovirus. Genus demarcation based on host, vector, number and length of genomic DNAs, and presence of specific DNAs. Nanoviruses infect eudicots, while Babuviruses infect monocots. Host/Ecology: Host range is narrow. Nanoviruses infect eudicots, mainly Fabaceae. Babuviruses infect monocots, order Zingiberales. Transmitted by aphids in a circulative, non-propagative persistent manner. Viruses are restricted to the phloem tissue, and typically cause symptoms of stunting, reddening or yellowing of leaves, and sometimes leaf rolling and premature death. Geographical distribution is limited to the Old World.

name: Alphasatellitidae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: Circular, single-stranded DNA. Genome size: 1100-1380 nucleotides. Organization: Similar to DNA-R component of nanoviruses; contains an adenine-rich region and a satellite conserved region (SCR). Key proteins: Encodes a Rep protein (Cress-type Endonuclease). EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation: Satellite virus; requires helper Geminivirus (Begomoviruses, Mastrevirus, or Nanoviruses) for replication and packaging. HOST/ECOLOGY: Host range: Plants. Tropism: Phloem and sieve elements or phloem-limited tissues. Geographical distribution: Worldwide. Transmission: Vector-borne (insects). Replication: Nuclear. ssDNA converted to dsDNA by host factors. Bidirectional transcription from IR promoter. Replication initiated by REP cleavage via rolling circle. ssDNA can be converted to dsDNA for transcription/replication, encapsidated for virion formation, or transported to neighboring cells via plasmodesmata with viral movement proteins.

name: Kitaviridae
info: Family: Kitaviridae Genome Characteristics: ssRNA(+) viruses with multipartite genomes. Genomes are capped and polyadenylated. Number of genome components varies by genus: Blunervirus (4), Cilevirus (2), Higrevirus (3). Encodes replication (RdRP) and movement proteins. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm with a dsRNA intermediate, producing genome and subgenome-sized mRNAs. Translation is canonical. Evolutionary Context: Belongs to Realm Riboviria, Kingdom Orthornavirae, Phylum Kitrinoviricota, Class Alsuviricetes, Order Martellivirales. Contains 3 genera (Blunervirus, Cilevirus, Higrevirus) and 14 species. The family was established in 2019. Host/Ecology: Infects plants. Transmitted by mite vectors. Example species: tea plant necrotic ring blotch virus (genus Blunervirus, species Blunervirus camelliae).

name: Paulinoviridae
info: Family: Paulinoviridae Genome Characteristics: Members possess circular, single-stranded positive-sense DNA genomes ranging from 5.6 to 5.9 kb, encoding 8-10 proteins. Replication occurs via a rolling circle mechanism. Translation proceeds from mRNAs. Evolutionary Context: The family Paulinoviridae belongs to the realm Monodnaviria, kingdom Loebvirae, phylum Hofneiviricota, class Faserviricetes, and order Tubulavirales. It comprises two genera: Bifilivirus and Thomixvirus, encompassing three species. Taxonomic demarcation is based on genomic and virion characteristics. The name Paulinoviridae derives from the Latin "paulus," signifying "small," referencing the smaller genomes and fewer proteins compared to other Tubulavirales families. Bifilivirus is derived from the Latin "bifilum" meaning double thread, and Thomixvirus from the Latin "thomix" meaning cord, string, line, thread. Host/Ecology: Paulinoviridae viruses infect bacteria, specifically Actinomycetes and Deinococci. Virions are non-enveloped, flexible filaments with a diameter of 7-12 nm and a length of 620-830 nm. Geographical distribution and specific transmission patterns are not detailed.

name: Smacoviridae
info: Family: Smacoviridae GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: Circular ssDNA(+/-) Genome size: 2.3–3.1 kb Organization: Circular Replication: Rolling circle EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomy: Realm Monodnaviria, kingdom Shotokuvirae, phylum Cressdnaviricota, class Arfiviricetes, order Cremevirales Genera: 12 Species: 143 Demarcation: Based on sequence analysis and phylogenetic relationships. HOST/ECOLOGY: Host range: Diverse animals, including vertebrates; possibly archaea. Examples include baboons, bovine, cattle, cow, dragonfly, dromedary, feline, human, chicken, Indian peafowl, porcine, primate, and simian. Geographical distribution: Unknown, detected in environmental samples. Transmission: Unknown. Notes: Smacoviridae viruses were established in 2018. The name is derived from small circular ssDNA. Virions are predicted to be icosahedral. Translation mechanisms are unknown.

name: Artoviridae
info: Family: Artoviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome is a single-stranded, negative-sense, unsegmented RNA molecule, ranging from 11 to 12.5 kb in size. Genomes encode up to 5 structural proteins, including a nucleocapsid protein (N), glycoprotein (G), and an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP), designated as the large protein (L). The gene order is typically 3'-U1-U2-U3-(G)-L-5', where U1, U2, and U3 represent hypothetical proteins of unknown function. Evolutionary Context: Artoviridae belongs to the order Mononegavirales and is phylogenetically related to the families Bornaviridae, Lispiviridae, Mymonaviridae, and Nyamiviridae. The family includes two genera: Peropuvirus (9 species) and Hexartovirus (4 species). Taxonomic demarcation is based on phylogenetic analysis and biological properties. Host/Ecology: Artovirids infect a diverse range of invertebrate hosts, including barnacles, copepods, odonates, parasitoid wasps, pillworms, and woodlice. One species has been identified in eggplant. Geographical distribution varies depending on the host. For example, Pteromalus puparum negative-strand RNA virus 1 (PpNSRV-1) infects parasitoid wasps and is transmitted vertically. Lepeophtheirus salmonis negative-strand RNA virus 1 (LsNSRV-1) infects sea lice and has been detected in farmed Atlantic salmon in Norway.

name: Baculoviridae
info: Family: Baculoviridae Genome Characteristics: Circular, supercoiled dsDNA, 80-180 kbp in size, encoding 100-200 proteins. Contains 38 core genes involved in DNA replication, late gene transcription, and virion structure. Temporal gene regulation with early and late gene classes. Late genes transcribe from a 5'-TAAG-3' promoter motif. Putative replication origins are homologous repeat regions. Evolutionary Context: Belongs to the class Naldaviricetes, order Lefavirales, sharing structural, genetic, and biological characters with Nudiviridae, Hytrosaviridae, and Nimaviridae. Genera are distinguished by phylogeny, genome characteristics, host range, and occlusion body morphology. Key feature is the presence of pif-genes. Host/Ecology: Infects larval-stage insects of the orders Lepidoptera, Hymenoptera, and Diptera. Transmission occurs horizontally via contaminated food or egg surfaces, vertically within the egg, or experimentally via injection or cell culture infection. Viral replication begins in the insect midgut, followed by transmission to secondary tissues. Occlusion bodies (OBs) provide environmental stability. Persistent, asymptomatic infections are documented.

name: Amnoonviridae
info: Family: Amnoonviridae Genome Characteristics: Negative-sense RNA virus with a genome size of approximately 10.3 kb. The genome is segmented into 10 linear RNA molecules, each containing at least one open reading frame (ORF). RNA segments 1-3 encode subunits of the viral polymerase (RNA-directed RNA polymerase, RdRP), homologous to orthomyxovirid PB1, PB2, and PA. RNA segment 4 encodes a nucleoprotein. All segments have conserved complementary sequences at their 5' and 3' ends. Evolutionary Context: Belongs to the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Negarnaviricota, class Insthoviricetes, and order Articulavirales. Most closely related to orthomyxovirids. Contains one genus and one species. Host/Ecology: Known to infect actinopterygiid fish (tilapia) and squamate reptiles (Gulf tree gehyras). Tilapia lake virus (TiLV) has been detected in wild and farmed tilapia in Africa, Asia, and North America. TiLV causes systemic disease in tilapia, leading to high mortality. Experimentally infects zebrafish, Malawi cichlids, and Mozambique tilapia. Transmission patterns are still being researched.

name: Mimiviridae
info: Family: Mimiviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome consists of a single, linear, double-stranded DNA molecule of approximately 1,181,549 bp with 72% A+T content. It encodes approximately 1018 genes, including protein-coding genes, tRNAs, and non-coding mRNAs. The genome has inverted repeats of a 617-bp segment. Virions contain virus-encoded mRNAs. Virions contain at least 137 viral proteins, including structural components, transcription enzymes, and enzymes associated with oxidative pathways, protein/lipid modification, DNA topology, damage repair, and replication. Evolutionary Context: The family currently contains only one recognized genus, Mimivirus. Host/Ecology: Mimiviruses infect Acanthamoeba strains, including Acanthamoeba castellanii. They have been isolated from water sources. Metagenomic surveys suggest relatives are prevalent in marine environments, infecting heterotrophic protists. Transmission patterns in natural environments are not fully established. Initial findings suggested a link to pneumonia, but subsequent studies have not confirmed this. Mimivirus particles are internalized by phagocytic cells.

name: Pneumoviridae
info: Pneumoviridae is a family of enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses. The genome size ranges from 13.2 to 15.3 kb. Genomes encode 9-11 proteins, including nucleocapsid proteins (N, P, L), matrix proteins (M, M2-1), and envelope glycoproteins (F, G, SH). The RNA-dependent RNA polymerase complex includes P and L proteins; M2-1 is a processivity factor. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm. The family includes two genera: Orthopneumovirus and Metapneumovirus. Orthopneumoviruses have 10 genes, including NS1 and NS2, while Metapneumoviruses have 8. Gene order and intergenic region lengths also differ between genera. Viruses in both genera infect mammals; Metapneumoviruses also infect birds. Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) and human metapneumovirus (HMPV) are human pathogens. Transmission is primarily via aerosol droplets and contact. No known vectors exist. Pneumoviruses infect respiratory epithelial cells, causing respiratory disease. Infections are generally cleared by host immunity, but prolonged shedding can occur. The fusion (F) protein is a major neutralization antigen. The attachment (G) protein is a secondary neutralization antigen for Orthopneumoviruses. Antigenic subgroups exist within HRSV, HMPV, and avian metapneumovirus (AMPV), based on genetic and antigenic differences, particularly in the G protein. Pneumoviridae members share gene expression, replication strategies, and gene order similarities with other Mononegavirales families like Paramyxoviridae, Rhabdoviridae, and Filoviridae.

name: Vilmaviridae
info: Family: Vilmaviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, double-stranded DNA genome of 69-76 kb, encoding approximately 123-129 genes. Contains 1 to 12 tRNAs. Evolutionary Context: Based on ICTV criteria. Host/Ecology: Infects Mycobacteria. Exhibits a worldwide geographical distribution. Transmission occurs via passive diffusion through the medium. Virion Characteristics: Non-enveloped with a head-tail structure exhibiting Sipho-type morphology. The icosahedral head is approximately 80 nm in diameter. The non-contractile tail is about 350 nm in length. Replication: Cytoplasmic. Adsorption to host cell adhesion receptors via tail fibers. Viral DNA ejection into the host cytoplasm through a long flexible tail ejection system. Early and late gene transcription and translation. Genomic DNA replication. Assembly of an empty procapsid and genome packaging. Viral tail fiber and tail assembly. Virions are released via cell lysis.

name: Polycipiviridae
info: Family: Polycipiviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome consists of a single molecule of linear, positive-sense, non-segmented RNA, ranging from 10 to 12 kb. It is polycistronic, containing four or more 5'-proximal open reading frames (ORFs) and a long 3' ORF. The genome has a 3'-poly(A) tail and is presumed to have a small viral protein genome-linked (VPg) covalently attached to the 5'-end. Key conserved domains include superfamily III helicase, chymotrypsin-like serine protease, and superfamily I RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP). Evolutionary Context: Polycipiviridae belongs to the order Picornavirales. Genera are separated based on phylogenetic clustering based on protein sequence identities. Polycipiviruses have polyadenylated positive-sense RNA genomes that encode three jelly-roll capsid proteins, a superfamily III helicase, a 3C-like chymotrypsin-related protease and a superfamily I RdRP. Unlike other members of the order, with the exception of marnaviruses, the polycipivirus protease has serine rather than cysteine at the active site. Polycipiviruses also have a unique genome organization. Host/Ecology: The known host range is Arthropoda, with the majority of viruses derived from ants. Members of the type species Solenopsis invicta virus 2 appear to establish a chronic, asymptomatic infection in Solenopsis invicta ants. Transmission patterns for Solenopsis invicta virus 2 suggest food-borne transmission, probably by trophallaxis. Fire ant infections with SINV2 are associated with negative impacts on queen ants resulting in significant reductions in fecundity, longer claustral periods, and slower growth of newly established colonies.

name: Pospiviroidae
info: Family: Pospiviroidae Genome Characteristics: Members possess a single-stranded, circular RNA genome ranging from 246-375 nucleotides. The RNA adopts a rod-like or quasi rod-like conformation. A central conserved region (CCR) is crucial for replication. A terminal conserved region (TCR) or a terminal conserved hairpin (TCH) is also present. The genome contains five structural/functional domains: C (central), P (pathogenic), V (variable), TL (terminal left), and TR (terminal right). Replication occurs via an asymmetric RNA-RNA rolling-circle mechanism using host DNA-dependent RNA polymerase II. No translation occurs. Evolutionary Context: Genus demarcation relies on the type of CCR and the presence/absence of a TCR or TCH. Five genera are recognized: Apscaviroid, Cocadviroid, Coleviroid, Hostuviroid, and Pospiviroid. Pospiviroidae lack ribozymes, distinguishing them from Avsunviroidae. Host/Ecology: The host range includes various angiosperm plant species, primarily dicotyledons, though some infect monocotyledons. Transmission occurs through vegetative propagation, mechanical means, seed, and pollen. Aphid transmission is generally negligible. Bumblebees and whiteflies may act as vectors for some members. Infections can cause a range of symptoms, from severe disease to mild or no symptoms, depending on the viroid-host combination. Symptom expression is influenced by temperature and light intensity. Viroids move systemically through the phloem, potentially aided by plant proteins.

name: Bacilladnaviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: Circular, single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) with an approximately 800bp partially double-stranded region. Genome size and organization: Approximately 5-6 kb. Encodes 3 proteins. Key conserved domains: Cress-type Endonuclease (Rep). EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment: Information not provided. HOST/ECOLOGY: Known/predicted host range: Chaetoceros sp. (diatoms). Geographical distribution: Information not provided. Transmission patterns: Virus penetrates host cell. Uncoating occurs, and the viral ssDNA genome enters the nucleus. Viral ssDNA is converted to dsDNA using cellular factors. dsDNA transcription produces viral mRNAs, which are translated into viral proteins. Replication, potentially mediated by a Rep protein, occurs via rolling circle replication, producing ssDNA genomes. These ssDNA genomes can be converted to dsDNA for further transcription/replication or encapsidated by capsid proteins to form virions. Virions are released via cell lysis.

name: Matonaviridae
info: Matonaviridae is a family of enveloped viruses with single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genomes of 9.6-10 kb. The family contains one genus, Rubivirus, which includes Rubivirus rubellae (rubella virus, RuV), Rubivirus ruteetense (ruhugu virus, RuhV), and Rubivirus strelense (rustrela virus, RusV). Genome Characteristics: The genome is non-segmented, single-stranded, positive-sense RNA with two open reading frames encoding non-structural and structural proteins. Conserved domains include methyltransferase, ADP-ribose-1"-phosphatase, helicase, and RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP). Evolutionary Context: Rubiviruses were previously classified within Togaviridae but were moved to Matonaviridae due to differences in transmission, virion structure, and sequence relationships. Phylogenetic analysis shows similarities to Benyviridae, Hepeviridae, and Alphatetraviridae. Host/Ecology: RuV infects humans and is transmitted via the respiratory route, causing rubella. Postnatal infection is generally mild, but congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) can occur in infants born to infected pregnant women. RuhV infects bats, and RusV infects rodents and other mammals, causing encephalitis in some species. The zoonotic potential of RuhV and RusV is not fully known. RuV has a global distribution, while RuhV and RusV have been found in Uganda and Germany, respectively. Safe and effective live-attenuated vaccines against rubella are globally available.

name: Gammaflexiviridae
info: Family: Gammaflexiviridae Genome Characteristics: ssRNA, linear, positive-sense, 6827 nt (excluding poly(A) tail). Contains two major ORFs. ORF1 encodes a 153 kDa protein with methyltransferase and helicase motifs; readthrough yields a 212 kDa protein including an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) domain. ORF2 encodes a 32 kDa coat protein (CP). Evolutionary Context: Phylogenetic relationships to viruses in the order Tymovirales. Distinct readthrough translation strategy justifies separate family status. Host/Ecology: Known host is the plant pathogenic fungus Botrytis cinerea. Geographical distribution and transmission patterns are unknown. Virion Properties: Flexuous filaments, 720 nm in length and 13 nm in diameter. Composed of a single coat protein of 302 amino acids (32 kDa). Lipids and carbohydrates not reported. Antigenic Properties: Not known. Derivation of Name: Flexi: from flexus, Latin for “bent”. Mycoflexi: from mycovirus with flexuous virions.

name: Yadokariviridae
info: Family: Yadokariviridae Genome Characteristics: Non-segmented, linear, positive-sense (+) RNA genome, ranging from 3.6 to 6.3 kb. Genomes are typically monocistronic, encoding a polyprotein containing an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) and a smaller protein, often with a 2A-like self-cleaving peptide. Some members have bicistronic genomes. The RdRP contains key conserved domains. Some genomes are polyadenylated. Evolutionary Context: Phylum Pisuviricota. Forms the order Yadokarivirales. Yadokarivirids are capsidless viruses that rely on phylogenetically distant double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) viruses for capsids. Genus demarcation is based on RdRP amino acid sequence phylogeny and sequence similarity. Host/Ecology: Known hosts are fungi and possibly oomycetes. Geographical distribution includes Asia, Europe, and the Middle East. Transmission occurs via heterocapsids acquired from co-infecting dsRNA viruses. Each yadokarivirid species typically partners with a specific dsRNA virus species. Yadokarivirids exhibit complex symbiotic relationships (mutualistic, commensal, or harmful) with their capsid donor viruses and host fungi.

name: Sinhaliviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: ssRNA(+) Genome size and organization: Linear, 5.9-6.0 kb Key conserved domains: Not specified EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment: Established family in 2020. Realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Kitrinoviricota, class Magsaviricetes, order Nodamuvirales. Contains 1 genus and 2 species. HOST/ECOLOGY: Known/predicted host range: Invertebrates Geographical distribution: Not specified Transmission patterns: Not specified ADDITIONAL INFORMATION: Virion: Icosahedral, 30 nm diameter Replication: Cytoplasmic, genome-length dsRNA is transcribed/replicated Translation: Capped genome RNA is translated Name Derivation: Sinhaliviridae from Sinaivirus (defunct name) and Halictivirus; Sinaivirus from Sinaivirus (defunct name).

name: Adintoviridae
info: Family: Adintoviridae Genome Characteristics: Circular, double-stranded DNA genome ranging from 11 to 24 kb. Contains 10 to 21 open reading frames (ORFs). Encodes DNA-directed DNA polymerase B (DNApol) and Integrase (Int). Some members may encode jelly-roll fold capsid proteins. Evolutionary Context: Formerly named Adintoviridae, renamed Eupolintoviridae in 2023. Associated with Polinton virus DNA transposons. Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not explicitly documented. Host/Ecology: Infects both vertebrates and invertebrates. Geographical distribution and transmission patterns are undocumented. Replication and gene expression mechanisms are also undocumented.

name: Pleolipoviridae
info: Family: Pleolipoviridae Genome Characteristics: The Pleolipoviridae family comprises archaeal viruses with pseudo-spherical, pleomorphic virions lacking a protein capsid. The genome can be circular single-stranded DNA (7-11 kb), circular double-stranded DNA (8-17 kb), or linear double-stranded DNA (approximately 16 kb). Genomes contain 8-35 predicted ORFs. A conserved block of collinear genes encodes major structural proteins, a putative NTPase, and other proteins. Alphapleolipoviruses encode rolling circle replication initiation proteins. Betapleolipoviruses encode proteins with unknown function, some with a winged helix-turn-helix domain. Gammapleolipoviruses encode a type B DNA polymerase. Virions contain one or two types of internal membrane protein and one or two types of spike protein. Lipids are derived non-selectively from host cell membranes. Evolutionary Context: Genera are differentiated by genome type and phylogenomic analysis. Alphapleolipovirus genomes are circular ssDNA or dsDNA. Betapleolipovirus genomes are circular dsDNA. Gammapleolipovirus genomes are linear dsDNA. Pleolipoviruses form a distinct group with no significant amino acid similarity to other viral structural proteins. Host/Ecology: Pleolipoviruses infect extremely halophilic archaea in the class Halobacteria (phylum Euryarchaeota), specifically Halorubrum, Haloarcula, Halogeometricum or Natrinema strains. They exhibit a narrow host range and a persistent, non-lytic life cycle, sometimes temperate with integration into the host chromosome. They are found in hypersaline environments globally. Transmission occurs via budding.

name: Quadriviridae
info: Family: Quadriviridae Genome Characteristics: The Quadriviridae family comprises non-enveloped viruses with a quadripartite, linear, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genome. The genome consists of four segments, ranging from 3.5 to 5.0 kbp, totaling 16.8-17.1 kbp. Each segment contains a single large open reading frame (ORF). The largest segment (dsRNA1) encodes a hypothetical protein, dsRNA2 and dsRNA4 encode capsid proteins, and dsRNA3 encodes RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP). Conserved terminal sequences are present in all segments. Evolutionary Context: Phylogenetic analysis indicates that quadriviruses are most closely related to members of the genus Totivirus (family Totiviridae). Taxonomic reorganization of the family Totiviridae may be warranted based on the phylogenetic affinity between Quadriviridae and certain Totiviridae members. Host/Ecology: Quadriviruses infect filamentous fungi, specifically Rosellinia necatrix. They are transmitted intracellularly via hyphal anastomosis. Vertical transmission through spores and horizontal transmission via vectors are not known. The viruses persist in their fungal hosts. Horizontal transmission between vegetatively incompatible mycelia can occur in the presence of Zn2+, which retards programmed cell death.

name: Aliceevansviridae
info: Family: Aliceevansviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, double-stranded DNA genome ranging from 34-50 kb, encoding approximately 50 genes. Key conserved domains not specified. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not specified. Host/Ecology: Host Range: Bacteria. Specifically, the phage attaches to the target cell adhesion receptor FhuA through its tail fibers. Geographical Distribution: Worldwide. Transmission: Passive diffusion through medium. Additional Information: Aliceevansviridae, including Brussowvirus, are temperate siphoviruses. Virions are non-enveloped with a head-tail structure exhibiting Sipho-type morphology. The icosahedral head is approximately 100 nm in diameter, and the non-contractile tail is about 400 nm in length. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm. The viral life cycle involves attachment to the host cell, ejection of viral DNA, transcription and translation of early and late genes, genome replication, procapsid assembly, genome packaging via a headful mechanism, tail fiber and tail assembly, and virion release via cell lysis.

name: Lavidaviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: dsDNA. Genome size: 18.3 kb. Genome organization: Circular. Number of ORFs: 21. Key conserved domains: Protease (Peptidase S74), Helicase. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment: Lavidaviridae (taxid:1914302), formerly Sputniviroviridae (2025). Satellite virus requiring Mimivirus co-infection. HOST/ECOLOGY: Host range: Protists infected by Mimivirus. Geographical distribution: Undocumented. Transmission patterns: Passive diffusion through water. Capsid: Non-enveloped, icosahedral (T=27 symmetry), 50 nm diameter. Gene Expression: Undocumented. Replication: Undocumented. Source: ViralZone Type: Family Name: Lavidaviridae

name: Metaviridae
info: Family: Metaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Metaviridae family comprises retrotransposons and reverse-transcribing viruses with long terminal repeats (LTRs), also known as Ty3/Gypsy LTR retroelements. The genome consists of two identical copies of linear, single-stranded, positive-sense RNA. Genome lengths vary from 3 kb to over 15 kb. Key conserved domains include Gag (capsid protein, nucleocapsid protein) and Pol (protease, reverse transcriptase, ribonuclease H, integrase). The typical genome architecture is 5'-LTR-CP-NC-PR-RT-RH-INT-LTR-3', with some members also encoding an envelope protein (SU-TM). Evolutionary Context: Metaviridae belongs to the order Ortervirales. Genera demarcation criteria are based on the presence (Errantivirus) or absence (Metavirus) of an env gene, though this criterion is inconsistent with evolutionary history. Host/Ecology: Metaviridae members are widely distributed in eukaryotes, including fungi, plants, and animals. They replicate via reverse transcription primed with a host-encoded tRNA. The viral membrane, when present, is derived from the host cell membrane. Integration into the host genome can be mutagenic, leading to the development of mechanisms to target integration into less disruptive loci. Some members target heterochromatin or centromeric regions. Host organisms have also developed mechanisms to modulate the activity of integrated metaviruses.

name: Aoguangviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Family Aoguangviridae members possess linear, double-stranded DNA genomes ranging from 90-100 kbp. Genomes exhibit a G+C content around 31.5% and encode a large number of proteins, including a complete virus-encoded DNA replisome. Genomes may exhibit terminal redundancy and/or circular permutation. Key conserved domains include a family B DNA polymerase, archaeo-eukaryotic DNA primase, and other replication/repair proteins. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Aoguangviridae is classified within the realm Duplodnaviria, kingdom Heunggongvirae, phylum Uroviricota, class Caudoviricetes, and order Magrovirales. Genus demarcation is suggested at 60% protein sequence identity, and species demarcation at 95% overall genome sequence identity. Aoguangviridae is closely related to other unclassified archaeal viruses within the order Magrovirales and distantly related to the family Druskaviridae. HOST/ECOLOGY: Aoguangviridae viruses infect marine archaea of the order Poseidoniales. These viruses are globally distributed in marine environments. Transmission patterns are currently unknown, but the absence of integrases/transposases suggests a lytic lifestyle. No members have been cultured; therefore, biological insights are derived from computational analysis.

name: Yangangviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: dsDNA, linear genome of 36-38 kb, encoding approximately 68 genes. Encodes Terminate [TerL], HNH endonuclease [Endo], DNA methyltransferase [MTase], and Protease (Peptidase M) [Pro]. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment unavailable. HOST/ECOLOGY: Host range: Nitrososphaeria marine archaea. Geographical distribution: Undocumented. Transmission patterns: Undocumented. Morphology: Non-enveloped, head-tail structure with Sipho-type morphology. Icosahedral head. Replication: Cytoplasmic. Gene expression: Undocumented. Source: ViralZone. Type: Family. Name: Yangangviridae.

name: Yanlukaviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: dsDNA, linear genome of approximately 35 kb, encoding about 68 putative genes. Encodes Terminase (TerL), Metallophosphatase (MPtase), Endonuclease (Endo), HnH endonuclease (HNH), DNA methyltransferases (MTase1, MTase2), and Protease (Pro). EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment is not documented. HOST/ECOLOGY: Natural host is Nitrososphaeria marine archaea. Geographical distribution and transmission patterns are undocumented. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION: Family Yanlukaviridae. Predicted to be non-enveloped with a head-tail structure exhibiting Sipho-type morphology. The head is icosahedral. Gene expression and replication (cytoplasmic) are undocumented. Information source: ViralZone.

name: Chaacviridae
info: Family: Chaacviridae Genome Characteristics: dsDNA, linear genomes of 10.2-10.8 kbp with inverted terminal repeats. Evolutionary Context: Realm Varidnaviria, kingdom Abadenavirae, phylum Produgelaviricota, class Belvinaviricetes, order Coyopavirales. Contains 2 genera and 3 species. Established in 2023. Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment information derived from ICTV Report Editors, Taxonomic Proposals, and the Master Species List. Host/Ecology: Infects anaerobic methanotrophic ANME-1 archaea. Geographical distribution inferred from metagenomic studies. Transmission patterns not explicitly established but inferred to occur within anaerobic methanotrophic environments. Virion: Predicted to have tailless icosahedral virions, known only from metagenomic studies. Etymology: Chaacviridae named after Chaac, the Mayan god of rain. Antichaacvirus derived from the Greek "anti" (opposed). Homochaacvirus derived from the Greek "homo" (same). Example: Methanophagales virus PBV304 (OP548099), species Homochaacvirus pescaderoense, genus Homochaacvirus.

name: Tulasviridae
info: Family: Tulasviridae Genome Characteristics:  Nucleic acid type: RNA, ambisense  Genome size and organization: Approximately 12.2 kb, non-segmented, linear. Contains 2-3 open reading frames (ORFs) encoding a nucleoprotein (NP), a large (L) protein with an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain, and a protein of unknown function (X).  Key conserved domains: RdRP domain in the L protein. Evolutionary Context:  Taxonomic demarcation criteria: Genus demarcation is based on monophyly and the number of ORFs (Orthotulasvirus: 3 ORFs; Paratulasvirus: 2 ORFs). Phylogenetically related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, and tospovirids. Host/Ecology:  Host range: Agaricomycete fungi, including Tulasnella sp. and Agrocybe praecox.  Geographical distribution: Detected in Italy (Tulasnella bunyavirales-like virus 1) and Japan (Agrocybe praecox tulasvirus 1).  Transmission patterns: Unknown. Taxonomy:  Realm: Riboviria  Kingdom: Orthornavirae  Phylum: Negarnaviricota  Class: Bunyaviricetes  Order: Elliovirales  Genera: Orthotulasvirus, Paratulasvirus  Species examples: Orthotulasvirus tulasnellae (e.g., Tulasnella bunyavirales-like virus 1), Agrocybe praecox tulasvirus 1.

name: Plectroviridae
info: Family: Plectroviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome is a supercoiled, circular, positive-sense single-stranded DNA molecule, ranging from 4.5 to 8.3 kb, encoding 4-13 proteins. G+C content varies from 22.2% to 33.3%. Key proteins include a major coat protein (7.5-19 kDa), DDE-type transposase (Vespertiliovirus), and replication protein (Suturavirus). Genome replication occurs via rolling-circle (Plectrovirus, Suturavirus) or transposition (Vespertiliovirus) mechanisms. UGA codon encodes tryptophan in Suturavirus and Vespertiliovirus. Evolutionary Context: Belongs to the order Tubulavirales, sharing morphological and genomic similarities with Inoviridae and Paulinoviridae. Genus demarcation is based on DNA sequence similarity (BLASTn) and >50% similarity of major coat protein and maturation protein sequences (BLASTp). Host/Ecology: Infects cell wall-less bacteria (Acholeplasma and Spiroplasma). Geographical distribution is not specified. Transmission occurs via extrusion of virions from host cells, establishing a chronic productive infection without cell lysis. Some members can form plaques. Vespertiliovirus alters spiroplasma genomes via transposition. Suturavirus integration can cause resistance to reinfection.

name: Mayoviridae
info: Family: Mayoviridae Genome Characteristics: ssRNA(+) genome, bisegmented, not polyadenylated. Replication occurs in the cytoplasm with a dsRNA intermediate, producing genome and subgenome-sized mRNAs. Translation is canonical. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation is based on molecular characteristics and host range. Taxonomy: Realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Kitrinoviricota, class Alsuviricetes, order Martellivirales. Contains 2 genera and 4 species. Host/Ecology: Infects plants and is transmitted by pollen. Example: privet leaf blotch-associated virus (species Idaeovirus ligustri, genus Idaeovirus). Geographical distribution is not specified. Virion: Non-enveloped, icosahedral. Nomenclature: Mayoviridae is named in honor of plant virologist Michael A Mayo. Idaeovirus is derived from Rubus idaeus, the host plant of raspberry bushy dwarf virus. Pteridovirus is derived from the Ancient Greek word for "fern". Established: 2020.

name: Tosoviridae
info: Family: Tosoviridae Genome Characteristics: Tosoviridae viruses possess a bi-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome of approximately 12.3 kb. The genome consists of a small (S) segment (about 5.7 kb) and a large (L) segment (about 6.6 kb), each containing two open reading frames (ORFs) in ambisense orientation. The S segment encodes a nucleoprotein (NP) and a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), while the L segment encodes a large (L) protein with an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain and a zinc-binding (Z) protein. The RdRP shows distant relation to other negarnaviricots, while the GPC is homologous to hantavirid actinoviruses. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria are not applicable as the family contains only one genus and one species. Host/Ecology: The known host range includes emydid and trionychid turtles (softshell turtles and cooters). An unclassified tosovirid has been found in eels in New Zealand. Transmission patterns are currently unknown.

Replication may be mediated by a Rep protein, and would occur by rolling circle producing ssDNA genomes. name: Nimaviridae
info: Family: Nimaviridae Genome Characteristics: The family Nimaviridae contains viruses with a single molecule of circular, double-stranded DNA genome ranging from 280 to 307 kbp. Transmission occurs through cannibalism of diseased individuals, waterborne exposure via gills, and vertical transmission from adults to offspring. WSSV has been identified in crustaceans from China, Japan, Korea, Southeast Asia, South Asia, the Middle East, and the Americas. Major targets of infection are tissues of ectodermal and mesodermal embryonic origin.
