These viruses possess icosahedral capsids (approximately 60 nm in diameter) and non-contractile helical tails (approximately 230 nm in length), exhibiting siphoviral morphology. Evolutionary Context: The family Anaerodiviridae was established in 2022. It is classified within the realm Duplodnaviria, kingdom Heunggongvirae, phylum Uroviricota, class Caudoviricetes, and order Methanobavirales. Taxonomic demarcation is based on viruses infecting methanogenic archaea. The family currently contains one genus (Metforvirus) and one species (Metforvirus limi). Host/Ecology: Anaerodiviridae viruses infect methanogenic archaea of the class Methanobacteria. The type species, Metforvirus limi, was isolated from Methanobacterium formicicum Khl10, a hydrogenotrophic methanogen. The name "Anaerodiviridae" is derived from "anaerobic digester," reflecting the source of isolation.

name: Nenyaviridae
info: Family: Nenyaviridae Genome Characteristics: ssDNA, circular, monopartite genome ranging from 1700 to 3000 bp. Replication occurs via double-stranded DNA intermediates, utilizing rolling circle replication initiated and terminated by the Rep protein. A conserved nonanucleotide sequence (AGTATTAC) within a stem-loop structure in the intergenic region is the site of ssDNA synthesis initiation. Evolutionary Context: Taxid: 2946189. Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not specified. Host/Ecology: Natural hosts are Entamoeba parasites. Geographical distribution is worldwide. Transmission patterns are not explicitly established, but virions are presumably released by cell lysis. Replication: Nuclear. Virus penetrates the host cell and the viral ssDNA genome enters the nucleus. Viral ssDNA is converted to dsDNA using cellular factors. Transcription of dsDNA produces viral mRNAs, which are translated into viral proteins. Replication is mediated by the Rep protein via rolling circle replication, producing ssDNA genomes. Newly synthesized ssDNA can be converted to dsDNA for further transcription/replication or encapsidated by capsid protein to form virions. Gene Expression: The viral DNA and complementary DNA encode two mRNAs for the Rep and capsid proteins. Enzymes: Cress-type Endonuclease [Rep]. Virion: Non-enveloped, round, presumably T=1 icosahedral symmetry.

name: Cremegaviridae
info: Family: Cremegaviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome is monopartite, linear, single-stranded positive-sense RNA, approximately 17 kb in size. It is capped and polyadenylated. The genome encodes a polyprotein that is processed into non-structural proteins, including an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), Nido-type capping enzymes (GDP polyribonucleotidyltransferase, N7methyltransferase, 2'O methylase), EndoU ribonuclease, polyprotein major protease (Peptidase S32), other proteases (Peptidase C31, Peptidase C32, Peptidase C33), and a helicase. Structural proteins are expressed as subgenomic RNAs. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not specified in provided information. Host/Ecology: The known natural hosts are turtles. The virus replicates in the cytoplasm. Attachment to host receptors mediates clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Fusion of the viral membrane with the endosomal membrane releases the ssRNA(+) genome into the cytoplasm. Replication occurs in viral factories, involving synthesis and proteolysis of replicase polyproteins, dsRNA intermediate, and subgenomic mRNAs. Assembly and ESCRT-independent budding occur at the membranes of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), intermediate compartments, and/or Golgi complex. Virions are released by exocytosis. The virion is enveloped, spherical, and approximately 45-60 nm in diameter, with an isometric core of 20-30 nm surrounded by a lipid-containing envelope. The RNA genome associates with the N protein to form the nucleocapsid.

name: Saparoviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: dsDNA. Genome size: 52-54 kbp, linear, circularly permuted. Organization: Icosahedral capsid with non-contractile helical tail (siphovirus-like morphology). Key conserved domains: Not specified. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation: Realm Duplodnaviria, kingdom Heunggongvirae, phylum Uroviricota, class Caudoviricetes. Established in 2022. Contains 2 genera and 2 species. HOST/ECOLOGY: Host range: Hyperhalophilic archaea of Haloarcula sp. Geographical distribution: Not specified. Transmission patterns: Not specified. Additional Information: Family name derivation: Saparoviridae from Finnish saparo, meaning pig tail. Example virus: Haloarcula californiae tailed virus 2 (KC292028), species Samsavirus crystalli, genus Samsavirus. Source: ICTV. Type: Family. Name: Saparoviridae.

name: Suolaviridae
info: Suolaviridae is a virus family established in 2022, belonging to the realm Duplodnaviria, kingdom Heunggongvirae, phylum Uroviricota, and class Caudoviricetes. The name is derived from the Finnish word "suola," meaning salt. GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Members of this family possess linear, double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) genomes of approximately 35 kbp. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: The family currently comprises one genus, Pormufvirus, and one species, Pormufvirus salinum. Taxonomic demarcation is based on genomic characteristics. HOST/ECOLOGY: Suolaviridae viruses infect hyperhalophilic archaea of the genus Halorubrum. Virions exhibit an icosahedral capsid with a non-contractile helical tail, displaying siphoviral morphology. An example is Halorubrum tailed virus 28 (MZ334528).

name: Pyrstoviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: dsDNA, linear. Genome size: ~42 kb. Genome organization: Encodes ~89 putative genes. Key conserved domains: Terminase (TerL, TerS), Endonuclease (Endo), HNH endonuclease (HNH1, HNH2, HNH3). EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment: Not specified. HOST/ECOLOGY: Known/predicted host range: Archaea. Geographical distribution: Not specified. Transmission patterns: Not specified. Replication: Cytoplasmic. Additional Information: Virion: Presumably non-enveloped, head-tail structure with Sipho-type morphology. Gene Expression: Undocumented. Etymology: Pyrstoviridae: from Finnish "pyrsto" (fish tail), referring to virion morphology. Reference Strain: Haloarcula tailed virus 3. Source: ViralZone. Type: Family. Name: Pyrstoviridae. TaxID: 2946181.

name: Aggregaviridae
info: Family: Aggregaviridae Genome Characteristics: dsDNA, circular genome of approximately 43 kb, encoding about 79 proteins. Genes are transcribed by operons. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation based on marine bacteria host. Host/Ecology: Host Range: Olleya marine bacteria. Geographical Distribution: Not specified. Transmission: Passive diffusion through medium. Virion: Non-enveloped, head-tail structure with Myo-type morphology. Icosahedral head diameter is approximately 43 nm. Contracted tail length is about 123 nm with myoviral morphology. Replication: Cytoplasmic. Adsorption via tail fibers. Viral DNA ejection into host cytoplasm via tail sheath contraction. Transcription and translation of early genes, followed by genome replication. Transcription and translation of late genes. Assembly of procapsid and genome packaging. Viral tail fiber and tail assembly. Virion release via cell lysis. Reference Strains: Olleya phage Harreka. Antiviral Drugs: None. Etymology: Aggregaviridae derived from the marine bacteria host found in aggregates.

name: Halomagnusviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Family Halomagnusviridae members possess linear, double-stranded DNA genomes, approximately 144 kbp in size. The viruses exhibit myoviral morphology, characterized by an icosahedral capsid and a contractile helical tail. Halogranum tailed virus 1 encodes 36 tRNAs for all universal genetic code amino acids. Prokaryotic translation occurs using viral mRNA and host ribosomes. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Halomagnusviridae is classified within the realm Duplodnaviria, kingdom Heunggongvirae, phylum Uroviricota, class Caudoviricetes, and order Thumleimavirales. The family currently comprises one genus (Hagravirus) and one species (Hagravirus capitaneum). Taxonomic demarcation is based on genomic and morphological characteristics. HOST/ECOLOGY: The known host range of Halomagnusviridae is limited to hyperhalophilic archaea of the class Halobacteria, specifically Halogranum sp. SS5-1. Replication is lytic. The geographical distribution is linked to the presence of susceptible haloarchaeal hosts. Transmission patterns are not explicitly detailed but presumed to occur through direct contact within hypersaline environments.

name: Hadakaviridae
info: Family: Hadakaviridae Genome Characteristics:  Nucleic acid type: Positive-sense (+) single-stranded RNA  Genome size and organization: Multi-segmented genome of 10-11 linear RNA segments (0.9-2.5 kb each, 14-15 kb total). Segments are monocistronic and non-polyadenylated. Double-stranded RNA replicative forms accumulate in infected cells.  Key conserved domains: Encodes an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP), a hypothetical protein, and a putative methyltransferase (MTR) homologous to those of Polymycoviridae. Some isolates encode a C2H2-type zinc finger protein. Conserved terminal sequences 5′-CGU and CCA-3′ or CCG-3′ are present on most segments. Evolutionary Context:  Taxonomic demarcation: One genus (Hadakavirus) with one species. Closely related to Polymycoviridae based on phylogenetic analysis of conserved proteins. Shows phylogenetic affinity to (+) RNA viruses in the phylum Pisuviricota. Host/Ecology:  Host range: Ascomycetous filamentous fungi (e.g., Fusarium oxysporum, F. nygamai, Colletotrichum fructicola).  Geographical distribution: Pakistan, China.  Transmission patterns: Vertical transmission through asexual spores.  Additional notes: Capsidless viruses, cannot be pelleted by ultracentrifugation, and RNA is susceptible to ribonuclease. Some members may be associated with lipid-layered vesicles. Some isolates cause mild growth reduction or infection delay in hosts.

name: Madisaviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: dsDNA, linear genome of 49 kbp, circularly permuted. Encodes conserved domains. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Family Madisaviridae, established in 2022. Taxonomy: Realm Duplodnaviria, kingdom Heunggongvirae, phylum Uroviricota, class Caudoviricetes. Contains 1 genus (Clampvirus) and 1 species (Clampvirus italiense). Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment available in ICTV Master Species List 37. HOST/ECOLOGY: Infects hyperhalophilic archaea of the species Haloarcula hispanica. Example virus: Haloarcula hispanica tailed virus 1 (KC292025). Lytic life cycle. Geographical distribution not specified, but virus was isolated in Margherita di Savoia, Italy. Transmission patterns not established. Virion: Icosahedral capsid and a non-contractile helical tail (siphoviral morphology). Derivation of name: Madisaviridae: truncation of Margherita di Savoia – the place of virus isolation.

name: Vertoviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: dsDNA genome, 55-58 kbp, circularly permuted. Encodes an invertible tail fiber locus. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Family Vertoviridae; Realm Duplodnaviria, kingdom Heunggongvirae, phylum Uroviricota, class Caudoviricetes. Contains 2 genera and 3 species. Taxonomic demarcation based on shared characteristics and phylogenetic relationships. Established in 2022. HOST/ECOLOGY: Infects hyperhalophilic archaea, including Natrialba magadii and Halobacterium salinarum. Geographical distribution presumed to be worldwide where suitable hosts exist. Transmission patterns not explicitly stated but assumed to be via direct contact or environmental persistence. ICTV Source.

name: Sphaerolipoviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Family Sphaerolipoviridae members possess a linear, double-stranded DNA genome, ranging from 28 to 31 kbp, with a GC content of 67-68%. The genome features inverted terminal repeats of approximately 300 bp with covalently bound terminal proteins. Genomes contain about 50 predicted open reading frames with conserved synteny. Twelve genes encode structural proteins, including major and minor capsid proteins, internal membrane proteins, and vertex complex proteins. The virion contains lipids selectively acquired from the host cell membrane. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Sphaerolipoviruses, along with families Matsushitaviridae and Simuloviridae, are classified within the order Halopanivirales, class Laserviricetes, phylum Dividoviricota, and kingdom Helvetiavirae. These families share structural similarities, including two single jelly-roll major capsid proteins and an internal lipid membrane. Sphaerolipoviruses exhibit a pseudo T=28 dextro capsid lattice, similar to Thermus bacteriophage P23-77. HOST/ECOLOGY: Sphaerolipoviruses infect halophilic archaea within the class Halobacteria (phylum Euryarchaeota), specifically Haloarcula and Halorubrum strains. The host range is narrow, with some evidence suggesting potential infectivity of Natrialba and Haloferax species. These viruses have been isolated from hypersaline environments in Europe, Asia, and Australia. The infection cycle is lytic, lasting 6-12 hours, with a burst size of 50-200 viruses per cell. Transmission occurs through a lytic life cycle.

name: Kolmioviridae
info: Family: Kolmioviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome is a non-segmented, negative-sense, covalently-closed circular RNA (cccRNA) of 1.5-1.7 kb. It contains ribozymes and forms a rod-like structure due to self-complementarity. Kolmiovirids encode at least one protein, delta antigen (DAg). Evolutionary Context: Viruses assigned to the eleven genera form a monophyletic clade based on phylogenetic analysis of delta antigen (DAg) homologs. Viruses from all eleven genera share at least two of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped spherical virions; (ii) circular negative-sense RNA genome containing ribozymes and encoding a DAg homolog; (iii) requiring an unrelated helper virus for assembly of infectious virions. Genus demarcation is based on DAg amino acid sequence similarity (≤60% between genera). Kolmiovirids are unrelated to other negative-sense RNA viruses but share similarities with viroids and related elements. Host/Ecology: Kolmiovirids infect a broad range of hosts, including amphibians, birds, fish, insects, mammals, and reptiles. Transmission is dependent on helper viruses, which provide envelope proteins for virion assembly. Host tropism is primarily determined by the distribution of the helper virus. Genera are associated with specific host groups: Daazvirus (salamanders), Dobrovirus (toads), Dalvirus (ducks/teals), Perithurisazvirus (tits/finches/munias), Dagazvirus (termites), Donvirus (termites), Deevirus (fish), Deltavirus (humans/marsupials), Perideltavirus (deer/squirrels/bats), Thurisazvirus (rodents/bats), Daletvirus (snakes). Deltaviruses are known to cause diseases in humans.

name: Yaraviridae
info: Yaraviridae GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: dsDNA, linear genome of approximately 45 kb. Encodes about 74 proteins. Contains a double jelly roll-fold major capsid protein (MCP). EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not specified. HOST/ECOLOGY: Host Range: Amoebae. Geographical Distribution: Brazil (site of initial isolation). Transmission: Passive diffusion through medium. Replication: Cytoplasmic. Adsorption to target cell, followed by viral DNA injection into the host cell cytoplasm. Early gene transcription and translation occur, followed by genomic DNA replication via a rolling-circle mechanism. Late gene transcription and translation then take place. Capsid proteins polymerize around a lipoprotein vesicle translocated in the cytoplasm by virion assembly factors. Genomic DNA is packaged into new virions. Mature virions are released from the cell by lysis. Virion: Presumably icosahedral, approximately 80 nm in diameter. Enzymes: Exonuclease (Exo), DNA lyase, Holliday-junction resolvase (HJ resolvase), DNA helicase ATPase (Helicase). Etymology: Yaraviridae: From Yara, a mythological character of the Tupi indigenous people of Brazil. Virus Reference Strain: Yaravirus brasiliensis. Source: ViralZone Type: Family

name: Ungulaviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: dsDNA, linear genome of approximately 20 kbp. Encodes heterodimeric major capsid proteins. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation is based on viruses infecting hyperthermophilic archaea of the genus Acidianus. Classified within the realm Adnaviria, kingdom Zilligvirae, phylum Taleaviricota, class Tokiviricetes, and order Ligamenvirales. Contains one genus (Captovirus) and one species (Captovirus yellowstonense). HOST/ECOLOGY: Infects hyperthermophilic archaea of the genus Acidianus. Geographical distribution is not specified but inferred to be in environments where Acidianus species thrive. Transmission patterns are not established in the provided information. Additional Information: Virions are filamentous, flexible, enveloped particles. They consist of a nucleoprotein core and terminal claw-like structures. The family name, Ungulaviridae, is derived from the Latin word "ungula," meaning "claw."

name: Corticoviridae
info: Family: Corticoviridae Genome Characteristics: The Corticoviridae family comprises viruses with icosahedral virions containing an internal membrane and a circular, double-stranded DNA genome of approximately 10 kbp. The G+C content ranges from 42.2% to 48.2%. Genomes encode structural and nonstructural proteins, with lipids forming an internal membrane with virus-specific membrane-associated proteins. Replication occurs via a rolling circle mechanism initiated by a virus-encoded protein. Evolutionary Context: Corticoviruses belong to the realm Varidnaviria, kingdom Abadenavirae, phylum Produgelaviricota, class Belvinaviricetes, and order Vinavirales. The family includes one genus with two species. Corticoviruses share structural similarities with other tailless icosahedral viruses containing internal membranes, such as those in the families Tectiviridae, Turriviridae, Simuloviridae, Sphaerolipoviridae, Finnlakeviridae and Matsushitaviridae. Host/Ecology: Corticoviruses infect gram-negative bacteria of the genus Pseudoalteromonas. Pseudoalteromonas virus PM2 is virulent and replicates in marine strains. Pseudoalteromonas phage Cr39582 is a prophage. Viral lipids are acquired from the host cytoplasmic membrane during virion assembly. Virions adsorb to host receptors via spike proteins, and the internal membrane mediates genome translocation. Mature virions are released by cell lysis. Integrated corticoviral genetic elements are commonly found within aquatic bacterial chromosomes.

name: Matshushitaviridae
info: Family: Matshushitaviridae Genome Characteristics: dsDNA, circular, 17-19 kb, encoding 37 proteins. Contains single jelly roll-fold major capsid protein. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria not assessed in provided information. Host/Ecology: Host Range: Thermophilic bacteria. Geographical Distribution: Hot spring in Hukuchi, Japan (site of initial isolation). Transmission: Passive diffusion through water. Virion: Non-enveloped, icosahedral virion with pseudo T=28 dextro symmetry. Virion size 50-80nm. Contains inner membrane vesicle enclosing genomic DNA. Key Enzymes: Probable REP Endonuclease (VP1), Phosphoadenosine phosphosulfate reductase, Transglycosylase, Endolysin (C8CHK7, C8CHK8). Gene Expression: Undocumented. Replication: Undocumented. Etymology: Named after a hot spring in Hukuchi, Japan. Virus Reference Strain: Thermus phage P23-77. Taxid: 2842322. Note: The correct name is Matsushitaviridae, despite a typo in some databases.

name: Asfarviridae
info: Family: Asfarviridae Genome Characteristics: The Asfarviridae family contains viruses with linear, double-stranded DNA genomes ranging from 170 to 194 kbp. The genome has complementary terminal loops and identical arrays of directly repeated units. Virions possess an internal core, internal lipid layer, icosahedral capsid, and outer lipid envelope. The genome encodes 151-167 genes. Evolutionary Context: Asfarviridae is classified within the realm Varidnaviria, kingdom Bamfordvirae, phylum Nucleocytoviricota, class Pokkesviricetes, and order Asfuvirales. Phylogenetic analysis places it within the nucleo-cytoplasmic large DNA virus superfamily, related to Poxviridae, Iridoviridae, Phycodnaviridae, and Mimiviridae. Host/Ecology: The known host range includes domestic pigs, wild boar, warthogs, and bush pigs. Transmission occurs through contact, ingestion, or via Ornithodoros ticks. The virus is endemic in Africa, where warthogs and bush pigs serve as reservoirs. It has spread to Europe and causes outbreaks in the Russian Federation and neighboring countries. The virus replicates in cells of the mononuclear phagocytic system.

name: Cruliviridae
info: Family: Cruliviridae Genome Characteristics: Negative-sense, tri-segmented RNA genome, 10.8-11.5 kb in size. Segments encode nucleoproteins (NPs), glycoproteins (GPs), RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP), and sometimes zinc-finger (Z) proteins. Conserved sequences flank individual genomic segments. Evolutionary Context: Belongs to the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Negarnaviricota, class Bunyaviricetes, order Elliovirales. Closely related to bunyaviral fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids. Species demarcation is based on phylogenetic analysis of the L protein nucleotide sequence. Contains one genus, Lincruvirus. Host/Ecology: Infects crustaceans, specifically portunid crabs (Chinese mitten crabs, European shore crabs, swimming crab Callinectes danae), unspecified crustaceans, and European brown shrimp. Geographical distribution includes China, Faroe Islands (Denmark), Brazil, and Belgium. Transmission patterns are not fully established, but replication involves endocytosis, vesicle formation, and release of mature virions.

name: Thaspiviridae
info: Family: Thaspiviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, double-stranded DNA genomes of 27-29 kbp with 176 bp terminal inverted repeats. GC content is approximately 29.8%. Encodes a protein-primed family B DNA polymerase. Genomes contain 48-51 open reading frames. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation is based on sequence identity (>95% nucleotide sequence identity for isolates of Nitmarvirus NSV1). Shares virion organization, genome architecture and replication mechanisms with Halspiviridae, but lacks significant sequence similarity and infects different archaeal phyla. Host/Ecology: Infects ammonia-oxidizing archaea of the genus Nitrosopumilus (phylum Thaumarchaeota), which are widespread in marine environments. Viruses are mesophilic and neutrophilic. Causes chronic, non-lytic infection, inhibiting host growth and reducing ammonia oxidation rates without causing host cell lysis. Cosmopolitan distribution in marine ecosystems. Transmission occurs via rapid adsorption to host cells.

name: Crepuscuviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Crepuscuviridae viruses possess non-segmented, linear, negative-sense RNA genomes of approximately 12.0 kb. The genome contains three open reading frames (ORFs) encoding a glycoprotein (GP), a nucleoprotein (NP), and a large (L) protein with an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria are not applicable as the family contains only one genus and one species. Crepuscuviridae viruses are closely related to jingchuviral aliusvirids, chuvirids, myriavirids, and natarevirids. HOST/ECOLOGY: The known host range is megalopteran insects (Corydalidae). The only classified member, megalopteran chu-related virus 119 (MCrV119), was found in Carabobo State, Venezuela. Transmission patterns and replication cycle are currently unknown.

name: Simuloviridae
info: Family: Simuloviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome is a circular, double-stranded DNA molecule, 16-19 kbp in size. It contains approximately 30 open reading frames (ORFs). Key conserved domains include genes related to replication, regulation, and virion structure. The virion contains two major capsid proteins, both with a single jelly-roll fold, and an A32-like genome packaging ATPase. G+C content is 61-64%. Evolutionary Context: Species demarcation uses 95% global genome identity. Members share structural similarities with Sphaerolipoviridae and Matsushitaviridae, all having icosahedral capsids, two single-jelly-roll major capsid proteins, and an internal lipid membrane enclosing dsDNA. These families are assigned to the order Halopanivirales, class Laserviricetes, phylum Dividoviricota, kingdom Helvetiavirae, and realm Varidnaviria. Host/Ecology: Simuloviridae infect halophilic archaea of the genera Natrinema and Haloterrigena (order Natrialbales), found in hypersaline environments. They are temperate viruses, existing as extrachromosomal episomes (proviruses) in host cells. The lytic cycle can be triggered, leading to cell lysis and virion production. Transmission patterns involve a lysis-lysogeny switch regulated by a MazE superfamily protein. Geographical distribution includes China, South Korea, and Bolivia.

name: Autolykiviridae
info: Family: Autolykiviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, double-stranded DNA genome of approximately 10 kb with inverted terminal repeats and terminal proteins covalently linked. Encodes about 21 proteins. Contains a DNA-directed DNA polymerase B [POL]. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation criteria not specified. Host/Ecology: Natural hosts are bacteria. Geographical distribution not specified. Transmission occurs via passive diffusion through medium. Virion: Presumably icosahedral, containing a lipid membrane within the capsid. Replication: Cytoplasmic. Adsorption to target cell, followed by injection of viral DNA into the host cell cytoplasm. Transcription and translation of early genes. Replication of genomic DNA via a rolling-circle mechanism. Transcription and translation of late genes. Capsid proteins polymerize around a lipoprotein vesicle translocated in the cytoplasm by virion assembly factors. Genomic DNA is packaged in new virions. Mature virions are released from the cell by lysis. Etymology: Autolykiviridae: from Autolykos, a Greek mythological character, who was described as being difficult to catch. Reference Strain: Paulavirus viph1008o.

name: Myriaviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Myriaviridae viruses possess non-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes of approximately 13.5 kb. The genome contains four open reading frames (ORFs) encoding a glycoprotein (GP), two proteins of unknown function, and a large (L) protein with an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Myriaviridae is a family within the order Jingchuvirales. It is most closely related to aliusvirids, chuvirids, crepuscuvirids, and natarevirids. Genus and species demarcation criteria are not applicable as the family contains only one genus (Myriavirus) and one species (Myriavirus myriapedis). HOST/ECOLOGY: The known host range includes myriapod arthropods. Húběi myriapoda virus 8 (HbMV8) has been associated with myriapods sampled in China. Unclassified myriavirids have been associated with cephalopods. Transmission patterns and replication cycle are currently unknown.

name: Natareviridae
info: Family: Natareviridae Genome Characteristics:  Nucleic acid type: Negative-sense, single-stranded RNA  Genome size: Approximately 12.9 kb, non-segmented  Genome organization: Four open reading frames (ORFs) encoding two glycoproteins (GPs), a nucleoprotein (NP), and a large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Evolutionary Context:  Taxonomic demarcation: Family includes a single genus (Charybdivirus) and a single species (Charybdivirus charybdis); therefore, genus and species demarcation criteria are not applicable. Closely related to jingchuviral aliusvirids, chuvirids, crepuscuvirids, and myriavirids. Host/Ecology:  Host range: Portunid crustaceans (e.g., Charybdis japonica)  Geographical distribution: China (Wēnzhōu crab virus 3 (WzCVV3))  Transmission: Unknown. Endogenized natarevirid elements in arthropod genomes suggest ancient association. Additional Information:  The name Natareviridae is derived from the Latin word "nato," meaning "swim, float."  The type species is Wēnzhōu crab virus 3 (WzCVV3).  Replication and translation mechanisms are currently unknown.

name: Ampullaviridae
info: Family: Ampullaviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, double-stranded DNA genome ranging from 22 to 28 kbp with terminal inverted repeats. GC content around 35%. Encodes approximately 57 proteins, including a protein-primed family B DNA polymerase, glycosyltransferase, thymidylate kinase, Cas4-like endonuclease, and DNA-binding proteins. Some genes exhibit small overlaps. Conserved proteins are found across different ampullaviruses. Evolutionary Context: Ampullaviruses share homologous protein-primed DNA polymerases with other archaeal viruses (Gammapleolipovirus, Nitmarvirus, Alphaovalivirus, Salterprovirus) and bacterial/eukaryotic viruses (Tectiviridae, Podoviridae, Adenoviridae, Lavidaviridae). They may represent ancestral virus forms. Taxonomic demarcation is based on genome sequence identity and virion morphology. Host/Ecology: Infects hyperthermophilic archaea of the genus Acidianus. Geographical distribution includes hot springs in Italy, Iceland, and the USA. Transmission is non-lytic, with virions released without apparent host cell lysis, increasing host generation time. Virions are champagne bottle-shaped, approximately 230 nm long and 4-75 nm wide, with a ring of filaments at the base.

name: Tristromaviridae
info: Family: Tristromaviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, double-stranded DNA of 16-18 kbp. The genome of Pyrobaculum filamentous virus 1 (PFV1) is 17,714 bp with 60 bp terminal inverted repeats, encoding 39 predicted proteins. G+C content is 45.4%. PFV1 virions contain three major capsid proteins (VP1, VP2, VP3) and at least five minor proteins. VP1 and VP2 bind viral dsDNA. VP3 is glycosylated. Some proteins share similarity with Thermoproteus tenax virus 1 (TTV1). PFV1 genome encodes a Cas4-like nuclease. Evolutionary Context: Belongs to Realm Adnaviria, kingdom Zilligvirae, phylum Taleaviricota, class Tokiviricetes, order Primavirales. Contains two genera and three species. TTV1 was reclassified into Tristromaviridae due to comparative genomics analysis. Host/Ecology: Infects hyperthermophilic archaea of the order Thermoproteales, specifically the genera Pyrobaculum (e.g., PFV1) and Thermoproteus (e.g., TTV1). PFV1 was isolated from a hot spring in Pozzuoli, Italy. TTV1 was isolated from a mud hole in Krafla, Iceland. Transmission occurs via cell lysis. PFV1 binds to host pili-like appendages.

name: Globuloviridae
info: Family: Globuloviridae Genome Characteristics: The virion contains a single molecule of linear, double-stranded DNA (dsDNA). Genome size is approximately 28.3 kb. The genome has inverted repeat sequences at the ends, containing multiple short direct repeats. Predicted proteins (38-48) show no significant sequence similarity to known proteins in databases. Evolutionary Context: Species within the Globulovirus genus are differentiated by virion size, host range, and genome size and nucleotide sequence. Host/Ecology: Known hosts are hyperthermophilic archaea of the genera Pyrobaculum and Thermoproteus. These hosts are strict anaerobes found in extreme geothermal environments (around 85°C, pH 6). Infection is non-cytocidal and does not cause host cell lysis. The viral genome does not integrate into the host chromosome. Virions are highly heat-stable, and prolonged exposure to oxygen does not affect infectivity. Virion Properties: Virions are spherical, 70-100 nm in diameter, with spherical protrusions (approximately 15 nm). Virions possess a lipid-containing envelope that encases a superhelical core of dsDNA and nucleoproteins. Virion buoyant density in sucrose is approximately 1.3 g/cm3. Virions contain a major structural protein (approximately 33 kDa) and two minor proteins (approximately 16 and 20 kDa). The major structural protein is highly hydrophobic. Virions contain modified host lipids.

name: Metaxyviridae
info: Family: Metaxyviridae Genome Characteristics: ssDNA(+) circular, multipartite genome. Evolutionary Context: Realm Monodnaviria, kingdom Shotokuvirae, phylum Cressdnaviricota, class Arfiviricetes, order Mulpavirales. The name Metaxyviridae, derived from the Greek "metaxy" (in-between), reflects the phylogenetic relationship of coconut foliar decay virus to Geminiviridae and Nanoviridae. Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment is based on phylogenetic relationship. Host/Ecology: Infects plants. Example: coconut foliar decay virus. Transmitted persistently via the plant hopper Myndus taffini. Geographical distribution is associated with the host plants. Additional Information: Virions are 20 nm isometric. Replication and translation mechanisms are currently unknown. Contains 1 genus (Cofodevirus) and 1 species (Cofodevirus kokonas). Established in 2021.

name: Mypoviridae
info: Family: Mypoviridae Genome Characteristics:  Nucleic acid type: Negative-sense RNA, tri-segmented (S, M, L)  Genome size: Approximately 16.0 kb (S segment ~2.6 kb, M segment ~3.5 kb, L segment ~9.9 kb)  Genome organization: Three monocistronic RNA segments encoding a nucleoprotein (NP), a glycoprotein (GP), and a large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Evolutionary Context:  Taxonomic demarcation criteria: Not applicable (single genus, single species).  Realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Negarnaviricota, class Bunyaviricetes, order Hareavirales. Host/Ecology:  Host range: Myriapods (centipedes/millipedes). Unclassified mypovirids have been detected in dipteran insects and soil samples.  Geographical distribution: Húběi myriapoda virus 5 detected in China. Unclassified mypovirids detected in Australia and China.  Transmission patterns: Unknown. Taxonomy:  Genus: Hubavirus  Species: Hubavirus myriapedis  Example Virus: Húběi myriapoda virus 5 (HbMV5)

name: Leisingerviridae
info: Leisingerviridae is a family of lytic, double-stranded DNA viruses infecting methanogenic archaea of the order Methanobacteriales. These viruses possess icosahedral capsids (approximately 55 nm in diameter) and non-contractile helical tails (approximately 210 nm in length), exhibiting siphoviral morphology. GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: The genome is linear, double-stranded DNA, approximately 26 kbp in size, circularly permuted, and terminally redundant. Key conserved domains are not specified in the provided information. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: The family is classified within the realm Duplodnaviria, kingdom Heunggongvirae, phylum Uroviricota, class Caudoviricetes, and order Methanobavirales. Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment details are not provided. HOST/ECOLOGY: The known host range includes Methanothermobacter marburgensis. The geographical distribution and transmission patterns are not specified in the provided information. Taxonomy includes one genus (Psimunavirus) and one species (Psimunavirus limi), exemplified by Methanobacterium phage psiM2. The family is named after Thomas Leisinger, who isolated the virus. Source: ICTV.

name: Halspiviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: dsDNA, linear. Genome size and organization: 14.5 kbp. Key conserved domains identified: Virus-encoded family B DNA polymerase involved in protein-primed replication. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment: Family established in 2020, not assigned to a higher taxon. Contains one genus and one species. Name derived from halophilic and spindle-shaped. HOST/ECOLOGY: Known/predicted host range: Halophilic archaeon Haloarcula hispanica (phylum Euryarchaeota). Geographical distribution: Not specified. Transmission patterns if established: Not specified. VIRION CHARACTERISTICS: Spindle (lemon)-shaped virions, approximately 75 nm (long-axis) and 35 nm (short axis). TAXONOMY: Family: Halspiviridae Genus: Salterprovirus Species: Salterprovirus australiense Example: His1 (AF191796)

name: Ovaliviridae
info: Family: Ovaliviridae Genome Characteristics: Linear, double-stranded DNA of 23,219 bp with 172 bp inverted terminal repeats. GC content is 33%. The genome is predicted to encode 38 proteins, including structural proteins (VP1-VP4), a glycosyltransferase, a B-family DNA polymerase, and a SAM-dependent methyltransferase. Some ORFs show homology to sequences in lipothrixviruses, rudiviruses, and Sulfolobus monocaudavirus 1 (Bicaudaviridae), suggesting possible horizontal gene transfer. The B-family DNA polymerase is similar to those from other archaeal viruses and plasmids. Evolutionary Context: Based on phylogenetic analysis of protein-primed DNA polymerases, Ovaliviridae is not closely related to any other known archaeal or bacterial virus. Seven SEV1 ORFs show sequence matches to other archaeal viruses. Host/Ecology: Infects hyperthermophilic archaea of the genus Sulfolobus, specifically Sulfolobus sp. A20. Isolated from an acidic hot spring (86-106°C, pH 2.2-2.5) in Laguna Fumarolica, Costa Rica. Infection slightly retards host cell growth. Virions are released through hexagonal openings on the host cell surface. Lytic lifecycle. Virion: Ellipsoid shaped, approximately 115 nm long and 78 nm wide. Enveloped virion with a striated capsid. The viral DNA forms a multilayered disk-like structure within the capsid. Six-fold symmetrical virus-associated pyramids appear on the surface of infected cells. Virions contain four major proteins (12-170 kDa). The distribution pattern of isoprenoid glycerol dibiphytanyl glycerol tetraethers in the virion envelope is similar to that in the host cell membrane.

name: Portogloboviridae
info: Family: Portogloboviridae Genome Characteristics: Circular, double-stranded DNA genome, approximately 20 kbp in size. Genome contains 45-46 open reading frames. GC content is around 38%. Encodes proteins with DNA-binding domains (zinc finger, helix-turn-helix, ribbon-helix-helix). Major capsid protein VP4 and minor capsid protein VP10 have jelly-roll folds. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation is based on 91.7% pairwise genome sequence identity between the two classified species. Ten ORFs share homology with viruses infecting Sulfolobales, including Rudiviridae, Lipothrixviridae, Fuselloviridae, and Turriviridae members. Host/Ecology: Infects hyperthermophilic archaea of the genus Saccharolobus (order Sulfolobales). Isolated from hot springs in Beppu, Japan. Viral replication occurs via chronic infection, without observable cell lysis. Transmission patterns are not fully understood. Portogloboviruses carry mini-CRISPR arrays targeting other viruses, suggesting a role in inter-viral competition. Virion: Icosahedral virions, 87 nm in diameter. Consists of an outer protein shell, inner lipid layer, and a nucleoprotein core wound into a spherical coil. Virion contains four major proteins (VP1-VP4) and six minor proteins (VP5-VP10). Lipids are selectively acquired from the host.

name: Finnlakeviridae
info: Family: Finnlakeviridae Genome Characteristics: The Finnlakeviridae family consists of viruses with a circular, single-stranded DNA genome of approximately 9.2 kb. The genome of Flavobacterium phage FLiP, a typical member, is 9,174 nucleotides long with a GC content of 34%. It contains 16 predicted coding sequences (CDSs), five of which encode structural proteins. The major capsid protein (MCP P8) is the most abundant protein. CDS14 shares similarity with lytic transglycosylases. The genome does not encode identifiable DNA or RNA polymerase, but CDS15 shows resemblance to rolling circle replication initiator proteins. Evolutionary Context: Flavobacterium phage FLiP exhibits limited sequence identity to other known viruses but shares structural similarities with Pseudoalteromonas phage PM2 (Corticoviridae) and members of the kingdom Bamfordvirae, particularly in capsid organization and MCP fold. Phylogenetic analysis places it within tailless prokaryotic DNA viruses with double-ß-barrel MCPs. Host/Ecology: Finnlakeviridae members infect Gram-negative bacteria of the genus Flavobacterium. Flavobacterium phage FLiP was isolated from a boreal freshwater habitat in Central Finland. It is a virulent virus that induces host cell lysis. Lipids form an internal membrane that contains virus-encoded proteins. The major lipid class is ceramide, differing from the host cytoplasmic membrane composition.

name: Wupedeviridae
info: Family: Wupedeviridae Genome Characteristics: Negative-sense RNA virus with a tri-segmented genome of approximately 20.5 kb. The genome segments encode a nucleoprotein (NP), a glycoprotein (GP), and a large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Evolutionary Context: Closely related to bunyaviral arenavirids, discoviridae, leishbuvirids, mypovirids, nairovirids, and phenuivirids. The family includes one genus (Wumivirus) and one species (Wumivirus millepedae). Host/Ecology: Infects polydesmid myriapods (millipedes). Wǔhàn millipede virus 2 (WhMV2) was detected in millipedes in China. Transmission patterns are currently unknown.

name: Avsunviroidae
info: Family: Avsunviroidae Genome Characteristics: The genome consists of single-stranded, circular RNA, ranging from 246 to 434 nucleotides. It forms rod-like or branched conformations and contains hammerhead ribozymes in both (+) and (-) polarity strands, which are crucial for replication. These viroids lack the central conserved region found in Pospiviroidae. Evolutionary Context: Species are grouped into genera based on hammerhead structure, G+C content, solubility in 2 M LiCl, and phylogenetic analysis. Avsunviroidae shows phylogenetic relationships to Pospiviroidae and ribozyme-containing viroid-like satellite RNAs, suggesting a possible origin in the RNA world. Host/Ecology: Avsunviroids infect angiosperms, often with a narrow host range limited to a single or a few related plant species. Replication occurs in plastids. Cell-to-cell and systemic movement likely occurs via plasmodesmata and phloem, respectively. Transmission can occur through seeds (ASBVd, ELVd) or infected pollen (PLMVd). Horizontal transmission via grafting and contaminated tools is common. Mechanical transmission is also possible. Taxonomic Demarcation: The family includes three genera: Avsunviroid, Pelamoviroid, and Elaviroid, comprising a total of five species. Genus demarcation relies on hammerhead structure, G+C content, LiCl solubility, and phylogenetic clustering.

name: Alvernaviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Nucleic acid type: ssRNA(+) Genome size and organization: Monopartite, linear genome of 4.4 kb with a stem-loop structure at the 3'-end. Key conserved domains: Encodes for RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRp), VPG-type capping protein (VPg?), and a polyprotein major protease (Pro). EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment: Not specified. HOST/ECOLOGY: Known/predicted host range: Dinoflagellates (Heterocapsa circularisquama). Geographical distribution: Not specified. Transmission patterns: Virus penetrates host cell, uncoats, and releases RNA into cytoplasm. Viral RNA is translated. Replication occurs in cytoplasmic viral factories, producing dsRNA from genomic ssRNA(+). dsRNA is transcribed/replicated to provide viral mRNAs/new ssRNA(+) genomes. Virus assembly, virions accumulate in the host cytoplasm forming a crystalline array. Cell lysis and virus release. Virion: Non-enveloped, spherical virion about 34 nm in diameter with T=3 icosahedral symmetry composed of 180 CP proteins that make bumps at the surface of the virion. The virion RNA is infectious and serves as both the genome and viral messenger RNA. ORF1 encodes the replicase and ORF2 encodes the capsid protein. Controls the host population possibly through lysis of the host cell. Ecology and disease: Controls the host population possibly through lysis of the host cell. Etymology: Alverna: from Alveolates infecting RNA virus. Reference strains: Heterocapsa circularisquama RNA virus 01 (strain 34).

name: Sarthroviridae
info: Family: Sarthroviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome is a linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) molecule of 796 nucleotides with a 3' poly(A) tail of 15-20 nucleotides. It contains a single open reading frame (ORF) encoding two capsid proteins (CP17 and CP16) of approximately 17 kDa and 16 kDa, respectively. The capsid proteins lack significant sequence similarity to other known proteins. Evolutionary Context: Sarthroviridae is classified within the realm Riboviria, order Tombendovirales. The family currently contains one genus, Macronovirus, with a single species, Macronovirus macrobrachii. Taxonomic demarcation is based on genomic and biological characteristics. Host/Ecology: Sarthroviridae members infect giant freshwater prawns (Macrobrachium rosenbergii). Specifically, Macronovirus macrobrachii (extra small virus, XSV) is a satellite virus dependent on Macrobrachium rosenbergii nodavirus (MrNV) for replication. Co-infection with MrNV causes white tail disease, leading to mass mortalities in prawn hatcheries and farms. XSV and MrNV have been detected in aquatic insects, suggesting a potential vector role. The virus has been isolated from diverse geographical locations, including the French West Indies, Thailand, Taiwan, China, and India. Transmission patterns are linked to the presence and spread of its helper virus, MrNV.

name: Sunviridae
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Family Sunviridae viruses possess a nonsegmented, negative-sense RNA genome of approximately 17.2 kb. The genome contains six open reading frames (ORFs) encoding at least six proteins: nucleocapsid protein (N), phosphoprotein (P), matrix protein (M), fusion protein (F), glycoprotein (G), and a large (L) protein with an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. A small ORF ("X") exists between the N and P ORFs, but its expression is uncertain. The RNA likely has a 3′-terminal free hydroxyl group and a 5′-triphosphate and is likely not polyadenylated. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria are not applicable as the family contains only one genus (Sunshinevirus) and one species (Sunshinevirus reptilis). Sunvirids are closely related to filovirids, paramyxovirids, and pneumovirids within the order Mononegavirales. HOST/ECOLOGY: Sunvirids have been isolated from squamate reptiles (pythonid and boid snakes) in Australia. Specifically, Sunshine Coast virus (SunCV) has been found in black-headed pythons, jungle carpet pythons, spotted pythons, and woma pythons. SunCV is associated with neurorespiratory disease in snakes, causing white matter spongiosis of the hindbrain. The virus is detected in the mouths and cloacas of infected snakes, suggesting transmission via oral and/or cloacal secretions. Vertical transmission is inefficient. A SunCV-related virus was associated with respiratory disease in captive sidewinders in North America, but no sequence data is available.

name: Pseudoviridae
info: Family: Pseudoviridae Genome Characteristics: The Pseudoviridae family consists of reverse-transcribing viruses with long terminal repeats (LTRs). The genome comprises two identical copies of linear, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA, ranging from 4 to 10 kb. The proviral form is a DNA sequence of similar size integrated into the host genome. Key genes include gag and pol, encoding structural proteins and enzymes for replication (protease, integrase, reverse transcriptase, and ribonuclease H). Some members, particularly in the genus Sirevirus, possess an additional env gene. Evolutionary Context: Pseudoviridae belongs to the order Ortervirales, sharing evolutionary history with Metaviridae, Belpaoviridae, Retroviridae, and Caulimoviridae. Genera demarcation (Pseudovirus, Hemivirus, Sirevirus) was initially based on primer binding site and env gene presence, but is under revision using phylogenetic criteria. Species demarcation relies on sequence identity thresholds in major coding regions (e.g., capsid, reverse transcriptase). Host/Ecology: Pseudoviruses are found integrated within the genomes of a wide range of eukaryotes including fungi, plants, and animals. They form icosahedral virus particles intracellularly but lack an extracellular phase (except potentially Sireviruses). Transmission is primarily vertical through germline integration. Geographical distribution is widespread, reflecting the broad host range. Integration site preferences vary, with some members targeting non-coding regions or heterochromatin to minimize disruption of host gene function.

name: Turriviridae
info: Family: Turriviridae Genome Characteristics: The Turriviridae family comprises viruses with a circular, double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) genome ranging from 16 to 17 kbp. The genome encodes for 34-38 CDSs. Key structural proteins, including the major capsid protein (MCP), contain a double jelly roll fold, a feature shared with viruses infecting eukaryotes, bacteria, and archaea. Virions contain a host-derived internal lipid membrane. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation is based on virion organization, sequence similarity, and gene synteny. MCP structure reveals relationships with other families like Adenoviridae, Tectiviridae, Corticoviridae, Chaacviridae and Skuldviridae. Host/Ecology: Turriviruses infect hyperthermophilic and acidophilic archaea of the genera Sulfolobus and Saccharolobus. These viruses are found in extreme environments such as acidic hot springs and volcanic areas. Sulfolobus turreted icosahedral virus 1 (STIV1) exhibits a lytic life cycle, utilizing a unique pyramid-dependent cell lysis mechanism. STIV2 life cycle is poorly understood. Some unclassified members can integrate into the host genome, suggesting both lytic and temperate lifestyles.

name: Spiraviridae
info: Family: Spiraviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome is a circular, positive-sense single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) molecule of 24,893 nucleotides with a G+C content of 46.7%. The genome contains 57 predicted open reading frames (ORFs), occupying 93.5% of the genome. Encodes proteins including a trypsin-like serine protease, tyrosine recombinase, thioredoxin-like proteins, carbohydrate metabolism proteins, and DNA-binding proteins. Lacks identifiable Rep proteins, suggesting a novel replication mechanism dependent on host machinery. Evolutionary Context: The family Spiraviridae comprises a single genus, Alphaspiravirus, with one species. No relationships with other viruses have been revealed. May represent ancestral virus forms. Taxonomic demarcation criteria assessment not explicitly stated. Host/Ecology: Infects hyperthermophilic archaea from the genus Aeropyrum. Specifically isolated from Aeropyrum permix in a coastal hot spring in Yamagawa, Kyushu island, Japan. Virions are released without apparent host cell lysis, establishing a chronic, non-lytic infection. Transmission patterns not explicitly established, but occurs in high-temperature environments. Geographical distribution is currently limited to the hot spring location in Japan.

name: Guttaviridae
info: Family: Guttaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Guttaviridae family consists of enveloped viruses with ovoid or droplet-shaped virions, 55-80 nm in diameter and 75-130 nm in length. The genome is a circular, double-stranded DNA molecule of approximately 14 kbp. Key features include an integrase of the tyrosine recombinase superfamily, a DnaA-like ATPase, a glycosidase, and several DNA-binding proteins containing helix-turn-helix motifs. The genome does not encode a DNA polymerase, suggesting reliance on the host replisome for replication. Evolutionary Context: Guttaviridae currently contains one genus, Betaguttavirus. Genus demarcation criteria are not defined due to the single genus. Guttaviruses share evolutionary relationships with fuselloviruses, indicated by shared genes for integrase and DnaA-like ATPase. The genus Alphaguttavirus was abolished in 2022 due to the loss of its sole member, Sulfolobus newzealandicus droplet-shaped virus (SNDV), which was never sequenced. Host/Ecology: Guttaviridae infects hyperthermophilic archaea, specifically within the phylum Crenarchaeota. Aeropyrum pernix ovoid virus 1 (APOV1) was isolated from Aeropyrum pernix in a coastal solfataric vent in Japan. APOV1 is a temperate virus that lysogenizes its host by integrating into the chromosome. Proviral excision, genome replication, and virion production are induced under suboptimal growth conditions, such as reduced aeration.

name: Clavaviridae
info: Family: Clavaviridae Genome Characteristics: The Clavaviridae family contains viruses with circular, double-stranded DNA genomes of approximately 5,278 bp. The genome has a G+C content of 52.7%. The genome contains 14 open reading frames (ORFs). The virion contains a single major capsid protein (VP1) of about 10 kDa and three minor capsid proteins (VP2-4) ranging from 9.5-21.5 kDa. The major capsid protein is heavily glycosylated. The genome is packaged as a left-handed superhelix. Evolutionary Context: Currently, Clavaviridae comprises a single genus, Clavavirus, with one species, Clavavirus yamagawaense. No significant sequence or structural similarities have been found with other known viruses. Taxonomic demarcation relies on host range and virion morphology. Host/Ecology: Clavaviridae members infect hyperthermophilic archaea of the genus Aeropyrum. Specifically, Aeropyrum pernix is a known host. The virus was isolated from a coastal hot spring in Yamagawa, Kyushu, Japan. The virus exhibits a non-lytic replication cycle, releasing virions without causing apparent host cell lysis. No integration into the host chromosome has been detected. Transmission patterns are not explicitly established but occur within hyperthermophilic environments.

name: Plasmaviridae
info: Family: Plasmaviridae Genome Characteristics: The genome consists of circular, supercoiled, double-stranded DNA of approximately 12 kbp. The genome of Acholeplasma virus L2 (AVL2) is 11,965 bp with a G+C content of 32%. It contains 15 ORFs, all encoded on the same strand. Replication is bidirectional from two origins and depends on the host DNA replisome. Key proteins include a carbohydrate-binding protein, a DNA-binding protein, an AAA+ ATPase, an integrase, and a transcriptional regulator. Evolutionary Context: Plasmaviruses share limited homology with other viruses, primarily the integrase. Virion organization is superficially similar to archaeal viruses of the family Pleolipoviridae, but this is likely convergent evolution. Host/Ecology: Plasmaviruses infect Acholeplasma species (wall-less bacteria of the class Mollicutes). Acholeplasma virus L2 infects Acholeplasma laidlawii. Related prophages are found in the genomes of various Acholeplasma species, integrated into tRNA genes. Virions are released by budding through the cell membrane without causing host cell lysis. Transmission patterns involve a non-cytocidal productive infectious cycle followed by a lysogenic cycle. Lysogens are inducible by UV-irradiation and mitomycin C treatment.

name: Mononegavirales
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Order Mononegavirales viruses contain a single molecule of linear, non-infectious, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA genome, ranging from 8.9 to 19 kb. The viral RNA lacks a capped 5’ terminus or a covalently associated protein and a poly(A) tail at the 3’ terminus. The 5’ and 3’ terminal regions exhibit inverse complementarity with conserved motifs. The genome comprises a linear sequence of genes with limited overlaps and short non-coding regions. Genes are expressed as individual transcription units bounded by short transcription start and termination sequences. The genome encodes 5-7 structural proteins, including envelope glycoproteins, a matrix protein, an RNA-binding protein, nucleocapsid-associated proteins, and a large polymerase protein. Some viruses encode non-structural proteins. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation criteria are based on conserved motifs in the terminal regions of the genome and similarities in transcription start and termination sequences within families. HOST/ECOLOGY: Mononegavirales viruses infect a wide range of hosts, including vertebrates, invertebrates, and plants. Filoviruses have been isolated from primates and swine. Paramyxoviruses occur only in vertebrates. Rhabdoviruses infect invertebrates, vertebrates, and plants. Bornaviruses have been isolated from various mammals and birds. Transmission patterns vary depending on the virus family and host. The site of multiplication is typically the cytoplasm, except for Bornaviridae, which replicates in the nucleus.

name: Picornavirales
info: Order: Picornavirales Genome Characteristics: The Picornavirales order comprises viruses with monopartite or bipartite, positive-sense RNA genomes, typically ranging from 7,000 to 12,500 nucleotides. Bipartite genomes consist of RNA1 (5800-8400 nt) and RNA2 (3200-7300 nt). Genomes possess a 5' VPg protein (3-5 kDa) and a 3' poly(A) tail, with exceptions. A key feature is the Hel-Pro-Pol domain, including a superfamily III helicase, a chymotrypsin-like proteinase, and a superfamily I RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Capsids are non-enveloped, icosahedral, approximately 30 nm in diameter, with pseudo-T=3 symmetry, containing 60 units of jelly-roll domains. Evolutionary Context: Taxonomic demarcation is based on shared properties like the Hel-Pro-Pol domain and virion structure. Similar domains exist in Caliciviridae and Potyviridae, but these families differ in particle structure, helicase type, and VPg size. Host/Ecology: Picornavirales infect a wide range of hosts, including vertebrates (Picornaviridae), plants (Secoviridae), arthropods (Dicistroviridae, Iflaviridae), and algae (Marnaviridae). Transmission patterns and specific host ranges vary among genera. Environmental genomic studies suggest a large number of uncharacterized picorna-like viruses exist in the ocean.

name: Jingchuvirales
info: Order: Jingchuvirales Genome Characteristics: Negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes ranging from 9.1 to 15.3 kb. Genomes can be nonsegmented linear, nonsegmented circular, bisegmented linear, or bisegmented circular. Genomes contain two to four open reading frames (ORFs) encoding a glycoprotein (GP), a nucleoprotein (NP), a large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain, and/or proteins of unknown function. Evolutionary Context: The order includes 5 families, 21 genera, and 58 species for 59 viruses. Viruses in different families have L protein sequences with less than 21% amino-acid identity. Viruses in different genera have L protein sequences with less than 31% amino-acid identity. Closely related to the order Mononegavirales. Host/Ecology: Associated with arachnids, barnacles, crustaceans, insects, fish, and reptiles in Africa, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. Specifically, found in araneaen and ixodidan arachnids; decapod and portunid crustaceans; blattodean, coleopteran, dermapteran, dipteran, hemipteran, hymenopteran, and odonatan insects; atheriniform and syngnathiform fish; and squamate reptiles. Also associated with cephalopods, termites, and turtles. Possible human infections have been suggested.

name: Belpaoviridae
info: Belpaoviridae is a family of reverse-transcribing viruses with long terminal repeats (LTRs), belonging to the order Ortervirales. GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: The genome consists of positive-sense linear single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) ranging from 4 to 10 kb. Belpaoviridae genomes typically encode Gag and Pol polyproteins, and in some cases, an Env-like protein. The Gag polyprotein is processed into capsid protein (CP) and nucleocapsid (NC) protein. The Pol polyprotein is processed into protease (PR), reverse transcriptase-ribonuclease H (RT-RH), and integrase (INT). Key conserved domains include CCHC zinc knuckle motifs in NC, DTG/ILG in PR, conserved regions in RT-RH, and a DD35E-like core in INT. The genome is flanked by LTRs, with a primer-binding site (PBS) and polypurine tract (PPT) present. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Belpaoviridae is closely related to Metaviridae, Pseudoviridae, Retroviridae, and Caulimoviridae within the Ortervirales order. Phylogenetic analysis reveals five clades: Tas, Bel, Pao, Sinbad, and Suzu, correlating with host origin. Species demarcation is based on less than 50% Gag protein sequence identity. HOST/ECOLOGY: Belpaoviridae members are found in metazoans, including vertebrates, insects, and nematodes. They are widely distributed within host genomes, often in intergenic regions and introns. Transmission patterns are not fully established, but some members may form infectious extracellular virions.

name: Nidovirales
info: Order: Nidovirales Genome Characteristics: Positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome. Genome size varies: large nidoviruses (26.4-31.7 kb) and small nidoviruses (12.7-15.7 kb). Genomes are capped and polyadenylated. Key conserved domains include a chymotrypsin-like protease (Mpro), an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), and a Zn-finger-like helicase (Zn-HEL). The replicase gene constellation tm-Mpro-tm_fs_RdRp_Zn-HEL is a diagnostic molecular marker. Evolutionary Context: Families Corona-, Arteri-, and Roniviridae form distinct phylogenetic clusters. Torovirinae (Bafini- and Torovirus) are closely related. Nidoviruses are distinguished from other RNA viruses by their replicase polyproteins. Homologs of nidovirus enzymes are found in viruses of the "Picornavirus-like" and "Alphavirus-like" supergroups. Host/Ecology: Diverse host range: birds, mammals (including humans), fish, and crustaceans. Geographical distribution varies depending on the virus. Transmission patterns include aerosols, fomites, fecal-oral route, and venereal transmission. Coronaviruses primarily target epithelia, causing respiratory and gastrointestinal diseases. Arteriviruses infect macrophages, causing arteritis. Roniviruses infect crustaceans, causing high mortality in acute infections. Bats are believed to play a pivotal role in CoV ecology and evolution. Nomenclature: Nido: from Latin nidus, "nest," referring to the nested set of mRNAs. Arteri: from equine arteritis. Corona: from Latin corona, "halo," referring to the virion appearance. Toro: from Latin torus, referring to the nucleocapsid morphology. Bafini: from bacilliform fish nidoviruses. Roni: from rod-shaped nidoviruses. Source: ICTV

name: Reovirales
info: Reovirales Order Summary GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: The order Reovirales comprises viruses with segmented, linear, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genomes. Genome size ranges from approximately 18 to 29 kbp, with 9 to 12 segments. Each segment typically encodes one protein, although some segments have multiple open reading frames. The positive-sense strand of each RNA duplex has a 5'-terminal cap, but lacks a 3'-poly(A) tail. Key conserved domains include an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) with transcriptase and replicase activity. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxonomic demarcation is based on RdRP sequence comparisons, host range, capsid structure, and genome segment number. Genera within the order share less than 30% RdRP amino acid sequence identity, with some exceptions. Phylogenetic analyses support co-evolution with hosts and vectors. The order is divided into two families: Spinareoviridae (turreted) and Sedoreoviridae (smooth). HOST/ECOLOGY: Reovirales viruses infect a broad range of hosts, including mammals, fish, birds, reptiles, arthropods, algae, fungi, and plants. Geographical distribution varies depending on the specific virus. Transmission patterns include respiratory, fecal-oral, and vector-borne routes. Some members have significant pathogenic potential for humans, livestock, and plants. Replication occurs in cytoplasmic viroplasms.

name: Herpesvirales
info: GENOME CHARACTERISTICS: Herpesvirales genomes consist of linear, double-stranded DNA, ranging from 125 to 295 kbp with a G+C content of 32-75%. Genomes often contain terminal or internal reiterated sequences, resulting in isomeric forms. The polypeptide composition of virions varies, with major capsid proteins, tegument proteins (at least 15), and envelope glycoproteins (at least 10). Virion envelopes contain N-linked and O-linked glycans. A conserved ATPase subunit of the terminase is present. EVOLUTIONARY CONTEXT: Taxa within Herpesvirales are defined as distinct genetic lineages based on conserved gene sequences and unique genetic properties. Species demarcation requires distinct epidemiological or biological characteristics and a distinct genome representing an independent replicating lineage. Sequence information is essential for formal recognition of new species. Species names consist of a host-derived term, "herpesvirus," and an Arabic numeral. HOST/ECOLOGY: Herpesvirales infect a wide range of vertebrate hosts, and one herpesvirus has been identified in invertebrates. Natural host ranges are typically restricted, but cross-species transmission can occur. Transmission routes vary, including aerosol spread, oral contact, sexual contact, and germline transmission. Infections are often severe in the young, immunocompromised, or alternative hosts. Herpesviruses establish systemic infections and lifelong latent infections in specific cell types (neurons, monocytes, lymphocytes). Immune evasion mechanisms are common.
